# dAI Radar: full dataset

> dAI Radar tracks shipping decentralized-AI / crypto-ML systems and traces each one back to the academic paper it is actually built on. Every claim is tagged "grounded" (directly sourced) or "inferred" (reasoned, not quoted); keep that distinction when answering from this data. A lineage is only asserted when a real citation chain exists.

Generated 2026-10-30T14:13:03+00:00 from https://dai.misbar.tech. Below are the verbatim markdown source files: systems/ (one per tracked system; its `foundation:` key names the foundations/ file it builds on), foundations/ (one per seed paper), and watch/log/ (daily watch runs, newest first). Each file starts with a FILE: line.

FILE: systems/akash-network.md
========================================================================

---
name: Akash Network
field: Decentralized GPU / compute marketplace
category: compute-markets
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (consensus citation); inferred (AI-specific framing); unverified (2026 migration endpoint)
website: "https://akash.network"
---

# Akash Network

## What it does

Akash is a decentralized marketplace for compute capacity: tenants publish a
deployment manifest describing what they need (CPU, GPU, storage), independent
providers bid competitively to host it, and the lowest qualifying bid wins. It
started as general-purpose cloud compute and has since leaned heavily into
GPU/AI workloads as that demand grew.

## Architecture summary

- Historically an application-specific **Cosmos SDK** chain using **Tendermint**
  Byzantine-fault-tolerant consensus (Proof-of-Stake) to handle escrow, leases,
  and provider payouts on-chain, while the actual compute runs off-chain on
  provider hardware (Docker/Kubernetes-based).
- **Reverse auction** is the core marketplace mechanism: tenants set terms,
  providers compete on price, settlement is in AKT.
- **GPU marketplace** ("Supercloud") shipped via Mainnet 6, August 2023;
  supports H100/A100/A6000/RTX4090/L40S across 150+ providers as of 2026.
  ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-gpu-marketplace-ai-compute/))
- **AkashML**, launched Nov 22 2025, adds a managed AI-inference layer with an
  OpenAI-compatible API that routes inference requests across available GPU
  providers on the network. ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-network-2026-gpu-market-leaves-cosmos/))
- **2026 base-chain migration (unverified endpoint, in progress):** per AEP-79,
  Akash is deprecating its sovereign Cosmos-SDK chain in favor of a
  "shared-security" model — buying BFT security from an established L1 rather
  than running its own validator set — driven by (a) capital inefficiency of
  self-staking and (b) a 2025 Cosmos SDK licensing change (Apache 2.0 →
  Source Available Evaluation License for the Enterprise module) that forced
  the issue. ~15 L1 candidates were evaluated; Solana was reported as the
  leading contender as of this research pass; migration targeted for Q4 2026.
  Not independently confirmed against Akash's own roadmap page beyond the
  secondary source below — reverify before treating "Solana" as settled.
  ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/akash-network-2026-gpu-market-leaves-cosmos/),
  [akash.network/roadmap/aep-79](https://akash.network/roadmap/aep-79/))

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Grounded, but not AI-specific:** Akash's whitepaper cites the Tendermint BFT
consensus algorithm directly (citation [9] in the original whitepaper) — "The
latest gossip on BFT consensus," Buchman, Kwon, Milosevic (2018) is the primary
academic specification underlying Tendermint. This is the one explicit
citation grounding found in Akash's own materials.

This is generic blockchain-consensus grounding, not anything specific to AI/ML
workloads — Akash's GPU marketplace and AkashML layer are a product build on
top of a general-purpose compute marketplace, not something with their own
distinct academic lineage. No foundations/ file created for this entry: per
this repo's rule, a foundations file is for AI/ML-relevant lineage, and
Tendermint's consensus grounding doesn't meet that bar even though it's a real
citation. (If a future watch-run finds Akash publishing something AI-specific
with its own citations — e.g. around AkashML's routing/verification approach —
that would be the point to reconsider.)

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base chain / consensus (as of 2026, pre-migration) | Cosmos SDK + Tendermint PoS | Akash whitepaper citation [9]; grounded |
| Marketplace mechanism | Reverse auction (price-competitive provider bidding) | Akash docs, grounded |
| GPU support | H100, A100, A6000, RTX 4090, L40S; 150+ providers, 30+ countries | hoge.gg, cross-referenced |
| AI-specific layer | AkashML (OpenAI-compatible inference API, routes across providers), launched 2025-11-22 | hoge.gg, single-source |
| Compute verification | **None found** — no cryptographic or other verification that a provider ran the workload as specified | hoge.gg analysis, single-source — flagged as a known limitation, not cross-confirmed elsewhere in this pass |
| Base-chain migration | In progress per AEP-79: Cosmos SDK → shared-security L1 (Solana reported as leading candidate), targeted Q4 2026 | akash.network/roadmap/aep-79, hoge.gg — endpoint unverified |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NONE FOUND | "Akash rents you a GPU; it does not prove what that GPU did." | hoge.gg analysis, single-source |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | Whichever provider wins the lease; a substituted or quantized model would go undetected | hoge.gg analysis, single-source |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | GENERIC ONLY | Whitepaper cites Tendermint BFT consensus: a real citation, but not AI-specific | Akash whitepaper citation [9], grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | GPU marketplace since Aug 2023, AkashML since Nov 2025; base-chain migration in progress | Akash docs + hoge.gg, cross-referenced |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Cosmos SDK + Tendermint chain, migrating to a shared-security L1 (Solana reported, unconfirmed) | Akash whitepaper; AEP-79 endpoint unverified |

## Known limitations

- **No compute verification.** Per the source above: "Akash rents you a GPU;
  it does not prove what that GPU did." A provider could in principle
  substitute a cheaper/quantized model for what was requested without
  detection — there is no proof-of-execution or attestation layer analogous to
  Gensyn's RepOps/bisection game or a TEE-attestation approach. This is a
  structural gap, not a bug, and the most important thing for a future
  watch-run to monitor if Akash ever adds a verification layer.
- **Mid-migration as of this writing.** The Cosmos-SDK → shared-security-L1
  transition (AEP-79) is a live, disruptive architecture change with an
  unconfirmed landing spot. Treat any consensus-layer claim in this file as
  provisional until the migration completes and is reverified.
- Economic/tokenomics grounding (AKT emission, staking requirements) comes
  from a 2019 economics whitepaper that predates the GPU marketplace and
  AkashML entirely — not re-verified against current parameters in this pass.

FILE: systems/allora.md
========================================================================

---
name: Allora Network
field: Decentralized ML forecasting / inference incentive networks
category: incentive-networks
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (architecture/status facts); no external academic lineage found
website: "https://www.allora.network"
---

## What it does

Allora is a decentralized network (a "Model Coordination Network") where
many independent ML models submit predictions/inferences on a given
topic; the network combines them into a single synthesized inference
that is intended to outperform any single contributing model, and pays
contributors based on the measured quality of their individual
contribution to that combined result.

## Architecture summary

- Built on the **Cosmos SDK**, using **CometBFT** as the underlying BFT
  consensus engine, with a **Delegated Proof-of-Stake (DPoS)** validator
  set securing the chain itself (this part is standard Cosmos-chain
  infrastructure, not Allora-specific).
- Allora-specific layer on top: **Workers** submit inferences/forecasts
  on a "topic"; **Reputers** stake-weight and score those submissions
  for accuracy; the network combines scored submissions into a single
  output via Allora's own **"Inference Synthesis"** mechanism.
- Rewards are distributed based on each participant's measured marginal
  contribution to the synthesized result, not raw output volume — intended
  to reward genuinely useful predictions over ones that just add noise.
- Mainnet (with the ALLO token) launched 2025-11-11, per Allora
  Foundation's own announcement
  ([allora.network/blog/allora-foundation-announces-launch-of-allora-mainnet-and-allo-token](https://www.allora.network/blog/allora-foundation-announces-launch-of-allora-mainnet-and-allo-token)).
  ALLO launched across multiple chains (Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain) in
  addition to Allora's own L1.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No external academic lineage was found, despite checking.** This is
worth stating plainly rather than forcing a fit:

- Allora's technical design is documented in its own self-published
  paper, *"Allora: a Self-Improving, Decentralized Machine Intelligence
  Network"* (Kruijssen, Emmons, Peluso, Ghaffar, Huang, Longmore, Kell —
  2024), published in "Allora Decentralized Intelligence," which is
  Allora's own research venue, not a third-party peer-reviewed journal.
  PDF: [research.assets.allora.network/allora.0x10001.pdf](https://research.assets.allora.network/allora.0x10001.pdf).
- Direct inspection of that PDF found **no citations to prior external
  academic work** grounding the "Inference Synthesis" mechanism, the
  Reputer scoring/reward design, or the stake-weighted consensus layer
  (the base-chain BFT/DPoS machinery is standard Cosmos tooling, not
  something Allora invented or needs to cite).
- A 2025 follow-on preprint by overlapping authors, *"Context-Aware
  Inference via Performance Forecasting in Decentralized Learning
  Networks"* (Pfeffer, Kruijssen, et al., [arxiv.org/pdf/2510.06444](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.06444)),
  extends the same in-house framework rather than introducing external
  grounding.
- Checked `docs.allora.network/learn/what-is-allora` as well — it
  points back to the same self-published whitepaper, no external
  citation trail there either.

Net: unlike EZKL (PLONK via Halo2) or Gensyn (explicit citations to
Proof-of-Learning, Agatha, etc.), Allora's core mechanism reads as an
original in-house construction, not an implementation of prior academic
work. **No `foundations/` file was created for this entry** — creating
one would misrepresent a self-published whitepaper as an external
foundational seed paper in the same sense as the other tracked systems'
entries. This should be revisited if Allora's team publishes something
that does engage with prior ensemble-learning/mechanism-design
literature (e.g. classic stacked-generalization or prediction-market
scoring-rule work), which "Inference Synthesis" and the Reputer reward
design resemble in spirit but do not cite directly.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base chain | Cosmos SDK + CometBFT, DPoS validator set | Allora whitepaper/docs, grounded |
| Core mechanism | Inference Synthesis — combines Worker submissions into one output, scored/weighted by Reputers | Allora whitepaper, grounded |
| Incentive design | Rewards based on measured marginal contribution to the synthesized result | Allora whitepaper, grounded |
| Token / cross-chain | ALLO token; mainnet + multichain (Ethereum, Base, BNB Chain) launch 2025-11-11 | Allora Foundation announcement, grounded |
| Academic grounding | None found externally; architecture is self-published, not derived from cited prior work | Direct PDF inspection + docs site check, grounded (as a negative finding) |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PEER SCORING | Reputers stake-weight and score Workers' inferences for accuracy; Inference Synthesis combines them | Allora whitepaper, grounded |
| Trust rests on | STAKE MAJORITY | Stake-weighted Reputers on a DPoS chain; collusion resistance not independently analyzed | Allora whitepaper; classification inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Self-published whitepaper with no external citations for the core mechanism | Direct PDF inspection, grounded (as a negative finding) |
| Maturity | LIVE | Mainnet and ALLO token launched 2025-11-11 | Allora Foundation announcement, grounded |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Cosmos SDK + CometBFT L1; ALLO also on Ethereum, Base and BNB Chain | Allora whitepaper/docs, grounded |

## Known limitations

- No independent third-party audit of the Inference Synthesis or Reputer
  scoring mechanism was located in this pass.
- Because the core mechanism isn't grounded in external literature, there's
  no independent theoretical analysis to cross-check its claimed properties
  (e.g. collusion-resistance of the Reputer scoring) against — it has to be
  evaluated on the Allora team's own self-published analysis alone.
- Current economic/staking parameters (minimum stakes, slashing conditions)
  were not verified in this pass and should be checked against current
  docs.allora.network before citing specifics.

# alpha-beta-CROWN

## What it does

A GPU neural-network verifier combining linear bound propagation with
branch and bound. Certifies robustness to adversarial perturbations and
other properties (e.g. Lyapunov stability in control); handles large
convolutional networks, ResNets and Transformers.

## Architecture summary

- Components: CROWN, auto_LiRPA, α-CROWN (incomplete), β-CROWN
  (complete for ReLU), GenBaB (general nonlinearities), GCP-CROWN and
  BICCOS (cutting planes), BaB-Attack (falsifier), INVPROP.
- Led by Prof. Huan Zhang (UIUC) under Verified-Intelligence; BSD
  3-Clause.
- Reports winning VNN-COMP every year 2021-2026 (self-reported).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Grounded: the README asks users to cite CROWN (2018), auto_LiRPA,
α-CROWN, β-CROWN, then later extensions. See
`foundations/neural-network-verification.md`.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Soundness | Sound bounds; complete for ReLU via β-CROWN | README |
| Hardware | GPU | README |
| Competition | VNN-COMP wins 2021-2026 (self-reported) | README |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | FORMAL PROOF | Sound bounds certify robustness and other properties on specified input regions; complete for ReLU via beta-CROWN | README, grounded |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Soundness of the bound computations and of the verifier's implementation; SoundnessBench exists to test it | Known limitations; classification inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | CROWN (2018) and its successors, by the group that leads the project (Huan Zhang) | README citation list, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Maintained open-source verifier; VNN-COMP wins 2021-2026 (self-reported) | README, self-reported |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | — | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- Verifies properties of a model on specified input regions, not general
  "safety"; scales to large networks but not to frontier LLMs (not claimed
  by the README).
- Verifier bugs are a real risk: a benchmark (SoundnessBench,
  arXiv 2412.03154) exists to test whether verifiers, including this one,
  return sound answers.

FILE: systems/apple-private-cloud-compute.md
========================================================================

---
name: Apple Private Cloud Compute (PCC)
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
category: private-compute
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (architecture); no academic paper lineage — see Known limitations
website: "https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/"
---

## What it does

Private Cloud Compute (PCC) lets Apple Intelligence offload AI requests that
need more capability than an on-device model can provide, to Apple's own
servers, while keeping the same privacy guarantee as on-device processing.
Per Apple's own description: "Personal user data sent to PCC isn't accessible
to anyone other than the user — not even to Apple."
([security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/))

## Architecture summary

- **Hardware root of trust**: custom-built Apple silicon server hardware
  carrying the same Secure Enclave and Secure Boot technology used in
  iPhone/iPad. Certificates are rooted in each node's Secure Enclave UID.
- **Attestation**: before a device sends encrypted request data, it
  cryptographically verifies the target PCC node's attestation. Requests
  bypass load balancers and encrypt directly to the validated node.
- **Physical/manufacturing verification**: high-resolution imaging and
  tamper switches activated before sealing; data-center validation involves
  multiple independent Apple teams plus third-party observation.
- **Multi-vendor attestation**: for components whose compromise could
  exfiltrate data, attestation is rooted in at least two independent
  hardware vendors (Apple's own hardware plus, for some components, Google
  Cloud) rather than a single vendor's root of trust.
- **Stateless / no-retention design**: the Secure Enclave randomizes the
  data-volume encryption key on every reboot without persisting it;
  request-associated data is deleted on completion; address space is
  periodically recycled; there is no remote shell or interactive debugging
  interface into production nodes.
- **Public verifiability**: every production PCC software build's
  measurement is written to an append-only, cryptographically tamper-proof
  transparency log; binary images are published for independent inspection
  within 90 days; a Virtual Research Environment and source releases
  (the CloudAttestation and Thimble projects) let outside researchers
  verify the published software matches what's actually running.
- **Request anonymization (separate from the confidentiality claim above)**:
  RSA Blind Signatures (IETF RFC 9474) and an Oblivious HTTP relay (RFC 9458)
  are used so that request routing can't be linked back to a specific
  device/identity — this is about non-targetability, not about protecting
  the content of the request itself.

Source for all of the above:
[security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute](https://security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute/)
and [security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research](https://security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research/).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No academic paper is cited for the core confidentiality/attestation
design.** Checked Apple's own PCC security blog posts directly — the only
explicit external references are two IETF RFCs used for a narrower piece
of the system (request anonymization, not confidentiality of compute):

- **RSA Blind Signatures** — [RFC 9474](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9474)
- **Oblivious HTTP** — [RFC 9458](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9458)

The actual confidentiality/attestation mechanism (Secure Enclave, Secure
Boot, hardware-rooted certificates) is grounded entirely in Apple's own
prior engineering, documented in the **Apple Platform Security Guide**
([help.apple.com/pdf/security](https://help.apple.com/pdf/security/en_US/apple-platform-security-guide.pdf)),
not in an externally authored, independently reviewed paper. This is the
same kind of grounding gap flagged in this repo's Bittensor entry — stated
plainly rather than forced into a citation that isn't actually there.
No new `foundations/` file was created for this reason; there's no distinct
academic lineage to seed one with.

Independent *analysis* of PCC exists in the academic literature — e.g.
"Unlocking Apple's Private Cloud Compute: An Analysis of Privacy-Preserving
Artificial Intelligence" ([arXiv:2605.24239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.24239)) —
but that's third-party research examining PCC from the outside, not
something PCC's own design cites as foundational.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Attestation mechanism | Hardware-rooted attestation via Secure Enclave + Secure Boot; client verifies node attestation before sending data | security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute, grounded |
| Trust model | Hardware root of trust (custom Apple silicon); certs rooted in per-node Secure Enclave UID; physical manufacturing/data-center verification | Same source, grounded |
| Multi-vendor attestation | ≥2 independent hardware roots of trust for certain components (Apple + Google Cloud) | security.apple.com/blog/pcc-security-research, grounded |
| Public verifiability | Append-only transparency log of all production software measurements; binaries published within 90 days; source code (CloudAttestation, Thimble) released | security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute, grounded |
| Request anonymization | RSA Blind Signatures (RFC 9474) + Oblivious HTTP relay (RFC 9458) — prevents request-to-identity linkage | Same source, grounded |
| Maturity | Production; live since 2024 launch with Apple Intelligence; actively expanding per "Expanding Private Cloud Compute" post | security.apple.com/blog/expanding-pcc, grounded |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Device verifies the node's hardware attestation before sending; every production build is logged to an append-only transparency log | security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Apple silicon root of trust and Apple's manufacturing/data-center process; two vendors for some components | security.apple.com PCC posts, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Personal data "isn't accessible to anyone other than the user, not even to Apple"; stateless, no retention | security.apple.com/blog/private-cloud-compute, grounded |
| Lineage | STANDARDS | Apple's own engineering (Platform Security Guide) plus two IETF RFCs for request anonymization; no paper | Apple PCC security blog posts, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Production since the 2024 Apple Intelligence launch | security.apple.com/blog/expanding-pcc, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | No blockchain component appears in Apple's materials | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- **Fundamentally different trust model from the other tracked systems in
  this repo.** ZKML/FHE/MPC systems here derive their guarantees from
  cryptographic hardness assumptions, independent of any single hardware
  vendor. PCC's guarantee ultimately rests on hardware correctness and
  Apple's own manufacturing/physical-security process — a trust model that
  shouldn't be read as equivalent in kind just because it's also labeled
  "confidential computing." Worth keeping distinct in any cross-system
  comparison.
- No external academic paper grounds the core attestation design (see
  above) — this entry's grounding is strong on primary-source documentation
  but weak on independent academic lineage, by the nature of what PCC
  actually is.
- Independent security critiques of PCC beyond the one analysis paper
  found above were not surveyed in this pass — a candidate for a future
  watch-run if third-party security research on PCC accumulates.

# Atoma Network

## What it does

A decentralized, privacy-preserving inference layer on Sui. Announced May
2024 as a verifiable inference network serving Sui; reported live on Sui
mainnet in December 2024 (alpha, with a demo chat app "Utopia").

## Architecture summary

- AI processing runs in TEEs so inputs and outputs are isolated from the
  operators (press release).
- OpenAI-compatible API endpoints.
- Atoma's team paper, "Privacy-Preserving Decentralized AI with
  Confidential Computing" (Lee, Antonio, Khan; arXiv 2410.13752, Oct 2024),
  argues TEEs protect model parameters and user data on untrusted
  machines at lower cost than zkML ("prohibitive computational
  overhead"), says TEEs "face a few limitations", and outlines how they
  fit Atoma's framework. Only the abstract was read.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

The arXiv paper is Atoma's own framing, not a cited foundation of the
mechanism. Link to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md` is **inferred**.
It also positions itself against `/foundations/zkml.md`.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Chain | Sui | Decrypt / Chainwire |
| Verification | TEE-based (vs zkML) | arXiv 2410.13752 abstract |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | TEE-based verification, positioned as a practical alternative to zkML | arXiv 2410.13752 abstract |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | TEE hardware isolates inputs and outputs from operators | Decrypt / Chainwire press release |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Inputs and outputs isolated from node operators inside TEEs | Decrypt / Chainwire press release |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | Team paper (arXiv 2410.13752) is framing, not a cited foundation; TEE link inferred | File's lineage note, inferred |
| Maturity | OPEN QUESTION | Reported alpha on Sui mainnet in Dec 2024; nothing newer found | 2024 sources only, inferred |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Sui | Decrypt / Chainwire |

## Known limitations

- All sources are 2024; the current state of the network was not found.
  Treat as stale until checked against the project's repo and docs
  (docs.atoma.network was unreachable this pass).

FILE: systems/azure-confidential-ai.md

---
name: Azure Confidential AI
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
category: private-compute
foundation: foundations/ccf-confidential-computing.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (ledger lineage); inferred/vendor-spec (TEE hardware lineage)
website: "https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/confidential-computing/confidential-ai"
---

# Azure Confidential AI

## What it does

Microsoft's umbrella term for running AI training/inference inside
hardware-isolated Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) on Azure, so
that neither Microsoft (the cloud operator) nor other tenants can see
model weights or input data while the workload runs — and, in the
newer "Confidential Inferencing" variant, producing an auditable record
of exactly what code ran.

**Caution:** Microsoft has published more than one architecture under
this umbrella, and they are not identical (see below) — this entry
documents what was actually found for each, rather than collapsing them
into one story.

## Architecture summary

**1. Azure confidential VMs (the base layer)** — grounded directly from
Microsoft Learn (learn.microsoft.com/azure/confidential-computing/confidential-vm-overview):
- CPU TEE via AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX, hardware-enforced isolation from
  the hypervisor/host.
- A dedicated virtual TPM (vTPM, TPM 2.0 spec) per VM for attestation
  and key/secret storage.
- Boot-time attestation via Azure Attestation; the VM won't start if
  required isolation settings (e.g. SEV-SNP) aren't enabled.
- GPU confidential computing extension: the `NCCadsH100v5` VM series
  pairs SEV-SNP with NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core GPU confidential-computing
  mode, forming one TEE spanning CPU and GPU, with encrypted PCIe
  traffic between them.
- Secure key release: Azure Key Vault Managed HSM can be configured to
  release decryption keys only after Azure Attestation confirms the VM
  state.

**2. Azure AI Confidential Inferencing (preview, newer)** — grounded
from Microsoft's own techcommunity blog and learn.microsoft.com/azure/confidential-computing/confidential-ai:
- Inference runs inside the confidential GPU VM described above, with
  an integrity-protected disk image.
- A client obtains an HPKE public key from a KMS plus hardware
  attestation evidence and transparency evidence binding that key to
  the service's current secure-key-release policy, before sending an
  encrypted (OHTTP) request.
- An append-only **transparency ledger** records container hashes and
  deployment policies for the inference service, so what code ran is
  independently auditable. Microsoft's own docs state directly:
  **"Azure confidential ledger is built on the Confidential Consortium
  Framework (CCF)."**

**3. A third, simpler documented variant exists** —
`github.com/microsoft/confidential-ai` (inference/docs/arch.md)
describes a reference architecture using AMD SEV-SNP plus a custom
"attested TLS" extension and model-file encryption, with **no mention
of CCF, OHTTP, or a transparency ledger**. This looks like an earlier
or alternative reference design, not the same system as (2) — flagged
explicitly rather than merged into one narrative, since the two
documents describe materially different mechanisms.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Two separate lineages, with different grounding strength:

- **Transparency ledger → CCF (grounded):** Azure's own docs state the
  confidential ledger used in AI Confidential Inferencing is built on
  CCF. CCF itself is a Microsoft Research system with a direct academic
  paper — see `/foundations/ccf-confidential-computing.md`.
- **TEE hardware (vendor-spec, not an academic-paper lineage):** AMD
  SEV-SNP, Intel TDX, and NVIDIA H100 confidential computing are vendor
  hardware technologies with their own technical specifications, not
  Microsoft Research's own academic contribution. Microsoft's docs cite
  them by name (grounded: this is what Azure uses) but there is no
  single foundational *paper* here the way there is for CCF — treat any
  claim of a specific academic seed paper for the hardware TEE layer as
  unsupported unless found otherwise.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| CPU TEE | AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX | learn.microsoft.com/azure/confidential-computing/confidential-vm-overview, grounded |
| GPU TEE | NVIDIA H100 Tensor Core, confidential-computing mode (`NCCadsH100v5` series) | same source, grounded |
| Attestation | Azure Attestation (boot-time, hardware + firmware measurements); vTPM (TPM 2.0) per VM | same source, grounded |
| Key release | Azure Key Vault Managed HSM, gated on successful attestation | same source, grounded |
| Transparency/auditability | Append-only ledger (CCF-based) recording container hashes + deployment policy — **only in the AI Confidential Inferencing preview architecture**, not confirmed present in the simpler `microsoft/confidential-ai` reference design | techcommunity.microsoft.com Confidential Inferencing deep-dive, grounded for that specific architecture |
| Maturity | AI Confidential Inferencing explicitly described as **preview**, not GA, as of this research pass | techcommunity.microsoft.com, Azure AI Foundry blog, grounded |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Azure Attestation of hardware/firmware state; Confidential Inferencing adds a ledger of container hashes | learn.microsoft.com + techcommunity deep-dive, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX CPU TEE, plus NVIDIA H100 confidential mode for GPUs | learn.microsoft.com confidential-vm-overview, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Neither Microsoft nor other tenants can see weights or inputs while the workload runs | learn.microsoft.com confidential-ai, grounded |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Transparency ledger built on CCF (Microsoft Research); the TEE hardware is vendor spec with no paper | learn.microsoft.com (Azure confidential ledger), grounded |
| Maturity | PREVIEW | AI Confidential Inferencing is preview, not GA | techcommunity.microsoft.com, Azure AI Foundry blog, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | No public blockchain; auditability comes from the CCF-based confidential ledger | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- Two (at least) differently-architected "confidential AI" reference
  designs are publicly documented by Microsoft with no explicit
  statement of how they relate — a future watch-run should check
  whether these converge, or whether one supersedes the other.
- Hardware TEEs as a class (SEV-SNP, TDX, any vendor) have a history of
  disclosed side-channel attacks in the broader security literature;
  this entry did not locate a specific disclosed vulnerability against
  Azure's current deployment in this research pass, so no specific
  claim is made here — flagged as a general risk class worth a
  dedicated watch-run rather than an unsupported specific claim.
- AI Confidential Inferencing's preview status means the architecture
  (and this entry) may be out of date quickly; recheck before relying
  on specifics.

FILE: systems/bittensor.md

---
name: Bittensor
field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks
category: incentive-networks
foundation: foundations/decentralized-consensus-ml.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded
website: "https://bittensor.com"
---

# Bittensor

## What it does

Bittensor is a decentralized network in which independent operators ("miners")
run machine-learning models and are paid in the TAO token based on how
useful their outputs are judged to be by other network participants
("validators"). Instead of a central benchmark deciding what's useful, peers
rank each other, and rewards flow from that peer-ranking.

## Architecture summary

- **Subtensor**: the layer-0 blockchain (built on Polkadot Substrate) that
  records peer identity, stake, and the consensus/incentive state.
- **Subnets**: independently defined competitions, each specifying its own
  task (e.g. text generation, image generation) and its own validator
  scoring logic. As of 2026 the network has scaled to roughly 64-128 active
  subnets (sources disagree on the exact figure at time of writing; mainnet
  slot cap is 128, with an expansion to 256 planned). [[FalconX: State of
  Bittensor]](https://www.falconx.io/newsroom/state-of-bittensor-subnet-adoption-trends-network-mechanics-and-covenants-departure)
- **Dynamic TAO (dTAO)**: deployed to mainnet ~Feb 13, 2025. Replaced a
  single global emission pool with per-subnet "alpha" tokens and AMM pools,
  letting TAO holders stake directly into specific subnets rather than the
  network as a whole. [[CryptoBriefing]](https://cryptobriefing.com/bittensor-dynamic-tao-emission-model/)
- **Yuma Consensus (YC)**: the mechanism that turns validator rankings into
  miner payouts (see below).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Shapley (1952), "A Value for n-Person Games"** — explicitly cited in
Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves, Shaabana, Hu, Luus, Liu, Tasker-Steeves et al.), hosted
at [bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia), as the
theoretical basis for the peer-ranking mechanism: Shapley values are used to
fairly attribute each peer's contribution to the network's informational
output across permutations of participants.

The whitepaper (*"Bittensor: A Peer-to-Peer Intelligence Market,"* Yuma Rao,
[bittensor.com/whitepaper](https://www.bittensor.com/whitepaper)) separately
cites Fisher Information pruning (LeCun et al. 1989; Yu et al. 2017) as the
theoretical ideal behind how peer-significance weights are ranked, and cites
a cluster of standard deep-learning papers (Hinton et al. 2015 on
distillation/general intelligence, Devlin et al. 2019, Radford et al. 2019,
Shazeer et al. 2017) as background for why peer-to-peer intelligence markets
are plausible — these are context, not the mechanism's core theoretical
grounding.

**Note on naming**: the official academic paper describes the
Shapley-value-based ranking and trust-weighted consensus mechanism but does
not use the name "Yuma Consensus" anywhere in that document. "Yuma
Consensus" as a named, specific algorithm (stake-weighted median + outlier
clipping) appears in community/ecosystem documentation and later working
papers rather than in the cited academic source itself — flagged here as a
naming gap between the academic grounding and the term actually used in
practice.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Consensus/incentive mechanism | Yuma Consensus — stake-weighted median of validator rankings with outlier clipping; rewards require >50% stake-trust to avoid exponential penalty | [hoge.gg explainer](https://hoge.gg/yuma-consensus-2026-how-bittensor-decides-who-gets-paid/) (community source, not primary) |
| Theoretical basis for ranking | Shapley value attribution | [bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia) |
| Base chain | Subtensor (Polkadot Substrate) | docs.bittensor.com |
| Tokenomics model | Dynamic TAO — per-subnet alpha tokens + AMM pools, live since Feb 2025 | [CryptoBriefing](https://cryptobriefing.com/bittensor-dynamic-tao-emission-model/) |
| Subnet count | ~64-128 active, cap 128 (256 planned) | [FalconX](https://www.falconx.io/newsroom/state-of-bittensor-subnet-adoption-trends-network-mechanics-and-covenants-departure) |
| Maturity | Mainnet live, first emission halving Dec 2025 (7200 → 3600 TAO/day) | search aggregation, not independently verified against chain data |
| Collusion assumption | Honest nodes assumed to hold >50% of stake | bittensor.com/whitepaper |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PEER SCORING | Validators rank miners' outputs; Yuma Consensus turns stake-weighted rankings into payouts | hoge.gg explainer (community source, not primary) |
| Trust rests on | STAKE MAJORITY | Honest nodes assumed to hold more than 50% of stake | bittensor.com/whitepaper |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | Not part of the base protocol; one subnet (SN4 Targon) reportedly uses TEEs | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | Shapley (1952), cited in Bittensor's own paper as the basis for peer ranking | bittensor.com/academia |
| Maturity | LIVE | Mainnet; first emission halving Dec 2025 | Search aggregation, not independently verified |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Subtensor (Polkadot Substrate) | docs.bittensor.com |

## Notable subnets

Subnets share Bittensor's core Yuma Consensus/Shapley grounding above —
they don't get separate top-level system files here, since what differs
per subnet is the task and validator scoring logic, not the base
architecture. This is a snapshot of significant subnets as of this
check, not a directory; the ecosystem reorders fast (market caps below
are from a March 2026 search, already stale by the time you read this).

| Subnet | Task | Notable technical distinction | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| SN3 — τemplar | Decentralized LLM pretraining | Trained Covenant-72B (72.7B params) across 70+ independently-owned nodes; top subnet by alpha-token market cap as of March 2026 (~$135M) | [KuCoin](https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/templar-bittensor-sn3-trains-72-7b-parameter-model-in-decentralized-network), [CoinGecko](https://www.coingecko.com/learn/top-bittensor-subnets-dtao) |
| SN9 — IOTA (Macrocosmos) | Distributed LLM pretraining | Own technical primer, not just a Bittensor doc — "Incentivised Orchestrated Training Architecture" (arXiv:2507.17766); demonstrated distributed pretraining of 700M–14B-param models surpassing baselines (Aug 2024) | [arXiv:2507.17766](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.17766v1), [Macrocosmos whitepaper](https://www.macrocosmos.ai/research/pretraining_whitepaper.pdf) |
| SN4 — Targon | Confidential-compute AI cloud | TEE-based verifiable inference — uses NVIDIA's nvTrust SDK on H200 GPUs to attest jobs ran honestly/confidentially; same underlying claim category (TEE attestation) as the big-tech confidential-AI entries in this repo, worth cross-referencing later | [search aggregation — unverified against Targon's own docs this pass] |
| SN13 — Data Universe | Decentralized data collection | Collects/distributes data (e.g. Reddit, X/Twitter) for AI training and real-time insight use cases | [Macrocosmos docs](https://docs.macrocosmos.ai/subnets/subnet-13-data-universe) |
| SN64 — Chutes | Serverless AI inference compute | Lets developers deploy/scale models without managing infra; public access layer for models produced by other subnets (e.g. SN120) | [tao.bot / X](https://x.com/taodotbot/status/1988931791802040588) |
| SN120 — Affine | Incentivized RL training arena | Validators reward only the Pareto-frontier model across RL tasks (program synthesis, reasoning, coding); explicitly designed sybil/copy/overfitting-proof, with winning models surfaced publicly via SN64 | [X thread](https://x.com/Gabensor_tt/status/1964748989800067301) |
| SN51 — Lium | Decentralized GPU rental marketplace | Sells raw GPU-hours as an input other subnets consume; overtook Chutes as top subnet by one ranking in 2026 | [TAO Daily](https://taodaily.io/lium-flips-chutes-as-bittensors-top-subnet-while-scaling-high-speed-gpu-rentals/) |
| SN62 — Ridges AI | Autonomous coding agents | Agents that find/fix bugs and write/ship code autonomously | [tao.bot / X](https://x.com/taodotbot/status/1988931791802040588) |

**Worth promoting to a dedicated top-level file later:** SN9's IOTA has
its own arXiv technical primer independent of Bittensor's base
citations — unlike most subnets, it's arguably a distinct research
contribution in the decentralized-training field (comparable to
Gensyn/Prime Intellect/Nous in this repo), not just a configuration of
Bittensor's incentive layer. SN4 Targon is also worth a closer look
given the overlap with this repo's confidential-computing-for-AI
entries — flagging rather than building either out now.

## Known limitations

- **Weight copying**: validators can copy other validators' submitted
  weights to earn rewards without doing the underlying evaluation work,
  free-riding on honest validators. Acknowledged as a known issue — a
  working paper titled *"Weight Copying in Bittensor"* (Opentensor, May
  2024) exists specifically addressing it, though the document's full
  content could not be retrieved directly for this entry (link redirected
  to a generic docs page: https://docs.learnbittensor.org/papers/BT_Weight_Copier-29May2024.pdf).
  Flagged as inferred-exists, content-unverified.
- **Governance centralization tension**: validator/stake concentration has
  drawn scrutiny over how decentralized the network actually is in
  practice. [Yellow.com research](https://yellow.com/research/bittensor-decentralized-ai-market-control-2026)
  raises this; not independently verified here.
- **Naming/documentation gap**: as noted above, the specific "Yuma
  Consensus" algorithm described in secondary sources isn't the same
  document as the academic paper citing Shapley values — the primary
  academic source and the commonly-cited mechanism name don't fully line up,
  which makes precise grounding harder than for the other tracked systems.

---
name: C2PA (Content Credentials)
field: Content provenance for AI-generated media
category: ownership
foundation:
last_updated: 2026-10-27
confidence: grounded (spec); secondary (adoption news)
website: "https://c2pa.org"
---

# C2PA (Content Credentials)

## What it does

An open standard for tamper-evident provenance metadata on media. It does
not judge content as good or bad, only whether assertions are validly
signed and bound to the asset.

## Architecture summary

- **Assertions** bundle into a signed **claim**; claim + signature +
  assertions form a **manifest**.
- **Hard bindings** (cryptographic hashes) tie a manifest to exact bytes;
  **soft bindings** (fingerprints, invisible watermarks) let a stripped
  manifest be recovered. The spec forbids using a soft binding as a hard one.
- Trust is anchored in X.509 signer certificates and a C2PA Trust List;
  time-stamps keep manifests valid after credentials expire.
- Adoption (secondary): OpenAI joined the steering committee and pledged
  SynthID alongside Content Credentials on 2026-05-19; EU AI Act
  Article 50 is reported enforceable from 2026-08-02.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Informed by Project Origin and the Content Authenticity Initiative (per
the spec). No academic foundation filed.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Integrity | Hash binding + signature | C2PA spec 2.2 |
| Trust | Trust List of certificate anchors | C2PA spec 2.2 |
| Opt-in | Yes | C2PA spec 2.2 |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | SIGNATURE | Signed claims bound to exact bytes by hash; proves who asserted what, not whether it is true | C2PA spec 2.2, grounded |
| Trust rests on | CERTIFICATE ISSUERS | X.509 signer certificates anchored in the C2PA Trust List | C2PA spec 2.2, grounded |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | STANDARDS | Informed by Project Origin and the Content Authenticity Initiative; no paper | C2PA spec, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Published spec (2.2); OpenAI joined the steering committee in May 2026 | C2PA spec; adoption from secondary sources, inferred |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | Centralized trust via a certificate list, unlike crypto-native registries | Known limitations; classification inferred |

## Known limitations

- Metadata is lost if stripped; soft bindings and watermarks are the
  fallback. SynthID covers only Google outputs and is detected with
  proprietary infrastructure (secondary source).
- Only ~100k of 580k characters of the spec were read; the threat model
  lives in separate Security Considerations and Harms Modelling docs.
- Centralized trust (a certificate list), unlike the crypto-native
  approaches in `/systems/story-protocol.md`.

---
name: Chutes
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
category: private-compute
foundation: foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md
last_updated: 2026-10-27
confidence: grounded (TEE mode, per Chutes' own post); unverified (Bittensor relationship)
website: "https://chutes.ai"
---

# Chutes

## What it does

A serverless AI inference platform that added a TEE serving mode (public
announcement dated 2026-05-07) for confidential LLM inference.

## Architecture summary

- **Hardware:** Intel TDX for CPU isolation plus NVIDIA confidential
  computing for the GPU.
- **Attestation:** measured boot (RTMR measurements); a hardware-signed TD
  Quote is checked by validators against a known-good configuration; NVIDIA
  GPU attestation is verified; the LUKS-encrypted root filesystem unlocks
  only after attestation; Kubernetes admission allows only cosign-signed
  images.
- **Optional E2EE:** on eligible TEE-backed instances, prompts are
  encrypted client-side and decrypted only inside a verified TEE.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

No paper cited. Lineage to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md` is
**inferred**. The announcement page does not mention Bittensor; the
common description of Chutes as a Bittensor subnet comes from outside this
pass and is **unverified here**.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation | Intel TDX + NVIDIA CC | Chutes post |
| E2EE | Optional, eligible instances only | Chutes post |
| Image policy | cosign-signed images only | Chutes post |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Validators check a hardware-signed TDX quote and NVIDIA GPU attestation against a known-good configuration | Chutes post, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Intel TDX and NVIDIA confidential computing; only cosign-signed images admitted | Chutes post, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | TEE serving mode; optional client-side E2EE on eligible instances, not the default | Chutes post, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | Chutes post, inferred link |
| Maturity | LIVE | TEE serving mode announced 2026-05-07 on a running inference platform | Chutes post, grounded |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | Commonly described as a Bittensor subnet; unverified in this pass | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- E2EE is not the default for all inference.
- Narrower runtime paths and more complexity than standard inference.
- The post itself says "We do not present TEEs as a silver bullet" and
  notes TEEs still need software validation and auditability.

========================================================================
FILE: systems/ezkl.md
========================================================================

---
name: EZKL
field: ZKML / verifiable inference
category: verifiable-inference
foundation: foundations/zkml.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (proving-system lineage); inferred (some matrix cells)
website: "https://github.com/zkonduit/ezkl"
---

## What it does

EZKL (zkonduit/ezkl) compiles ONNX-format ML models (exported from
PyTorch, TensorFlow, sklearn, etc.) into a zero-knowledge circuit, so
that a model inference can be proven correct without revealing the
model weights and/or inputs, and verified cheaply — including on-chain
in the EVM, in a browser, or on-device.

## Architecture summary

- Takes an ONNX graph + sample input, compiles a corresponding proving
  circuit, generates a proof of correct execution, and a matching
  verifier (including Solidity verifier contracts for EVM chains).
- Backend proving system: **Halo2**. EZKL's own README states: "In the
  backend we use the collaboratively-developed
  [Halo2](https://github.com/privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2) as a
  proof system." ([github.com/zkonduit/ezkl](https://github.com/zkonduit/ezkl))
- EZKL uses a modified variant of Halo2 that swaps in **KZG polynomial
  commitments** (rather than the discrete-log/IPA commitment Halo2
  originally shipped with) specifically to get smaller proofs and
  cheaper on-chain verification. This is a deliberate deviation from
  vanilla Halo2, not an assumption — flagged as inferred-from-general
  sourcing rather than a single explicit EZKL doc quote; worth
  rechecking against current docs.ezkl.xyz if this matters for a
  specific decision.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Two-hop grounding, not a direct citation** — EZKL's own docs don't
cite an academic paper directly. The chain is:

1. EZKL's README/docs explicitly name **Halo2**
   ([privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2](https://github.com/privacy-scaling-explorations/halo2))
   as the proof system it uses.
2. Halo2's own design book explicitly states: *"The arithmetization
   used by Halo 2 comes from [PLONK](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953),
   or more precisely its extension UltraPLONK that supports custom
   gates and lookup arguments."*
   ([zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html](https://zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html))

So: EZKL → (names) Halo2 → (cites) PLONK paper. See
`/foundations/zkml.md` for the paper itself. Halo2 does **not**, per
its own arithmetization page, discuss the original "Halo" recursive-
proof-composition paper (Bowe/Grigg/Hopwood 2019) — that lineage looked
plausible going in but didn't hold up under direct source-checking, so
it's dropped rather than asserted.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Proving system | Halo2 (modified) | EZKL README, grounded |
| Arithmetization | PLONKish (UltraPLONK: custom gates + lookup arguments) | Halo2 design book, grounded |
| Commitment scheme | KZG (EZKL's fork), not vanilla Halo2's IPA | General sourcing, **inferred** — recheck before relying on this |
| Trust model | Requires a KZG structured reference string (SRS/ptau); EZKL can auto-download or generate one | docs.ezkl.xyz/getting-started/setup, grounded |
| SRS size | Hundreds of MB to several GB depending on circuit size | General sourcing, inferred |
| On-chain verification | Yes — generates Solidity verifier contracts, EVM-compatible | EZKL project description, grounded |
| Maturity | Active, widely used reference implementation in the ZKML space; not formally audited to my knowledge as of this check | Inferred — not independently verified this pass |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PROOF | Halo2 zero-knowledge proof of the inference; verifiers run in the EVM, a browser, or on-device | EZKL README, grounded |
| Trust rests on | MATH + SETUP | Cryptographic soundness plus a KZG structured reference string (SRS/ptau) from a setup ceremony | docs.ezkl.xyz/getting-started/setup, grounded |
| Confidentiality | CRYPTOGRAPHIC | Zero-knowledge: inference proven correct without revealing model weights and/or inputs | EZKL project description, grounded |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | Two hops: EZKL names Halo2; Halo2's design book cites PLONK | EZKL README + Halo2 design book, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Active, widely used reference implementation; audit status not checked | Inferred, not independently verified this pass |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | No chain of its own; generates Solidity verifier contracts for EVM chains | EZKL project description, grounded |

## Known limitations

- SRS/setup size scales with circuit complexity and can become a real
  deployment cost for larger models.
- Relies on a trusted-setup ceremony for KZG (weaker trust assumption
  than a fully transparent setup) — this is a direct consequence of
  choosing KZG over Halo2's original commitment scheme.
- This entry did not independently verify audit status, current proof
  latency numbers, or maximum practical model size — flag these as
  open follow-ups rather than treating the matrix as complete.

========================================================================
FILE: systems/fetch-ai.md
========================================================================

---
name: Fetch.ai (uAgents)
field: Decentralized AI agent / marketplace protocols
category: agents
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (architecture description, team-authored); inferred (some matrix cells)
website: "https://github.com/fetchai/uAgents"
---

## What it does

Fetch.ai provides a framework (uAgents, Python) and blockchain infrastructure
for building autonomous software agents that can discover each other,
communicate, and transact. Agents register on-chain for discoverability and
settle value exchange via Fetch.ai's own token (FET).

**ASI Alliance context:** Fetch.ai merged with SingularityNET and Ocean
Protocol in 2024 to form the Artificial Superintelligence Alliance (ASI),
unifying their tokens (FET/AGIX/OCEAN → ASI) under one brand. CUDOS
(distributed GPU compute) joined in Oct 2024. Ocean Protocol subsequently
**withdrew from the alliance in Oct 2025**, with an associated lawsuit
settled (286M FET returned) — this entry focuses on Fetch.ai's own
technical stack, not the alliance's business structure, which is actively
in flux. ([0xgreythorn Medium overview](https://0xgreythorn.medium.com/fetch-ai-the-asi-alliance-decentralized-ai-powerhouse-b39c40ec4a56))

## Architecture summary

- **uAgents**: a Python library for building event-driven agents — each
  agent has a cryptographic identity (address derived from a keypair, not
  an IP), listens for messages, and responds via decorated handlers. State
  persists via a key-value store; agent-to-agent messaging uses a typed
  "Agent Chat Protocol." ([github.com/fetchai/uAgents](https://github.com/fetchai/uAgents))
- **Almanac**: a smart contract on Fetch.ai's own chain where agents
  register for discoverability; paired with a Fetch Name Service (FNS) for
  human-readable discovery and the Fetch Ledger for record-keeping.
- **Base chain**: an independent Cosmos-SDK chain using CometBFT (formerly
  Tendermint) consensus, with IBC interoperability to other Cosmos chains —
  not an Ethereum L2/L1.
- **Agentverse / ASI:One**: a hosted platform and LLM-orchestration layer
  that translates natural-language goals into multi-agent workflows on top
  of the uAgents substrate.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Primary technical source:** *"Fetch.ai: An Architecture for Modern
Multi-Agent Systems"* (arXiv:2510.18699) — authors Michael J. Wooldridge,
Attila Bagoly, Jonathan J. Ward, Emanuele La Malfa, Gabriel Paludo Licks.
This is a team-authored architecture paper (the submitting/corresponding
author is affiliated with Fetch.ai), not an external citation the product
docs point to — the same pattern as Gensyn's and Nillion's team-authored
protocol papers being treated as the grounding source. Notably, co-author
Michael Wooldridge is himself one of the foundational multi-agent-systems
theorists (co-author of the field's standard textbook, *An Introduction to
MultiAgent Systems*), which is a stronger-than-usual signal for this kind
of self-published grounding.

**Honest gap:** the paper's abstract states it bridges "decades of
foundational multi-agent systems (MAS) research," but does not point to
one specific external seed paper the way EZKL → Halo2 → PLONK did, and
Fetch.ai's own uAgents GitHub README cites **no academic papers or
whitepapers at all** — confirmed by direct fetch, not inferred. So unlike
most other entries in this repo, there is no crisp single foundational
citation to point to here beyond the team's own architecture description.
No new `foundations/` file created for this reason — forcing one would
mean inventing a seed paper that isn't actually referenced.

The original 2019 tokenomics/protocol whitepaper (*"FETCH: Technical
Introduction"*) describes the earlier Autonomous Economic Agents (AEA) /
Open Economic Framework design; current production architecture (above)
has superseded parts of that design, similar to how Gensyn's litepaper was
superseded by Verde.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Agent framework | uAgents (Python) | github.com/fetchai/uAgents |
| Identity scheme | Cryptographic keypair-derived address, not IP-based | uAgents README |
| Discovery mechanism | Almanac smart contract + Fetch Name Service | uAgents README |
| Base chain | Independent Cosmos-SDK chain, CometBFT consensus, IBC-interoperable | web search aggregation, not independently verified against chain docs |
| LLM orchestration layer | ASI:One — translates natural-language goals into multi-agent workflows | arXiv:2510.18699 abstract |
| Alliance structure | ASI Alliance (Fetch.ai + SingularityNET; Ocean Protocol withdrew Oct 2025) | 0xgreythorn Medium overview — secondary source, not independently verified |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NOT COVERED | Agents authenticate by keypair-derived address; nothing described checks what an agent computes | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Trust rests on | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Team-authored architecture paper (arXiv 2510.18699); the uAgents README cites no papers | arXiv 2510.18699 + uAgents README, grounded |
| Maturity | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Cosmos-SDK chain with CometBFT and IBC; agents register in the Almanac contract | Web search aggregation, not independently verified, inferred |

## Known limitations

- No independent academic citation grounds the current architecture beyond
  the team's own paper — treat claims of novelty against prior MAS research
  with the same caution the paper itself invites ("decades of... research"
  is a claim of continuity, not a specific, checkable citation).
- The ASI Alliance's business structure is actively unstable (Ocean
  Protocol's 2025 withdrawal plus a settled lawsuit) — any claim about
  "the alliance" as a unified technical entity should be rechecked against
  current status before relying on it.
- Property matrix entries sourced from secondary blog coverage (alliance
  structure, some chain details) rather than primary Fetch.ai documentation
  were not independently cross-verified in this pass.

# Flower

## What it does

An open federated learning framework ("a friendly federated learning
framework") for moving existing ML workloads into a federated setting.
Maintained by Flower Labs GmbH. Docs at v1.42.x.

## Architecture summary

- Components: SuperLink, SuperNodes, ServerApp, ClientApp. Deployment
  options: managed SuperLink, Docker, Helm, Slurm, SuperGrid.
- Privacy features documented: differential privacy (strategies, local-DP
  mod, privacy accountants), **SecAgg / SecAgg+** mods and a
  SecAggPlusWorkflow, TLS, SuperNode authentication, audit logging.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

The docs name SecAgg and SecAgg+ directly, so the link to
`foundations/secure-aggregation.md` (Bonawitz et al., 2017) is grounded
for the SecAgg mod; SecAgg+ is a later refinement of it by other authors,
not covered by that paper. The Flower framework paper itself was not
cited on the page reviewed.

FILE: systems/gensyn.md

---
name: Gensyn
field: Decentralized / distributed training
category: training
foundation: foundations/decentralized-training.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded
website: "https://www.gensyn.ai"
---

# Gensyn

## What it does

Gensyn is a protocol for decentralized ML compute: clients submit training
jobs, untrusted third-party providers execute them, and a verification layer
lets the client trust the result without controlling or re-running all of the
provider's hardware.

## Architecture summary

Current production system is **Verde** (per Gensyn's own research blog,
Oct 2026 check), which replaced the older litepaper-era design built around
four roles (Submitters, Solvers, Verifiers, Whistleblowers) and a Truebit-style
challenge game. Verde combines two pieces:

- **RepOps (Reproducible Operators)**: forces a fixed operation ordering for
  ML operators so that execution is bitwise-reproducible across different
  hardware, closing the floating-point non-associativity gap that previously
  made exact-match verification unreliable across GPUs/vendors.
- **Two-level bisection game**: providers commit to each training iteration
  via Merkle trees; disputes are resolved by bisecting first at the iteration
  level, then the operation level, so a referee only has to re-check a small,
  pinpointed slice of the computation instead of re-running the whole job.

Source: [Verde: Verification System In Production](https://www.gensyn.ai/research/verde-verification-system-in-production)
(Gensyn's own research blog).

Note: the older litepaper (docs.gensyn.ai/litepaper) describes a different,
earlier design — a Truebit-style incentive game with Submitter/Solver/
Verifier/Whistleblower roles and a graph-based "pinpoint protocol." That
litepaper is confirmed by Gensyn's own ecosystem write-ups to be **outdated**
relative to Verde. Documented here for lineage, not as current architecture.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

See [foundations/decentralized-training.md](../foundations/decentralized-training.md)
for the primary seed paper (Proof-of-Learning). Verde's own research post
additionally cites, as directly relevant prior work:

- **Refereed Delegation of Computation** — [dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2046707.2046759](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2046707.2046759)
  — the referee/dispute-arbitration pattern Verde's bisection game descends from.
- **Agatha** — [arxiv.org/abs/2105.04919](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04919) — prior
  execution-verification approach Verde explicitly improves on.
- **Toploc** — [arxiv.org/abs/2501.16007](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.16007) — another
  prior approach Verde positions itself against (couldn't extend to training,
  per Gensyn's own description).
- **Proof-of-Training-Data** — [arxiv.org/abs/2307.00682](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.00682)
- Verde's own full research paper: [arxiv.org/abs/2502.19405](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.19405)

Confidence: grounded — all five citations above came directly from Gensyn's
own research blog post, not inferred.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Verification mechanism | RepOps (bitwise-reproducible ops) + two-level bisection/dispute game | Verde research post |
| Trust model | Optimistic — provider's result accepted unless a referee is triggered to arbitrate a disputed step | Verde research post |
| Re-execution cost on dispute | Only the pinpointed iteration/operation, not the full job | Verde research post |
| Legacy design (superseded) | Truebit-style 4-role game (Submitter/Solver/Verifier/Whistleblower) | docs.gensyn.ai/litepaper (confirmed outdated) |
| Maturity | Verde described as "in production" by Gensyn as of this research post | Verde research post title |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | DISPUTE GAME | Verde: RepOps makes execution bitwise-reproducible; disputes are bisected down to one operation for a referee | Verde research post |
| Trust rests on | ONE HONEST PARTY | Optimistic: a provider's result stands unless someone disputes it and triggers the referee | Verde research post; one-honest-party reading inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | Proof-of-Learning (IEEE S&P 2021), plus Refereed Delegation, Agatha and Toploc cited by Verde | Gensyn research blog, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Verde described as "in production" by Gensyn | Verde research post title |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- The litepaper's incentive-game numbers (staking, slashing, jackpot rewards)
  are from the superseded design; current economic parameters for Verde were
  not found in this pass and should be checked directly against Gensyn's
  current docs before citing specifics.
- RepOps's bitwise-reproducibility claim depends on providers running the
  mandated fixed operation ordering; no independent third-party audit of this
  claim was located in this pass — flagged as a candidate for a future watch
  run if an independent analysis is published.

FILE: systems/giza-orion.md

---
name: Giza / Orion
field: ZKML / verifiable inference (STARK-based)
category: verifiable-inference
foundation: foundations/zkml-stark.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (what it was built on, historically); status itself is grounded as largely inactive
website: "https://github.com/gizatechxyz/orion"
---

## What it does

Giza originally built **Orion**, a framework for compiling ML models (via
ONNX) into Cairo programs so that ML inference could be proven correct
using zk-STARKs and verified on-chain on StarkNet — the STARK-based
counterpart to EZKL's Halo2/PLONK approach. The stack: ONNX model →
Giza Transpiler → Cairo program (Sierra/CASM) → STARK proof → on-chain
verification via SHARP (Starknet's shared prover).

**This product no longer exists in that form.** Giza pivoted away from
ZKML entirely toward on-chain DeFi agents (ARMA, Pulse), and by 2026
those were wound down too. See "Known limitations" / current status
below before treating this as an active reference implementation.

## Architecture summary

- Original stack: ONNX → Cairo 1.0 (via the Orion ONNX-in-Cairo runtime)
  → STARK proof generated via Cairo's execution trace → SHARP
  (SHARed Prover) aggregates proofs for verification on Ethereum.
- Orion itself was archived 2025-03-03
  ([gizatechxyz/orion](https://github.com/gizatechxyz/orion)).
- Giza pivoted to verifiable DeFi agents (ARMA, Pulse) without the ZKML
  verification layer attached — the agents ran, but proof-of-correct-
  inference was not part of that product.
- A next-generation ML proving stack, **LuminAIR**, built on StarkWare's
  newer **S-two (stwo)** prover (Circle STARKs) was announced as the
  long-term differentiator but, per independent review, its repository
  "had no commits in over eight months" as of the review and "the
  on-chain Cairo verifier is still roadmap"
  ([ownyourmind.ai/projects/giza](https://ownyourmind.ai/projects/giza/)).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Two-hop, weaker grounding than the EZKL→Halo2→PLONK chain** — the
analogous chain here is Giza/Orion → Cairo → the original STARK paper,
but the second hop could not be directly confirmed:

1. Orion compiled models to **Cairo**, StarkWare's STARK-friendly CPU
   architecture — this is explicit in Orion's own announcement and docs.
2. Cairo's own paper — *"Cairo: a Turing-complete STARK-friendly CPU
   architecture"* (Goldberg, Papini, Riabzev, eprint 2021/1063) — is the
   natural second hop to the original STARK paper (Ben-Sasson, Bentov,
   Horesh, Riabzev, *"Scalable, transparent, and post-quantum secure
   computational integrity,"* eprint 2018/046). **This citation could
   not be confirmed in-text**: the Cairo paper's PDF returned a 403 on
   fetch, and the visible abstract/metadata did not explicitly cite the
   2018/046 paper. The association is strong by authorship/org (Cairo's
   authors are StarkWare; Ben-Sasson, StarkWare's co-founder, co-authored
   the original STARK paper) but this is **inferred, not grounded** —
   flagged exactly because it didn't survive the same direct-quote check
   used elsewhere in this repo (e.g. the EZKL entry's Halo2 citation).
3. Starknet's own SHARP documentation
   ([docs.starknet.io/learn/protocol/sharp](https://docs.starknet.io/learn/protocol/sharp))
   cites no academic papers at all — only blog posts and third-party
   write-ups (Nethermind, zkSecurity, LambdaClass).

See `foundations/zkml-stark.md` — created as a separate file from
`foundations/zkml.md` because this is a STARK lineage, not a PLONK one;
forcing them into one file would misrepresent two different proof
systems as one lineage.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Proving system (original Orion) | Cairo execution → STARK proof via SHARP | Orion docs/announcement, grounded |
| Proving system (next-gen, unreleased) | LuminAIR on S-two (stwo) prover, Circle STARKs | [ownyourmind.ai review](https://ownyourmind.ai/projects/giza/), grounded |
| Trust model | Transparent setup (STARK, no trusted ceremony) — a structural advantage over EZKL's KZG trusted setup | Standard STARK property, inferred from Cairo's design, not Giza-specific confirmation |
| On-chain verification | Yes, originally — via SHARP on Ethereum | Starknet SHARP docs |
| **Maturity** | **Largely inactive as of Oct 2026**: Orion archived 2025-03-03; ARMA/Pulse DeFi agents wound down Feb–Mar 2026 (wind-down announced 2026-02-26, migration deadline 2026-03-26); GitHub orgs show no pushes since 2026-03-23; LuminAIR unreleased, no commits in 8+ months per review | [ownyourmind.ai](https://ownyourmind.ai/projects/giza/), corroborated independently via WebSearch (GitHub push dates, on-chain balance drop from ~$4.85M to ~$14K by 2026-06-24) |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PROOF | Original Orion: STARK proof of Cairo execution, aggregated by SHARP | Orion docs/announcement, grounded |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Transparent setup (STARK, no trusted ceremony) | Standard STARK property, inferred from Cairo's design |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | Orion compiles to Cairo; Cairo's link to the original STARK paper (eprint 2018/046) couldn't be confirmed in-text | Orion docs, grounded; Cairo to STARK hop inferred |
| Maturity | INACTIVE | Orion archived 2025-03-03; successor DeFi agents wound down Feb-Mar 2026; LuminAIR unreleased | ownyourmind.ai review, corroborated via GitHub push dates and on-chain balances, grounded |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Originally verified on Ethereum via SHARP, Starknet's shared prover | Starknet SHARP docs, grounded |

## Known limitations

- **This is the clearest "status" flag in the repo so far**: unlike
  EZKL, Gensyn, Zama, Nillion, and Bittensor (all actively developed),
  Giza/Orion's original ZKML product is archived and its successor
  product line (ARMA/Pulse) has also been wound down. The announced
  next-gen ML-proving stack (LuminAIR) is unreleased and appears
  stalled. Treat this entry as historical/architectural reference, not
  as a currently-deployable system.
- Marketing materials (e.g. "$19M assets under agent") diverge sharply
  from on-chain measurement (~$12,800 in agent positions as of
  2026-10-04 per the independent review) — a useful general reminder to
  check on-chain data over marketing figures for any system in this
  space, not just this one.
- The STARK-lineage citation (Cairo paper → original STARK paper) is
  inferred, not confirmed — worth a recheck if someone can access the
  full Cairo paper text directly.
