FILE: systems/google-confidential-federated-learning.md
========================================================================

---
name: Google Confidential Federated Learning (TensorFlow Federated + TEE confidentiality)
field: Federated learning / confidential aggregation
category: private-compute
foundation: foundations/secure-aggregation.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded
website: "https://research.google/blog/federated-learning-collaborative-machine-learning-without-centralized-training-data/"
---

# Google Confidential Federated Learning

## What it does

Google trains production ML models (e.g. Gboard's next-word prediction) on
data that never leaves users' devices. Each device computes a local model
update on its own data; only the update — not the raw data — is sent to a
server, which aggregates updates across many devices into an improved
global model. The "confidential" layer adds server-side trusted execution
environments (TEEs) so that even the aggregation server itself cannot see
individual updates, with the privacy properties externally auditable rather
than taken on trust.

## Architecture summary

- **Base mechanism**: Federated Averaging — devices compute local SGD
  updates, a server averages them into a new global model, raw data is
  never centralized.
- **Confidentiality layer** ("Confidential Federated Computations", 2024):
  devices encrypt their uploads with keys controlled by a TEE-hosted Key
  Management Service (KMS). The KMS only releases decryption keys to
  specific, pre-approved TEE binaries — so the server operator cannot
  access plaintext updates even with full infrastructure access.
- **External verifiability**: access policies (which binaries may process
  which data) are published to Rekor, Sigstore's public transparency log,
  and the TEE binaries are reproducibly buildable from open-source code —
  so an outside auditor can check that the system is actually doing what
  it claims, not just trusting Google's word for it. This is the piece
  that lets Google claim *externally verifiable* differential privacy
  rather than DP that depends on trusting the service operator.
- Per secondary reporting (MarkTechPost, Oct 2026 — primary source page
  returned a 403 during this research pass, so this specific detail is
  less directly confirmed than the rest): this architecture is now live in
  production for Gboard.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Grounded via a direct citation chain from Google's own federated-learning
announcement, not inference:

- Google's 2017 FL announcement post
  ([research.google/blog](https://research.google/blog/federated-learning-collaborative-machine-learning-without-centralized-training-data/))
  directly links to **"Communication-Efficient Learning of Deep Networks
  from Decentralized Data"** (McMahan, Moore, Ramage, Hampson, y Arcas —
  [arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629](https://arxiv.org/abs/1602.05629), AISTATS
  2017) as the Federated Averaging algorithm itself — the base ML
  mechanism, not the crypto piece.
- The same post directly links to **"Practical Secure Aggregation for
  Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning"** (Bonawitz, Ivanov, Kreuter,
  Marcedone, McMahan, Patel, Ramage, Segal, Seth —
  [eprint.iacr.org/2017/281](http://eprint.iacr.org/2017/281), ACM CCS
  2017) as "a Secure Aggregation protocol that uses cryptographic
  techniques" so the server only ever sees an aggregate, never individual
  updates. This is the actual crypto-for-ML contribution — see
  `/foundations/secure-aggregation.md`.
- Direct authorship continuity: both Kallista Bonawitz (Secure Aggregation
  author) and Brendan McMahan (FedAvg author) are listed authors on the
  2024 "Confidential Federated Computations" paper
  ([arxiv.org/abs/2404.10764](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.10764)) that
  introduces the TEE-based confidentiality layer — the same people,
  extending their own prior work, not a third party building on it later.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Base algorithm | Federated Averaging (local SGD + server-side averaging) | McMahan et al. 2017, cited directly by Google's FL announcement |
| Aggregation privacy | Cryptographic Secure Aggregation (server sees only the sum/average, never individual updates) | Bonawitz et al. 2017, cited directly by Google's FL announcement |
| Server-side confidentiality | TEE-hosted KMS; decryption keys released only to pre-approved, reproducibly-built binaries | "Confidential Federated Computations," arxiv 2404.10764 |
| External verifiability mechanism | Access policies published to Rekor (Sigstore transparency log); TEE binaries reproducibly buildable from open source | arxiv 2404.10764 |
| Production usage | Gboard (per secondary reporting; primary source page was unreachable this pass — flagged as less directly confirmed) | MarkTechPost, Oct 2026 — inferred/secondary, recheck against Google's own primary source when accessible |
| Trust model | Does not require trusting the server operator's word — relies on TEE hardware security + externally auditable transparency log | arxiv 2404.10764 |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | TEE-hosted KMS releases keys only to pre-approved, reproducibly built binaries; policies published to Rekor | arxiv 2404.10764, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | TEE hardware security plus an externally auditable transparency log, not the operator's word | arxiv 2404.10764, grounded |
| Confidentiality | CRYPTOGRAPHIC + ENCLAVE | Raw data stays on device; Secure Aggregation shows the server only the aggregate; TEEs hide individual updates from the operator | Bonawitz et al. 2017 + arxiv 2404.10764, grounded |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | FedAvg (AISTATS 2017) and Secure Aggregation (CCS 2017), by Google authors who also wrote the 2024 TEE paper | Google's FL announcement post, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | In production for Gboard, per secondary reporting | MarkTechPost, Oct 2026, inferred/secondary |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | No blockchain component appears in Google's materials | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- TEE-based confidentiality inherits TEE hardware's own threat model —
  side-channel attacks against TEEs are an active research area; this
  entry does not independently assess that risk, it only documents what
  Google's own papers claim.
- The Gboard production-deployment claim in this entry rests on secondary
  reporting, not a directly-fetched primary source (the MarkTechPost
  article returned an HTTP 403 during this research pass) — worth
  re-verifying against Google's own blog/papers directly in a future pass.
- This entry does not independently verify the differential-privacy
  epsilon values or noise parameters actually used in production — only
  that the mechanism for achieving verifiable DP is as described in the
  cited papers.

FILE: systems/io-net.md
========================================================================

---
name: io.net
field: Decentralized GPU / compute marketplace
category: compute-markets
foundation: foundations/distributed-compute-scheduling.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (orchestration-engine lineage); no academic grounding found (trust/verification layer)
website: "https://io.net"
---

## What it does

io.net aggregates underutilized GPUs (data centers, crypto miners,
independent providers) across many countries into an on-demand,
clusterable compute marketplace, primarily marketed at AI
training/inference workloads.

## Architecture summary

- **IO-SDK** is io.net's own orchestration layer. Its own docs state
  directly: *"IO-SDK is our specialized fork of Ray, a core technology
  driving io.net's capabilities"* and name the base version as Ray 2.3.0.
  ([io.net/docs/guides/architecture/io-architecture](https://io.net/docs/guides/architecture/io-architecture))
- Backend stack layered on top: Kubernetes/Prefect/Airflow for
  orchestration, Ray/Ludwig/PyTorch/Keras/TensorFlow for execution,
  S3/HDFS for storage, Docker for containerization, Grafana/Datadog/
  Prometheus/NVIDIA DCGM for monitoring (per io.net's own architecture
  docs).
- **Resource-integrity mechanisms** (io.net-specific, not inherited from
  Ray): a "Proof-of-Work" and "Proof of Time-Lock" (PoTL) pair that
  check a provided GPU/CPU is real and stays dedicated to the rented
  workload for its full rental period, plus a daily "Cluster
  Verification Job" standardized benchmark that workers must pass to
  stay in the active pool.
- **Confidential compute**: io.net supports NVIDIA H200-based hardware
  confidential computing, using SPDM 1.1 for device authentication,
  X.509 PKI, OCSP, and TCG measurement/attestation specifications, via
  NVIDIA's own `nv-attestation-sdk`. Recommended mode is "Protected
  PCIe" (PPCIe), which puts an entire NVLink-connected GPU set into
  confidential mode together.
  ([io.net/docs/guides/clouds/confidential-compute-attestation-overview](https://io.net/docs/guides/clouds/confidential-compute-attestation-overview))

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Two-hop grounding for the orchestration engine, no grounding found for
the trust/verification layer:**

1. io.net's own docs name **Ray** (specifically IO-SDK as a fork of Ray
   2.3.0) as the technology underlying its clustering/task-orchestration
   capability — direct quote above.
2. Ray is itself an academic systems project: *"Ray: A Distributed
   Framework for Emerging AI Applications"* — P. Moritz, R. Nishihara,
   S. Wang, A. Tumanov, R. Liaw, E. Liang, M. Elibol, Z. Yang, W. Paul,
   M. I. Jordan, I. Stoica (UC Berkeley), OSDI 2018.
   ([usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-moritz.pdf](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-moritz.pdf))

See `/foundations/distributed-compute-scheduling.md`.

**Important distinction:** this lineage grounds io.net's *compute
orchestration engine only*. The parts of io.net that are actually about
decentralization/trust — PoW/PoTL resource verification, the Cluster
Verification Job, the confidential-compute attestation chain — are not
shown by io.net's own docs to descend from any specific academic paper.
They're described in terms of industry standards (SPDM, TCG, X.509) and
NVIDIA's own tooling, not a citable research lineage. Flagged as
no-academic-grounding-found rather than inferring one.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestration engine | IO-SDK, a fork of Ray 2.3.0 | io.net architecture docs, grounded |
| Resource-integrity check | Proof-of-Work + Proof of Time-Lock (PoTL) | io.net support docs, grounded |
| Recurring verification | Daily Cluster Verification Job (standardized benchmark) | io.net support docs, grounded |
| Confidential compute | NVIDIA H200 hardware CC, Protected PCIe mode, SPDM 1.1 + TCG attestation | io.net docs, grounded |
| Trust model (compute delivery) | Verification-by-benchmark + continuous monitoring, not cryptographic proof of correct execution | io.net docs, grounded — note this is weaker than the ZK/proof-based verification used by systems like EZKL or Gensyn |
| Maturity | Live production marketplace, actively marketed/benchmarked | io.net site, grounded |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | SPOT CHECK | Proof-of-Work + Proof of Time-Lock check the GPU is real and dedicated, plus a daily benchmark; not proof of correct execution | io.net support docs, grounded |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | GPU providers, policed by benchmarks and continuous monitoring rather than proofs | io.net docs, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Supports NVIDIA H200 confidential computing (Protected PCIe mode, SPDM attestation) | io.net confidential-compute docs, grounded |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | IO-SDK forks Ray (OSDI 2018). Grounds orchestration only, not the trust layer | io.net architecture docs, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Live production marketplace | io.net site, grounded |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- The resource-verification layer (PoW/PoTL/benchmarking) checks that a
  GPU exists and stays dedicated, not that any specific computation on
  it was executed correctly — a materially weaker guarantee than
  proof-based verification (contrast with Gensyn's RepOps+bisection or
  EZKL's ZK proofs). Worth keeping this distinction visible if io.net is
  ever compared against those systems on the same axis.
- No academic citation lineage found for the decentralization/trust
  mechanisms specifically — only for the underlying Ray-based
  orchestration layer, which is a general-purpose distributed-computing
  technology, not AI- or crypto-specific.
- This entry did not independently verify PoW/PoTL implementation
  details beyond what io.net's own support docs describe at a
  conceptual level.

FILE: systems/lagrange-labs.md
========================================================================

---
name: Lagrange Labs (DeepProve)
field: ZKML / verifiable inference
category: verifiable-inference
foundation: foundations/zkml-sumcheck.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (core technique lineage); inferred (trust model, some performance framing)
website: "https://www.lagrange.dev"
---

## What it does

DeepProve is Lagrange Labs' zkML system: it generates zero-knowledge
proofs that a specific LLM produced a specific output sequence from a
specific input, without re-running the model or trusting the party that
did. Unlike earlier zkML work limited to single tokens or isolated
components, DeepProve targets full end-to-end LLM inference — it
certifies that the whole output sequence is correct rather than
encoding the entire inference computation in-circuit, which is what
lets it avoid the quadratic circuit blowup or expensive RAM modeling
that sank earlier approaches.

Lagrange Labs is a separate project from, but shares the "ZK
coprocessor" branding with, Lagrange's other product line — a
decentralized ZK Prover Network / ZK Coprocessor for proving SQL
queries over on-chain data, which (per Lagrange's own docs) uses
Plonky2. **DeepProve is not that system** — it's a distinct proving
construction built specifically for ML inference. Don't conflate the
two when reading Lagrange's broader materials.

## Architecture summary

- Core building blocks, per DeepProve's own paper abstract: the
  **sum-check protocol** and **lookup arguments**, used to verify
  individual LLM operators (multi-head attention, layer normalization,
  grouped-query attention, rotary positional embeddings) without
  encoding the full computation as one monolithic circuit.
- Native format support: ONNX, safetensors, and GGUF — so models
  exported from PyTorch, TensorFlow, JAX, or Hugging Face run through
  DeepProve unchanged (no custom model-authoring step required).
- Positioned explicitly against two named prior systems: **zkGPT**
  (USENIX'25, single-token proofs) and **zkLLM** (CCS'24, proved only
  the Softmax component) — DeepProve's claimed contribution is doing
  both end-to-end and faster.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Two-hop grounding**, same pattern as this repo's EZKL entry:

1. DeepProve's own paper — *"DeepProve: Verifiable End-to-End Large
   Language Model Inference"* (IACR ePrint
   [2026/1112](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1112), accepted CCS 2026;
   authors include Yupeng Zhang and Charalampos Papamanthou, both
   established authors in prior sum-check-based SNARK literature) —
   explicitly names the **sum-check protocol** as a core building
   block in its own abstract.
2. The sum-check protocol's original paper: Lund, Fortnow, Karloff,
   Nisan, *"Algebraic methods for interactive proof systems,"* Journal
   of the ACM 39(4), 1992. This is the standard, widely-cited origin
   of the technique (confirmed via multiple independent sources,
   including the paper's own author describing it on social media as
   his most-cited work specifically because of its zkSNARK reuse).

**Not confirmed from a direct source in this pass:** whether DeepProve's
paper cites the 1992 paper by name in its bibliography, versus citing
an intermediate sum-check-based SNARK (GKR, Libra, Virgo, Spartan,
HyperPlonk, or Lasso/Jolt, all of which build on the same 1992
technique) — the abstract fetch used for this entry didn't expose the
full reference list. Treat the specific DeepProve→1992-paper link as
the standard lineage for "a sum-check-based proving system," not as a
confirmed direct citation in DeepProve's own bibliography.

See `foundations/zkml-sumcheck.md` — this is a **separate lineage**
from `foundations/zkml.md` (PLONK/Halo2, used by EZKL). Both files
share the field "ZKML / verifiable inference" but root in genuinely
different proving techniques (PLONKish arithmetization vs.
sum-check-based verification), so they're kept as distinct foundation
entries rather than merged.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Proving technique | Sum-check protocol + lookup arguments (not PLONKish arithmetization) | DeepProve paper abstract, grounded |
| Model format support | ONNX, safetensors, GGUF | DeepProve paper abstract / lagrange.dev, grounded |
| Claimed proving speedup | 20–60× faster than prior SOTA (paper abstract framing); a separate press release states "60×faster / 671× faster verification" — the two framings weren't reconciled in this pass, may refer to different baselines/benchmarks | DeepProve paper abstract; Lagrange press release — **flagged discrepancy, not resolved** |
| Example throughput | GPT-2: 174 tokens/min; Gemma 3: 86 tokens/min; verification in 1–3.7 seconds | DeepProve paper abstract, grounded |
| Production track record | 12M+ cryptographic proofs generated, 3M+ AI inferences verified end-to-end, as of the open-source release (June 2026) | Lagrange press release, grounded |
| Trust model (trusted setup or transparent) | Not confirmed from a direct source in this pass — sum-check-based systems are *typically* transparent (no CRS), but DeepProve's specific underlying polynomial commitment scheme wasn't identified here | **Inferred, unverified** — recheck before relying on this |
| Maturity | Open-sourced June 2026; github.com/Lagrange-Labs/deep-prove; live dashboard at deep-prove.lagrange.dev | Lagrange press release / blog, grounded |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PROOF | Sum-check + lookup-argument proofs of end-to-end LLM inference; verification in 1-3.7 s | DeepProve paper abstract, grounded |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Cryptographic soundness; whether a trusted setup is needed is unconfirmed (sum-check systems are typically transparent) | Inferred, unverified, see Property matrix |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | The file describes proving correctness, not what DeepProve keeps hidden | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | DeepProve names the sum-check protocol (Lund, Fortnow, Karloff, Nisan 1992); a direct bibliography citation is unconfirmed | DeepProve paper abstract; 1992 link is the standard lineage, inferred |
| Maturity | LIVE | Open-sourced June 2026; 12M+ proofs and 3M+ inferences verified, per Lagrange | Lagrange press release, grounded |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- Throughput (174 tokens/min for GPT-2, a small model by current
  standards) is far below normal plaintext LLM serving throughput —
  the "faster than prior zkML work" framing is a comparison against
  other zero-knowledge approaches, not against unproven inference.
  Worth keeping in mind when judging practicality.
- The proving-speedup framing differs between DeepProve's own paper
  abstract (20–60×) and Lagrange's press release (60× / 671×) — not
  reconciled in this pass; don't cite a single number without checking
  which baseline it refers to.
- Trust model (trusted setup vs. transparent) not independently
  confirmed here — flagged as an open follow-up, same category as
  EZKL's unresolved SRS-size claims elsewhere in this repo.

# Marabou

## What it does

An SMT-based framework for verifying deep neural networks: given a network
and a property it returns a guarantee or a counter-example input. Calls
itself "a research product."

## Architecture summary

- Inputs: ONNX (main), .nnet, TensorFlow; properties via Python or VNNLIB.
- Default solver is single-threaded with DeepPoly bound tightening and
  DeepSoI; also multi-worker and Split-and-Conquer modes; optional Gurobi.
- Version 2.0 tool paper: arXiv 2401.14461. A 2026 tutorial covers a
  proof-producing version (secondary source).
- About 348 stars; Windows support discontinued.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Marabou's approach (SMT/LP) differs from CROWN's bound propagation, so
the link to `foundations/neural-network-verification.md` is **inferred**
as a peer technique in the same field, not a citation. The README does
not state the license; the COPYING file was not read.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Method | SMT + bound tightening | README |
| Output | Proof or counter-example | README |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | FORMAL PROOF | SMT-based: returns a guarantee that the property holds, or a counter-example input | README, grounded |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Soundness of the SMT/LP reasoning and its implementation; verifier soundness is a research concern | Known limitations; classification inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Marabou 2.0 tool paper (arXiv 2401.14461); the link to CROWN is a peer technique, not a citation | README, grounded; foundation link inferred |
| Maturity | RESEARCH | Calls itself "a research product" | README, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | — | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- Complete SMT-style verification scales worse than GPU bound-propagation
  tools on large networks (general, not stated in the README).
- Verifier soundness is itself a research concern (SoundnessBench).

---
name: Modulus Labs
field: ZKML / verifiable inference

# Modulus Labs

## What it does

Modulus Labs built "proof of AI inference" systems — ZK proofs that a specific
model, with specific weights, produced a specific output on specific input —
so AI can act on-chain (trading bots, games, recommendation systems) without
requiring anyone to trust the model operator or re-run the computation to
check it.

**Status: the company no longer operates independently.** The team joined
Tools for Humanity (the organization behind Worldcoin/World) in late 2024.
Modulus Labs itself is now a historical reference rather than an active
vendor, though its open-source tooling — particularly the Remainder prover —
continued to be used/cited after that move.
([hoge.gg: "The zk-ML Toolchain in 2026"](https://hoge.gg/zkml-toolchain-2026-which-proving-system-ships/))

## Architecture summary

- **halo2_ml** — Modulus's own GitHub repo, described by Modulus as a
  "Foundation for speedy Machine Learning operations in Halo2 Prover."
  ([github.com/Modulus-Labs/halo2_ml](https://github.com/Modulus-Labs/halo2_ml))
  This is the same backend lineage as EZKL (see Built on, below).
- **Remainder** — Modulus's custom prover, described in third-party coverage
  as "a Halo2 variant tuned for ML" ([hoge.gg](https://hoge.gg/zkml-toolchain-2026-which-proving-system-ships/)).
  Introduced in their own paper "Scaling Intelligence: Verifiable Decision
  Forest Inference with Remainder" (Feb 2024), specifically targeting
  efficient verification of decision-forest/tree-ensemble models rather than
  neural nets. **Flagged as inferred, not fully grounded**: exactly how
  Remainder's internals relate to vanilla Halo2 (same arithmetization? a
  distinct backend reusing only Halo2's commitment layer?) was not confirmed
  from primary sources in this pass — recheck the actual paper
  (`github.com/Modulus-Labs/Papers/remainder-paper.pdf`) before relying on
  implementation-level claims.
- Demos (proof-of-concept, not production infra): **RockyBot** — described as
  the first fully on-chain AI deployment to mainnet, proving that an RNN/LSTM
  trading bot's decisions matched its model's predictions via zk-SNARKs;
  **Leela vs the World** — on-chain AI chess; demonstrated proofs of GPT-2-
  and Twitter-recommendation-algorithm-scale inference.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Same two-hop chain as EZKL — Modulus names **Halo2** directly (via their own
`halo2_ml` repo description) as their proving backend, and Halo2's own design
book cites **PLONK** (eprint.iacr.org/2019/953) as the source of its
arithmetization. See [foundations/zkml.md](../foundations/zkml.md) for the
paper itself — no new foundations file needed here since the lineage is the
same, not a separate one. The genuinely novel piece is Modulus's *own*
research output, not something they're built on:

- **"The Cost of Intelligence: Proving Machine Learning Inference with
  Zero-Knowledge"** (Daniel Shorr et al., Jan 2023, Ethereum Foundation grant)
  — the first benchmark of ZK proof systems (Groth16, Gemini, Winterfell,
  Halo2, Plonky2, zkCNN) against a common suite of ML inference workloads.
  Headline result: an 18M-parameter MLP proved in ~50s using Plonky2.
  ([github.com/Modulus-Labs/Papers](https://github.com/Modulus-Labs/Papers))
- **"Scaling Intelligence: Verifiable Decision Forest Inference with
  Remainder"** (Feb 2024) — introduces the Remainder technique above.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Proving system (neural nets) | Halo2-based (`halo2_ml`) | Modulus's own GitHub repo description, grounded |
| Proving system (decision forests) | Remainder (Halo2 variant per third-party source) | hoge.gg, cross-check against primary paper recommended |
| Own research contribution | First cross-system ZK-proving benchmark for ML ("Cost of Intelligence") | Modulus-Labs/Papers repo, grounded |
| Demonstrated scale | 18M-parameter MLP (2023 benchmark); later demos at GPT-2/recommendation-algorithm scale | Cost of Intelligence paper; secondary coverage for later demos, not independently verified |
| Organizational status | Team absorbed into Tools for Humanity (World) in late 2024; not operating as an independent vendor | hoge.gg, 2026 retrospective coverage |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PROOF | Zero-knowledge proofs of inference: halo2_ml for neural nets, Remainder for decision forests | Modulus GitHub repo description, grounded; Remainder details secondary |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Cryptographic soundness; commitment scheme and setup not documented in this file | Inferred from the proving system, see Property matrix |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | Same chain as EZKL: halo2_ml names Halo2; Halo2 cites PLONK | Modulus GitHub + Halo2 design book, grounded |
| Maturity | INACTIVE | Team joined Tools for Humanity (World) in late 2024; repos not assumed maintained | hoge.gg 2026 retrospective coverage |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Demos ran on existing chains (RockyBot trading bot, on-chain chess); no chain of its own | Architecture summary demo descriptions, inferred |

## Known limitations

- The company's defunct status means none of the repos above should be
  assumed actively maintained — check commit history directly before relying
  on any of this for current tooling decisions.
- Remainder's precise relationship to vanilla Halo2 was not confirmed from
  the primary paper in this pass; treat the "Halo2 variant" characterization
  as secondary-sourced, not primary-confirmed.
- The large-scale demos (GPT-2, Twitter recommendation algorithm) are
  demonstrations, not production-maintained systems — no evidence found of
  ongoing operation of either.

# Morpheus

## What it does

A decentralized marketplace for open-weight model inference. Providers
stake/offer compute; a router (built on Lumerin's code, originally for
decentralized Bitcoin mining) connects sessions to providers, with
smart-contract payment. Originally pitched around personal "Smart Agents";
a 2026-08 THORChain write-up describes it as an inference marketplace.

## Architecture summary

- Contracts on Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base (secondary source).
- MOR rewards compute providers and gives holders a share of network
  compute activity (launched with a $20M provider reward program).
- Phala announced TEE-based verifiable compute for Morpheus/Lumerin
  (2024). A TEE provider with Secret Network models was added 2026-08-07
  (see `/systems/secret-network.md`).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

No paper is cited. Foundation intentionally left empty: no real
citation chain was found.

## Property matrix

|---|---|---|

| Privacy | Optional, via TEE providers | Secret Network post |
| Usage | 39B tokens processed (single podcast write-up) | THORChain blog |

## Comparison axes

| Confidentiality | PER APP | Base inference isn't private; privacy depends on choosing a TEE provider | Secret Network post, inferred |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the router is built on Lumerin's Bitcoin-mining code | File's lineage note, inferred |
| Maturity | LIVE | 39B tokens processed, per a single podcast write-up | THORChain blog, inferred |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Contracts on Ethereum, Arbitrum and Base | Secondary source, inferred |

## Known limitations

  docs were not reached (morpheus.network is an unrelated supply-chain
  company). Verify against the project's own documentation.

  chosen.

---

# NEAR AI Cloud

## What it does

Private LLM inference where prompts, weights and outputs are claimed to
be hidden from the cloud provider, model provider and NEAR itself.

## Architecture summary

- **Private LLM nodes:** 8x NVIDIA H200, TDX-enabled CPUs, running a
  Private-ML-SDK for secure execution, attestation and signing.
- **LLM Gateway** (`cloud-api.near.ai`): handles model registration,
  routing, attestation-report storage, API keys; itself runs in a TEE.
- **Verification:** each TEE emits evidence; gateway TLS attestation binds
  the connection endpoint to the attestation report; responses can be
  signed by an attested signer. Optional client-side E2EE.
- dstack (see `/systems/phala-dstack.md`) lists NEAR AI as a production
  user (claimed by the dstack repo).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None cited; **inferred** link to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md`.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| CPU TEE | Intel TDX | NEAR AI docs |
| GPU TEE | NVIDIA confidential computing (H200) | NEAR AI docs |
| Response verification | Optional signed responses | NEAR AI docs |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Each TEE emits evidence; gateway TLS attestation binds the endpoint; responses can be signed by an attested signer | NEAR AI docs, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Intel TDX CPUs and NVIDIA H200 confidential GPUs; the docs call attestation "evidence, not a guarantee" | NEAR AI docs, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Prompts, weights and outputs claimed hidden from cloud, model provider and NEAR; optional E2EE | NEAR AI docs, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | NEAR AI docs, inferred link |
| Maturity | LIVE | Documented API; listed as a production user by the dstack repo (self-reported) | NEAR AI docs + dstack README, inferred |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- Direct completions endpoints skip the gateway, are experimental, and
  have known verification limits.
- Unsigned responses are not response-verified; TLS alone protects
  transit only.
- The docs state attestation is "evidence, not a guarantee"; strong
  wording ("technically impossible") is unsupported by audits or
  performance figures on the page.

FILE: systems/nillion.md

---
name: Nillion
field: Secure MPC for ML
category: private-compute
foundation: foundations/mpc-ml.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded

---

# Nillion

## What it does

Nillion is a decentralized network for storing and computing on encrypted
("blind") data without ever reconstructing the plaintext on any single
node. Data is split and distributed across independent nodes; computation
happens directly on the shares via secure multi-party computation (MPC),
and only the final result is reassembled.

## Architecture summary

- **Nil Message Compute (NMC)** is Nillion's branding for its MPC layer.
  It combines **One-Time Masking (OTM)** with **Linear Secret Sharing
  (LSS)** so that a network of nodes can jointly store and process
  confidential data with information-theoretic security (unconditionally
  secure, not just computationally hard to break).
- The production MPC protocol built on top of this is internally called
  **Curl**, extended from LSSS to efficiently support non-linear
  operations (division, square roots, trig, logs) that plain linear
  secret sharing can't do without extra machinery.
- In 2026 Nillion migrated its base chain from Cosmos to Ethereum,
  launching a new L1 called **Blacklight** (mainnet live 2026-10-05).
  Node operators stake NIL (minimum 70,000 NIL) to run nodes and verify
  computations. The original Cosmos-based L2 is being wound down, with
  users told to bridge assets to the new L1.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Paper:** "Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in
Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase"
— Miguel de Vega (Nillion), Andrei Lapets (Reity), Stanisław Jarecki
(UC Irvine), Wicher Malten (Nillion), Mehmet Ugurbil (Nillion), Wyatt
Howe (UCLA).
PDF: https://nillion.pub/sum-of-products-lsss-non-interactive.pdf
(originally posted to IACR ePrint as 2023/1740, later withdrawn from
ePrint but mirrored on Nillion's own site).

**Grounding source:** Nillion's own team announced this paper directly
as the basis for their non-interactive MPC protocol for non-linear
computation — see "Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol
for Non-Linear Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479)
and the MPC Alliance's coverage of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six authors are Nillion staff, so this is effectively
Nillion publishing its own core protocol paper — about as direct a
grounding as this kind of claim can get.

**How it's used:** the paper's contribution — evaluating arithmetic
sum-of-products expressions (which covers the multiplications needed
for non-linear ops) within LSSS using a preprocessing phase instead of
interactive communication during computation — is the specific technique
that lets Curl/NMC do non-linear math without the usual back-and-forth
communication overhead of classic MPC protocols.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Underlying primitive | One-Time Masking + Linear Secret Sharing (LSS) | Nillion docs/marketing materials, cross-confirmed across multiple sources |
| Security model | Information-theoretic (unconditional) for the core LSS layer | Nillion technical articles |
| Core protocol name | Curl (non-interactive MPC extension over LSSS) | Nillion Medium post, MPC Alliance coverage |
| Base chain | Ethereum L1 ("Blacklight", launched 2026-10-05); migrated from Cosmos | TradingView/CoinMarketCal news, chain migration coverage |
| Node staking requirement | Minimum 70,000 NIL per node | Blacklight L1 launch coverage |
| Maturity | Mainnet live; L2 (prior Cosmos-based network) being sunset in 2026 | TokenPost, Bitget coverage of L2 shutdown |
| Reported uptime | 100% over trailing 90 days (as reported, not independently verified) | status.nillion.com |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NOT COVERED | Node operators stake NIL to run nodes and verify computations; the verification mechanism isn't described | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Trust rests on | MATH | Information-theoretic (unconditional) security for the core linear-secret-sharing layer | Nillion technical articles |
| Confidentiality | CRYPTOGRAPHIC | Data is secret-shared across nodes and computed on via MPC; plaintext is never reconstructed on one node | Nillion docs, cross-confirmed |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Sum-of-products in LSSS paper, four of six authors at Nillion; withdrawn from ePrint | Nillion Medium post + MPC Alliance coverage, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Blacklight mainnet live 2026-10-05; the prior Cosmos-based L2 is being sunset | TokenPost, Bitget coverage |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Blacklight, a new L1 reported as an Ethereum L1; migrated from Cosmos | TradingView/CoinMarketCal news |

## Known limitations

- The specific foundational paper above was **withdrawn from IACR ePrint**
  (official listing shows 2023/1740 withdrawn 2024-06-28); the only
  available copy is now self-hosted by Nillion at nillion.pub. Worth
  tracking why it was withdrawn — could be a correction, a priority
  dispute, or something more substantive. Flagged here as an open
  question rather than resolved.
- Nillion markets both MPC and homomorphic-encryption-style techniques
  under the "blind computation" umbrella; some public-facing material
  blurs which specific guarantee (information-theoretic MPC vs.
  computationally-secure HE) applies to which product surface. Treat
  marketing claims about "which crypto is doing the work" with caution
  until cross-checked against the underlying protocol docs.
- Mid-2026 chain migration (Cosmos → Ethereum L1) and L2 shutdown is
  recent and operationally disruptive — a useful thing to watch for
  whether it introduces new trust assumptions (e.g. bridge security)
  not present in the original MPC design.

---

# Nous Research — Psyche

## What it does

Psyche is Nous Research's network for training large language models
using compute contributed from geographically dispersed, heterogeneous
machines across the internet, rather than a single co-located cluster.
It targets the bandwidth bottleneck that normally makes training over
consumer/Ethernet-class links impractical.

## Architecture summary

- Built on **DisTrO** (Distributed Training Over-the-Internet), Nous's
  in-house distributed optimizer stack, which in turn builds on **DeMo**
  (Decoupled Momentum Optimization), Nous's earlier optimizer paper.
  Nous's own Psyche page states directly: *"Building on DisTrO and its
  predecessor DeMo, Psyche reduces data transfer by several orders of
  magnitude."* ([nousresearch.com/nous-psyche](https://nousresearch.com/nous-psyche))
- Mechanism: decouples local momentum updates, applies a fast
  orthonormal transform (DCT) plus top-k sparsification, and reuses the
  momentum buffer as error feedback — described by Nous as compressing
  gradient communication the way JPEG compresses an image.
- Coordination layer runs on **Solana**: a smart-contract coordinator
  stores run metadata, handles state transitions, supplies randomness
  for node assignment, and acts as the synchronization authority across
  participants. Chosen specifically for fault-tolerance and censorship
  resistance, per Nous's own description.
- Largest known run to date: a 40B-parameter pretraining run on the
  testnet (May 2025), described by Nous as the largest internet-distributed
  pretraining run at the time.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

See [foundations/distributed-optimization.md](../foundations/distributed-optimization.md)
for the seed paper. Grounding is direct and strong: DeMo
(arXiv:2411.19870) is authored by Nous Research staff themselves (Bowen
Peng, Jeffrey Quesnelle, Diederik P. Kingma), and Psyche's own
documentation explicitly names both DisTrO and DeMo as what it's built
on — not an inferred or two-hop connection.

This is a **distinct lineage** from `foundations/decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, used for Gensyn): that paper addresses verifying
that training happened as claimed; DeMo/DisTrO addresses a different
problem — making distributed optimization communication-efficient
enough to train over the open internet at all. Same broad field,
genuinely different citation lineage, hence a separate foundations file
rather than reusing Gensyn's.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Core technique | DeMo (momentum decomposition) + DisTrO (compression/sync runtime) | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |
| Reported communication reduction | DeMo: up to 85x less data per GPU than AdamW-DDP (arXiv:2411.19870); Psyche: "several orders of magnitude" per Nous | arXiv:2411.19870 + Nous's own page, grounded |
| Coordination/trust layer | Solana smart contract (metadata, state transitions, randomness, sync authority) | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |
| Verification mechanism | **Not solved** — Nous states a theoretical model exists but "a practical implementation is still an open problem" | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |
| Maturity | No formal mainnet as of this check; Nous explicitly avoids using the term and describes current operation as a post-testnet phase, not a graduation | Search aggregation across Nous's own Sept. 2025 post and docs; node/participant counts not independently verifiable |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NONE FOUND | Nous: a practical verification implementation "is still an open problem" | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | Compute contributors; Solana coordinates the run, but nothing yet verifies their updates | Classification inferred from the Verification mechanism row |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | DeMo (arXiv 2411.19870), by Nous Research staff | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |
| Maturity | PREVIEW | No formal mainnet; a post-testnet phase; 40B-parameter testnet run in May 2025 | Search aggregation across Nous's own post and docs |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Solana smart-contract coordinator (metadata, state, randomness, sync) | nousresearch.com/nous-psyche, grounded |

## Known limitations

- **Verification is explicitly unsolved.** Nous's own materials state
  this plainly rather than claiming a solution: floating-point
  non-determinism accumulates across billions of operations, DisTrO's
  compression introduces further cross-node variability, and bitwise
  verification is described as "difficult (but not impossible)." There
  is no deployed mechanism analogous to Gensyn's RepOps/bisection game
  for this network as of this check.
- The "balance problem" — how much cross-node divergence is acceptable
  before it could hide an attacker's influence — is described by Nous
  as an open empirical question, not yet answered.
- Network scale (node/participant counts) is not independently
  verifiable from public sources at this time.

FILE: systems/nvidia-confidential-computing.md
========================================================================

---
name: NVIDIA Confidential Computing (H100/H200/Blackwell)
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
category: private-compute
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (standards lineage); grounded (performance, independent third-party source)
website: "https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-on-h100-gpus-for-secure-and-trustworthy-ai/"
---

## What it does

Lets a cloud tenant run AI inference/training on a GPU while keeping both
the model weights and the input data encrypted in GPU memory and
protected from the cloud operator, the hypervisor, and other tenants —
extended from CPU confidential computing (already common for general
workloads) to the GPU itself, which previously sat outside the trust
boundary entirely.

## Architecture summary

- The H100 (GA April 2024) is, per NVIDIA's own developer blog, "the
  world's first native Confidential Computing GPU." Confidential mode
  ("CC-On") anchors a hardware root of trust on-die; secure boot ensures
  only verified firmware runs.
- **Attestation chain**: the GPU driver uses **SPDM** (Security Protocol
  and Data Model) for session establishment, producing a cryptographically
  signed attestation report an external verifier can check before trusting
  the GPU's state.
  ([developer.nvidia.com](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-on-h100-gpus-for-secure-and-trustworthy-ai/))
- **Does not implement a standalone GPU TEE** — it extends an existing
  *CPU* TEE's trust boundary to include the GPU. Per NVIDIA's own blog,
  it requires a CPU TEE already in place: AMD Genoa/Milan with
  **SEV-SNP** enabled, or Intel Sapphire Rapids with **TDX**. The GPU's
  DMA engine encrypts CPU↔GPU data transfer (AES-GCM-256) so the data
  stays encrypted across that boundary.
  ([developer.nvidia.com](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/confidential-computing-on-h100-gpus-for-secure-and-trustworthy-ai/))
- Definition of "confidential computing" used throughout NVIDIA's own
  material is explicitly attributed to the **Confidential Computing
  Consortium** (an industry body, not an academic source):
  "protection of data in use by performing computation in a
  hardware-based, attested trusted execution environment (TEE), per the
  Confidential Computing Consortium."

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No single academic seed paper — the grounding here is a set of named
industry standards, not a citation chain.** NVIDIA's own material cites:

- **SPDM** (DMTF's Security Protocol and Data Model) — the attestation
  protocol used for the GPU's chain of trust.
- **Confidential Computing Consortium**'s definition of confidential
  computing — the threat model NVIDIA's design targets.
- **AMD SEV-SNP** and **Intel TDX** — the CPU TEE technologies the GPU's
  trust boundary is extended from; NVIDIA's confidential mode has no
  independent trust root of its own at the CPU level, it depends on one
  of these already being active.

This repo's `foundations/` files assume an academic-paper-shaped seed
citation (paper, authors, year, venue). Forcing that shape onto an
industry-standards lineage would misrepresent what's actually being
cited, so no `foundations/` file was created for this entry — document
the standards directly here instead, per the repo's existing rule to
flag weak/absent academic grounding rather than invent it. Worth
checking later whether the Apple Private Cloud Compute entry (also TEE
based) has the same shape — if so, both entries documenting "standards,
not papers" directly is the right pattern, not a shared paper citation.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Attestation protocol | SPDM (DMTF standard) | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Trust model | Extends an existing CPU TEE (AMD SEV-SNP or Intel TDX) — no independent GPU-only trust root | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| CPU TEE dependency | Requires AMD Genoa/Milan+SEV-SNP or Intel Sapphire Rapids+TDX already active on the host | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Data-in-transit protection | AES-GCM-256 on the GPU's DMA engine for CPU↔GPU transfer | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Hardware availability | H100 (GA April 2024), extended in later generations (H200/Blackwell) | NVIDIA developer blog + industry reporting, grounded |
| Performance overhead | Independent study (arXiv 2505.16501): confidential mode shows 20–30% higher latency, 45–70% lower throughput, ~50% lower GPU utilization vs. non-confidential mode, attributed mainly to encrypt/decrypt overhead when loading models | [arXiv:2505.16501](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.16501), grounded (independent third-party measurement, not NVIDIA's own figure) |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | SPDM-signed attestation report an external verifier checks before trusting the GPU's state | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | NVIDIA's on-die root of trust plus the host's CPU TEE (SEV-SNP or TDX); no GPU-only trust root | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Weights and inputs encrypted in GPU memory; AES-GCM-256 on CPU-GPU transfers | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Lineage | STANDARDS | SPDM, the Confidential Computing Consortium's definition, SEV-SNP/TDX; no academic paper | NVIDIA developer blog, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | H100 GA April 2024, extended in H200/Blackwell; 20-30% higher latency in confidential mode per an independent study | NVIDIA developer blog + arXiv:2505.16501, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | A hardware feature; no blockchain component | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- Confidential mode's performance cost is substantial per the independent
  study above — this is a real adoption barrier for latency-sensitive
  inference, not a marketing footnote.
- Trust still partially rests on the CPU vendor's TEE implementation
  (SEV-SNP/TDX) and its own attestation guarantees — a GPU-level
  vulnerability in NVIDIA's implementation isn't the only thing that
  could break the model; a flaw in the underlying CPU TEE would too.
- This entry did not independently verify Blackwell-generation-specific
  changes to the attestation chain — flagged as an open follow-up.

---
name: Oasis (Sapphire / ROFL)

# Oasis (Sapphire / ROFL)

## What it does

**Sapphire** is an EVM-compatible chain with encrypted transactions and
confidential smart contracts. **ROFL** (Runtime Off-Chain Logic) runs
apps in TEEs on Oasis nodes, managed by Sapphire.

## Architecture summary

- ROFL apps ship as Docker-like containers or single executables,
  depending on the TCB and threat model wanted.
- Permissionless node pool for registration, deployment and billing; a
  built-in Key Management Service derives and stores secrets inside the TEE.
- Sapphire contracts can verify the origin of ROFL transactions.
- AI examples: a private Telegram bot running an Ollama LLM inside ROFL;
  "provable AI learning" and trustless-agent use cases listed.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None cited. **Inferred** link to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md`.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| TEE | Intel SGX / TDX | Oasis ROFL docs |
| Key management | Built-in KMS in TEE | Oasis ROFL docs |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | ROFL apps run in TEEs; Sapphire contracts can verify the origin of ROFL transactions; attestation details unread | Oasis ROFL docs overview, inferred |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Intel SGX / TDX, with a key management service inside the TEE | Oasis ROFL docs, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Encrypted transactions and confidential contracts (Sapphire); TEE-hosted apps (ROFL) | Oasis docs overview, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | Oasis docs, inferred link |
| Maturity | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Sapphire, an EVM-compatible confidential chain | Oasis docs overview, grounded |

## Known limitations

- Overview page gives no attestation details, token/billing model, or
  limitations; read the attestation docs before raising confidence.
- GPU-based inference was not covered by the page (the examples are
  CPU-scale).

FILE: systems/ocean-protocol.md

---
name: Ocean Protocol
field: AI data marketplace / provenance
category: ownership
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (architecture); no academic lineage found for core privacy mechanism
website: "https://oceanprotocol.com"
---

## What it does

Ocean Protocol is a Web3 data marketplace: data owners publish datasets as
NFTs (ERC-721) with access rights sold as datatokens (ERC-20), and buyers
can either download data they've licensed or — via Compute-to-Data (C2D)
— run an approved algorithm against a dataset without the dataset ever
leaving the owner's infrastructure, so only the computation's output is
exposed, not the raw data.

## Architecture summary

- **Data NFTs + datatokens**: the data NFT represents the underlying IP;
  datatokens are per-asset ERC-20 access-right tokens. Smart contracts for
  publishing, pricing, and access control run on Ethereum mainnet; Ocean
  is also deployed across Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Energy Web Chain,
  Optimism, and Moonriver.
  ([docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks](https://docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks))
- **Compute-to-Data (C2D) privacy mechanism**: per Ocean's own
  architecture docs, privacy comes from **process isolation, not
  cryptography**. Each job runs in a dedicated, ephemeral Kubernetes pod
  that loads the dataset and algorithm, executes, publishes the result,
  then deletes the dataset, algorithm, and itself.
  ([docs.oceanprotocol.com/developers/compute-to-data/compute-to-data-architecture](https://docs.oceanprotocol.com/developers/compute-to-data/compute-to-data-architecture))
  Components: **Ocean Provider** (credentials/access control),
  **Operator Service** (HTTP API, workflow orchestration),
  **Operator Engine** (Kubernetes-backed execution).
- **Oasis Sapphire deployment**: Ocean's "Predictoor" product specifically
  is deployed on Oasis Sapphire mainnet, which *is* a confidential
  (TEE-based) EVM. This is a genuinely cryptographic/hardware-confidential
  privacy mechanism — but per Ocean's own docs, this Sapphire deployment
  does not currently support `ocean.js`, `ocean.py`, or Ocean Market, i.e.
  it isn't the mechanism behind the core data-marketplace/C2D product
  described above. Don't conflate the two.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No academic paper found that Ocean's own docs cite for the C2D privacy
mechanism itself.** Checked the C2D architecture page and the technical
whitepaper search results directly: the architecture is described
operationally (isolated Kubernetes pods, ephemeral execution) with no
citation to a specific academic paper, cryptographic primitive, or formal
security proof for *why* this gives the privacy property claimed. This is
the Bittensor-style situation — rather than force a citation, this is
flagged as **inferred/not grounded**: C2D is better described as an
engineering pattern (sandboxed compute-near-data) than as an
implementation of a specific cited cryptographic scheme.

No new `foundations/` file created — there's nothing to seed it with that
would survive the same source-checking bar used elsewhere in this repo.
If Ocean's team ever publishes a paper specifically justifying C2D's
security properties, revisit this.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Privacy mechanism | Process/container isolation (ephemeral Kubernetes pods) — **not** cryptographic (MPC/FHE/ZK) | Ocean C2D architecture docs, grounded |
| Cryptographic confidential-compute option | Exists only for the separate Predictoor product on Oasis Sapphire (TEE-based); not used by core C2D/Ocean Market | docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks + Oasis partnership announcements, grounded |
| Data representation | Data NFT (ERC-721) + per-asset datatoken (ERC-20) | Ocean docs, grounded |
| Base chain(s) | Ethereum mainnet (core contracts) + Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Energy Web Chain, Optimism, Moonriver, Oasis Sapphire (Predictoor only) | docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks, grounded |
| Maturity | Actively maintained; ocean-node v1.0.3 (Mar 2026), ocean.js v6.0.0 (Feb 2026) | repo release history via search, inferred-from-aggregation not primary-source-verified this pass |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NONE FOUND | A buyer has no cryptographic proof the algorithm ran only against the claimed dataset | Ocean C2D architecture docs, grounded |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | The data owner's Kubernetes infrastructure, or a provider they trust | Ocean C2D architecture docs, grounded |
| Confidentiality | ISOLATION | Compute-to-Data runs in an ephemeral pod; raw data never leaves the owner. Not cryptographic (TEE only for the separate Predictoor product) | Ocean C2D architecture docs, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited for the C2D privacy mechanism | Direct check of C2D docs + whitepaper search, grounded (as a negative finding) |
| Maturity | LIVE | Actively maintained; ocean-node v1.0.3 (Mar 2026), ocean.js v6.0.0 (Feb 2026) | Release history via search, inferred-from-aggregation |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Ethereum mainnet core contracts, plus Polygon, BNB Smart Chain, Energy Web, Optimism, Moonriver | docs.oceanprotocol.com/discover/networks, grounded |

## Known limitations

- The core privacy claim ("your data never leaves your infrastructure")
  rests on trusting the isolation of a Kubernetes pod operated by the
  data owner's own infrastructure (or a provider they trust), not on a
  cryptographic guarantee independently verifiable by the buyer. A buyer
  has no cryptographic proof that the algorithm actually ran only against
  the claimed dataset, or that the pod wasn't tampered with — this is a
  materially weaker trust model than the MPC/FHE/ZK-based systems
  elsewhere in this repo, and should not be described as "privacy-
  preserving" in the same sense as those.
- The one part of Ocean's stack with real cryptographic/hardware backing
  (Oasis Sapphire's TEE-based confidential EVM) is scoped to a single
  product (Predictoor) and explicitly not integrated with the main
  data-marketplace tooling as of this check — worth re-checking if that
  changes.
- Maturity/release claims above came from secondary aggregation during
  this research pass, not a primary-source changelog read — treat as
  approximate.

---
name: Olas (formerly Autonolas)
field: Decentralized AI agent / marketplace protocols
category: agents
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (architecture); no formal academic lineage found (see below)

# Olas (formerly Autonolas)

## What it does

Olas is an open-source stack plus on-chain protocol for building, running,
and monetizing "agent services" — groups of independent off-chain programs
(agents) that coordinate to perform a task (e.g. DAO treasury management,
custom oracles, keeper bots). The blockchain layer registers and secures
these services and provides the economic incentive for developers to build
and compose reusable agent components.

## Architecture summary

Per Olas's own developer docs and whitepaper, the stack has four parts:

- **Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) architecture** — an agent service is composed
  of independently-developed code components combined via software
  composition.
- **State-Minimized Consensus Gadgets** — a lightweight consensus mechanism
  so that a group of agent instances running the same service can agree on
  shared state without requiring full blockchain-level consensus for every
  interaction.
- **Agent Communication Network (ACN)** — a distributed hash table (DHT)
  that maps an agent's wallet address to its current network location, so
  agents can find and message each other without a central directory.
  ([stack.olas.network/open-aea/acn](https://stack.olas.network/open-aea/acn/))
- **On-chain protocol** — smart contracts that register agents, agent
  "blueprints," and components as NFTs, and handle the incentive/reward
  mechanism for composing them.
  ([olas.network whitepaper](https://olas.network/documents/whitepaper/Whitepaper%20v1.0.pdf))

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No formal academic foundational paper found** — flagged explicitly rather
than forced, following this repo's grounding rule.

- The ACN's own documentation describes it as a DHT with "consistent
  hashing" and "structured overlays" but does **not** cite a specific
  academic DHT paper (e.g. Kademlia / Maymounkov & Mazières) by name,
  confirmed by direct inspection of the ACN docs page.
- The whitepaper's own citations, per visible excerpts, are economic/
  composability essays rather than peer-reviewed CS or cryptography papers:
  a Vitalik Buterin article, Carlota Perez's work on technological
  revolutions, Tim Wu, a Placeholder VC investment thesis, and Jesse
  Walden's essay "4 eras of blockchain computing: degrees of
  composability." These ground Olas's *economic* thesis (why composable,
  incentivized software components matter), not its *technical* mechanism.
  The full PDF could not be parsed for a complete references list in this
  pass (binary/compressed text layer, no local PDF-text tool available) —
  this is based on visible search-result excerpts, not a full read: treat
  as partial evidence, not a complete citation audit.

This is the same pattern seen with Bittensor: real, working architecture,
but the public-facing academic grounding is thin-to-absent for the core
technical mechanism. No `foundations/` file created for this entry, per
the repo's rule to skip one when there's nothing real to cite.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Coordination mechanism | Off-chain multi-agent system + on-chain service registry | olas.network whitepaper, docs.olas.network — grounded |
| Agent discovery | ACN (DHT mapping wallet address → network location) | stack.olas.network/open-aea/acn — grounded |
| Consensus | "State-minimized consensus gadgets" for shared state among agent instances | Olas whitepaper summary (via search excerpt) — grounded but not independently verified in full text |
| On-chain registration | Agents/components/blueprints registered as NFTs | olas.network whitepaper — grounded |
| Base chain(s) | Deployed on multiple smart-contract chains (not single-chain) | docs.olas.network — grounded, specific chain list not verified this pass |
| Maturity | Active, cites >9.9M agent-to-agent (A2A) transactions as of a 2026 blog post | olas.network blog ("Olas: The 2021 Origin Story...") — grounded but self-reported, not independently audited |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | CONSENSUS | Several instances of an agent service agree on shared state via consensus gadgets | Olas whitepaper summary, full text not verified; classification inferred |
| Trust rests on | NOT COVERED | The fault threshold of the consensus gadgets isn't stated | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No formal paper: the ACN DHT cites no DHT paper; whitepaper citations are economic essays | ACN docs + whitepaper excerpts, grounded (partial evidence) |
| Maturity | LIVE | Active; more than 9.9M agent-to-agent transactions, self-reported | olas.network blog, self-reported |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Multiple smart-contract chains; agents and components registered as NFTs | docs.olas.network, grounded; chain list not verified |

## Known limitations

- No independently verified academic grounding for the ACN's DHT design or
  the consensus-gadget mechanism — these may be sound engineering without
  being novel research, but that distinction isn't established here.
- The whitepaper's full PDF was not fully machine-readable in this research
  pass; the citation list above is based on partial search-result excerpts,
  not a complete read. Worth a follow-up pass with a proper PDF-text tool.
- Self-reported transaction-volume figures (9.9M A2A transactions) were not
  cross-checked against independent on-chain data.

# Opacus

## What it does

A library for training PyTorch models with differential privacy,
requiring minimal code changes (`make_private()` with `noise_multiplier`
and `max_grad_norm`, which are DP-SGD parameters).

## Architecture summary

- Cites its technical report (Yousefpour et al., arXiv:2109.12298), Fast
  Gradient Clipping (2009.03106) and Ghost Clipping (2110.05679, added
  Aug 2024), and LoRA support (Dec 2024 tutorial).
- Under the `meta-pytorch` GitHub org; Apache-2.0; about 2k stars.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

The README does not cite Abadi et al. Link to
`foundations/differential-privacy.md` is **inferred** from the DP-SGD
parameters.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Guarantee | (epsilon, delta)-DP via DP-SGD | README parameters |
| Overhead | "little impact" (project's own claim) | README |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Trust rests on | MATH | DP's guarantee is mathematical, given the noise and clipping parameters chosen | README parameters; classification inferred |
| Confidentiality | DIFFERENTIAL PRIVACY | (epsilon, delta)-DP via DP-SGD; limits what the trained model reveals, not data during training | README, grounded |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Cites its own technical report (arXiv 2109.12298); the link to Abadi et al.'s DP-SGD is inferred | README, grounded; foundation link inferred |
| Maturity | LIVE | Library under meta-pytorch, Apache-2.0; latest dated README updates are from 2024 | README, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | — | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- DP protects what the trained model reveals, not data during training.
- Most recent dated README updates are from 2024; maintenance cadence
  was not checked beyond that.

---
name: OpenLedger

last_updated: 2026-10-27

# OpenLedger

## What it does

A blockchain for AI data attribution: users upload data to shared
"datanets"; developers train models on them; a "Proof of Attribution"
system records lineage of datasets, models and agents on-chain so outputs
trace to contributors and payouts route through smart contracts.

## Architecture summary

- OPEN mainnet launched (The Block article dated 2025-11-18); $8M seed
  led by Polychain Capital and Borderless Capital (July 2024 report).
  The article does not state the chain architecture.
- "Payable AI": datanets collect datasets; payments route through smart
  contracts per on-chain attribution trails.
- 2026 roadmap describes a nine-layer platform (company-paid announcement,
  limited independent validation).
- Joint licensed-training standard with Story Protocol (2026-01-29); see
  `/systems/story-protocol.md`.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None found. Foundation intentionally empty; how "Proof of Attribution"
works technically was not found in the sources read.

# OpenMined (PySyft)

## What it does

An open-source Python library for "data science on data that remains in
someone else's server": the data owner keeps data in place and approves
what leaves.

## Architecture summary

- Current line is `syft` 0.10+ (README: successor to `syft-client`;
  legacy <=0.9 users pin `syft<0.10`).
- Data scientists submit Python jobs; owners approve; jobs run in a
  sandboxed virtual environment and only approved outputs are returned.
- Transport via existing cloud storage (e.g. Google Drive) or P2P like
  WebRTC. An enclave section exists in the repo; maturity unknown.
- Apache-2.0.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None cited. Older surveys describe PySyft as focused on SMPC and HE, but
the current README doesn't mention them or differential privacy, so no
lineage is asserted; foundation intentionally empty.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Trust model | Owner-approved job execution | README |
| Differential privacy | Not mentioned in README | README |

## Comparison axes

| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | The data owner's review of submitted code and outputs, not cryptography | README, grounded |
| Confidentiality | ISOLATION | Data stays on the owner's server; jobs run in a sandbox and only approved outputs are returned | README, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | The current README cites no SMPC, HE or DP lineage | README, grounded (as a negative finding) |
| Maturity | NOT COVERED | Current line is syft 0.10+; no scale or audit information | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | — | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- The current model is approval-based, so protection depends on owner
  review of code and outputs rather than cryptography.
- Setup friction (Google OAuth token per role); no performance, scale or
  audit information on the page.

---
name: ORA Protocol
field: Optimistic on-chain AI verification
category: verifiable-inference
foundation: foundations/optimistic-ml.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded
website: "https://docs.ora.io"
---

# ORA Protocol

## What it does

ORA runs a verifiable AI oracle: large ML models (LLaMA, Stable
Diffusion, DeepSeek, Mistral, Qwen) execute off-chain, and smart
contracts on Ethereum and several L2s can trust the result without
re-running the model themselves, through an optimistic dispute
mechanism rather than a cryptographic proof. Its flagship product is
the On-Chain AI Oracle (OAO).

## Architecture summary

- **opML (Optimistic Machine Learning)** — ORA's own mechanism (see
  foundations entry) for getting ML inference results trusted on-chain
  without the cost of zkML's proof generation. Results are accepted
  optimistically; a challenge window lets any validator dispute a
  result, triggering a bisection game that narrows the disagreement to
  one computation step, resolved on-chain by a **Fraud Proof VM
  (FPVM)**.
- **System components**: the opML contract (handles fraud proofs and
  challenges), the AIOracle contract (connects opML nodes to on-chain
  callers), user contracts (initiate inference requests), and ORA Nodes
  running the **Tora client** (execute inference off-chain, submit or
  validate results).
- Trust model is "AnyTrust": security holds as long as at least one
  honest, economically incentivized validator is watching and willing
  to dispute within the challenge window — not a cryptographic
  guarantee, an economic/game-theoretic one.
- Founded Sept. 2022 as "Hyper Oracle"; chief scientist Cathie So is an
  ex-Ethereum Foundation zkML researcher, which is also why ORA's docs
  explicitly position opML *against* zkML (cost/scale trade-off) rather
  than treating them as unrelated.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

See [foundations/optimistic-ml.md](../foundations/optimistic-ml.md) —
the opML paper (arXiv 2401.17555) is co-authored by ORA's own
co-founder and chief scientist, making this a direct, team's-own-paper
grounding, not an inferred lineage.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Verification mechanism | Optimistic acceptance + bisection-game fraud proof (Fraud Proof VM) | opML paper; ORA docs via search, grounded |
| Trust model | AnyTrust — one honest, incentivized validator sufficient | ORA docs summary (iq.wiki), grounded |
| Cryptographic guarantee | None — economic/game-theoretic, not a proof of correctness | opML paper, grounded |
| Deployed chains | Ethereum mainnet (launched ~Mar 2024), Optimism, Base, Arbitrum (as of 2026 reporting) | Blockworks/Bitget launch coverage + 2026 search aggregation — chain list for 2026 not independently verified against ORA's own current docs this pass |
| Supported models (reported) | LLaMA/LLaMA2/LLaMA3, Stable Diffusion, DeepSeek, Mistral, Qwen, Grok (via integration) | Search aggregation — not cross-checked against ORA's current docs this pass |
| Maturity | Live on multiple mainnets since 2024; ORA's own docs site (docs.ora.io) could not be reached directly during this research pass (DNS failure) — findings here rely on search aggregation and third-party summaries (iq.wiki, Blockworks, Bitget), not a direct docs read | Flagged explicitly — recheck against docs.ora.io directly in a future pass |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | DISPUTE GAME | Results accepted optimistically; a challenge triggers a bisection game resolved on-chain by a Fraud Proof VM | opML paper; ORA docs via search, grounded |
| Trust rests on | ONE HONEST PARTY | AnyTrust: one honest, incentivized validator watching within the challenge window | ORA docs summary (iq.wiki), grounded |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | opML paper (arXiv 2401.17555), co-authored by ORA's co-founder and chief scientist | foundations/optimistic-ml.md, grounded |
| Maturity | LIVE | Live on multiple mainnets since 2024; docs.ora.io unreachable this pass | Third-party summaries only (iq.wiki, Blockworks, Bitget), inferred |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Ethereum mainnet, plus Optimism, Base and Arbitrum per 2026 reporting | Launch coverage + 2026 search aggregation, inferred |

## Known limitations

- **Verification pass for this entry relied on secondary sources.**
  `docs.ora.io` did not resolve during this research session (DNS
  lookup failure on every attempt) — every claim above that cites "ORA
  docs" is actually sourced through iq.wiki's summary of those docs or
  other third-party coverage, not a direct fetch. Worth a follow-up
  pass once docs.ora.io is reachable, specifically to confirm the
  current chain-deployment list and challenge-window duration.
- Optimistic/fraud-proof security is weaker than zkML's cryptographic
  guarantee by design — correctness depends on an economically
  rational, watching validator actually showing up within the dispute
  window. A result can finalize as "trusted" during any period with no
  active challenger, even if wrong.
- Challenge-window length (how long a result sits disputable before
  finalizing) was not found/confirmed in this pass — matters for
  latency-sensitive use cases and wasn't independently verified.

# Phala (dstack)

## What it does

Phala describes itself as a decentralized cloud for confidential
computing: apps run in TEEs and the code and hardware can be verified by
remote attestation. Products: Phala Cloud (deploy TEE apps), dstack
(open-source runtime), and GPU TEE for confidential AI.

## Architecture summary

- **dstack** runs Docker Compose workloads in confidential VMs. Components:
  a **Guest Agent** (generates TDX attestation quotes, provisions per-app
  keys, encrypts storage), a **KMS** in its own TEE that verifies quotes
  before releasing keys under policies defined in on-chain smart contracts,
  a **Gateway** (TLS termination, RA-TLS internally), and a **VMM** on
  bare-metal TDX hosts.
- Platforms: bare-metal Intel TDX (production path), AMD SEV-SNP
  (experimental), GCP Confidential VMs, AWS Nitro, and NVIDIA H100 /
  Blackwell confidential GPUs.
- Governance: dstack is a Linux Foundation Confidential Computing
  Consortium project; the repo includes a zkSecurity audit.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

No paper is cited in Phala's docs or the dstack repo. Lineage to
`foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md` is **inferred** from the shared
TEE-attestation mechanism only.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation | Intel TDX CVMs (+ NVIDIA CC GPUs) | dstack README |
| Key release | KMS in TEE, policy on-chain | dstack README |
| Audit | zkSecurity (PDF in repo) | dstack README |
| Production users | OpenRouter, NEAR AI (as claimed by the repo) | dstack README |
| Overhead | ~2-5% CPU for TDX (general claim, not benchmarked on the page) | dstack FAQ |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Guest agent issues TDX quotes; a KMS in its own TEE verifies them before releasing keys | dstack README, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Hardware vendors' attestation; side channels on TDX/SEV are out of scope | dstack README, grounded |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Workloads in confidential VMs (Intel TDX) with NVIDIA confidential GPUs | dstack README, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | dstack README, inferred link |
| Maturity | LIVE | Phala Cloud product; production users OpenRouter and NEAR AI (self-reported); zkSecurity audit in repo | dstack README, grounded |
| On-chain | OPEN QUESTION | Key-release policies live in on-chain contracts; which chain, and the network-level story, weren't verified | dstack README; network side unverified, inferred |

## Known limitations

- Trust roots in hardware vendors' attestation; side-channel attacks on
  TDX/SEV are out of scope of dstack's guarantees.
- Phala's docs index gave no token, chain, or limitations details; the
  network-level (non-dstack) story was not verified in this pass.
- Production users listed are self-reported by the repo.

---
name: Pluralis Research
field: Decentralized / distributed training
category: training
foundation: foundations/model-parallel-decentralized-training.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (core technique); inferred (some matrix cells)
