# Pluralis Research

## What it does

Pluralis Research runs **Protocol Learning**: large language models trained
collaboratively across the open internet on heterogeneous, unreliable
consumer/cloud hardware that no single participant fully owns — contrasted
with centralized datacenter training. Their production system for this is
called **Agora**.

## Architecture summary

- **Pipeline parallelism**: each participating device hosts one pipeline
  stage (e.g. one transformer block); multiple devices can replicate a stage
  for redundancy.
- **Data parallelism**, combined with the above, to distribute training
  further across the swarm.
- **Peer-to-peer routing**: participants join/leave dynamically without
  halting training.
- **Subspace Networks** (see Built on, below): the specific compression
  technique that makes cross-device communication cheap enough for this to
  work over consumer internet rather than datacenter interconnects — up to a
  100x reduction in inter-stage communication, by confining activations and
  gradients to a predefined low-dimensional subspace exploiting a recursive
  structure in transformer networks.
- Source: [pluralis.ai/docs](https://pluralis.ai/docs/) (Agora system
  overview).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Paper**: originally titled "Protocol Models: Scaling Decentralized
Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism," since retitled
(as of v3, 2026-07-09) to **"Subspace Networks: Scaling Decentralized
Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism."** Same arXiv ID
throughout: [arxiv.org/abs/2506.01260](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01260).
Authors: Sameera Ramasinghe, Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan, Gil Avraham, Yan Zuo,
Alexander Long — **affiliation explicitly listed as Pluralis Research** in
the paper itself (confirmed via the v1 HTML:
[arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1)).
Accepted at NeurIPS 2025.

**Grounding note**: this is the team's own paper, not a third-party citation
— same tier of grounding as Zama/Stoian et al. or Nillion's Curl paper
elsewhere in this repo (the system's own team publishing the core technique
directly), not a case of the product's docs citing someone else's work. The
title change between versions (Protocol Models → Subspace Networks, same
arXiv ID) was confirmed directly rather than assumed — an initial search hit
returned the old title and could have been reported as current without the
extra check.

**Not the same lineage as** `foundations/decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, arXiv:2103.05633, used by Gensyn) — that paper is about
*verifying* that training happened; this one is about making model-parallel
training communication-efficient enough to run over consumer internet at
all. Different problem, different citation lineage, hence a separate
foundations file rather than reusing the existing one despite the shared
field.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Parallelism approach | Hybrid: pipeline parallelism (one stage per device, replicated for redundancy) + data parallelism | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded |
| Core compression technique | Subspace Networks — up to ~100x inter-stage communication reduction | arXiv:2506.01260, grounded |
| Bandwidth target | Trains over consumer-grade internet (as low as ~80Mbps per search-aggregated reporting of the paper's claims) matching datacenter-connected (100Gbps) convergence | General sourcing of paper claims, **inferred** — recheck exact figures against the paper directly before citing precisely |
| Trust / verification mechanism | Informal points-and-leaderboard system for contributors; **no cryptographic or economic verification layer found** (no blockchain, no token, no dispute/fraud-proof game) | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded (as an absence, not just unconfirmed) |
| Maturity | Research-phase, active: Pluralis-13B run (Sept 2026, 62.4B tokens); prior Pluralis-8B (May 2026, 531.8B tokens) | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded |
| Node0 run (separate practical milestone) | Reported 7.5B-parameter run over ~3 weeks, 300+ participants, 1,642 GPUs | Cross-referenced across Pluralis's own GitHub (PluralisResearch/node0) and third-party coverage — **inferred/not independently re-verified this pass** |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NONE FOUND | Informal points-and-leaderboard; no cryptographic or economic verification layer | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded (as an absence) |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | Contributors, tracked only by points and a leaderboard | Classification inferred from the verification row |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Subspace Networks (arXiv 2506.01260, NeurIPS 2025), by Pluralis authors | arXiv 2506.01260, grounded |
| Maturity | RESEARCH | Research-phase runs: Pluralis-8B (May 2026), Pluralis-13B (Sept 2026) | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | No blockchain and no token | pluralis.ai/docs, grounded |

## Known limitations

- No cryptographic, economic, or formal verification layer for contributor
  honesty as of this check — unlike Gensyn's bisection/dispute game, Pluralis
  currently relies on an informal points/leaderboard system. This is a
  meaningful gap for a "decentralized AI + crypto" framing specifically:
  Pluralis solves the communication-efficiency half of decentralized
  training well, but not the trust/verification half.
- Bandwidth and compression figures above are drawn from aggregated
  reporting of the paper's claims, not independently re-derived from the
  paper's experiments section in this pass — worth a direct read of
  arXiv:2506.01260 before citing specific numbers.
- No blockchain/token component — if a future watch-run finds Pluralis
  adding one, that would be a genuine matrix-impacting change worth a
  companion note.

FILE: systems/prime-intellect.md

---
name: Prime Intellect
field: Decentralized / distributed training
category: training
foundation: foundations/diloco-distributed-training.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (training-framework lineage); inferred (protocol/incentive-layer specifics)
website: "https://www.primeintellect.ai"
---

# Prime Intellect

## What it does

Prime Intellect runs a GPU compute marketplace (50+ data centers, single-GPU
to multi-thousand-GPU clusters) and an open decentralized training stack on
top of it. Its best-known result is INTELLECT-1, the first openly
decentralized-trained 10B-parameter language model, trained across five
countries and three continents on up to 112 H100s running concurrently.

## Architecture summary

- **PRIME framework**: a fault-tolerant distributed training framework for
  unreliable, globally distributed nodes. Core piece is the
  **ElasticDeviceMesh**, which manages a dynamic global process group for
  fault-tolerant internet communication plus local process groups for
  intra-node communication, with live checkpoint recovery.
- PRIME combines **FSDP2** (intra-node sharded data parallelism) with
  **DiLoCo** (inter-node low-communication optimization) in a hybrid
  setup, plus a custom int8 all-reduce, to get a reported ~400x reduction
  in cross-node communication bandwidth versus standard data-parallel
  training.
- In the INTELLECT-1 run, nodes trained independently for ~38 minutes
  between synchronization steps, each sync taking ~1-7 minutes; reported
  compute utilization was 83% across continents and 96% when restricted to
  US-only nodes.
- Separately, Prime Intellect operates a "PI protocol" layer described as
  providing on-chain primitives for trust, collaboration, and collective
  ownership of resulting models by compute/data/code contributors — this
  layer is comparatively thin on technical documentation in what's
  publicly available; treat specifics as inferred, not grounded.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Paper:** "DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language
Models" — Arthur Douillard, Qixuan Feng, Andrei A. Rusu, Rachita
Chhaparia, Yani Donchev, Adhiguna Kuncoro, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Arthur
Szlam, Jiajun Shen (Google DeepMind). arXiv:2311.08105 (Nov 2023).

**Grounding source:** Prime Intellect's own OpenDiLoCo announcement states
directly: *"Introducing OpenDiLoCo, an open-source implementation and
scaling of DeepMind's Distributed Low-Communication (DiLoCo) method,
enabling globally distributed AI model training,"* and separately
describes OpenDiLoCo as *"a reproducible implementation of DeepMind's
DiLoCo experiments."*
([primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco))
This is direct, explicit grounding — not a multi-hop inference.

**How it's used:** DiLoCo's core idea — an inner optimizer (AdamW) doing
many local steps per worker, with an outer optimizer (Nesterov-momentum
SGD) periodically synchronizing pseudo-gradients across workers — is what
lets PRIME's workers train independently for tens of minutes between
syncs. Prime Intellect's own OpenDiLoCo paper (arXiv:2407.07852) extended
this to real multi-continent runs; the INTELLECT-1 technical report
(arXiv:2412.01152) layers FSDP2 and the ElasticDeviceMesh on top of that
same DiLoCo core for the 10B-parameter run.

This is a **distinct lineage** from `foundations/decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, cited by Gensyn): that paper addresses verifying that
training happened as claimed; DiLoCo addresses how to train efficiently
across poorly-connected nodes in the first place. Same field, different
problem, different seed paper — kept as a separate foundations file per
the repo's one-file-per-lineage rule.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Core training algorithm | DiLoCo (local SGD: AdamW inner optimizer + Nesterov-momentum outer optimizer) | DiLoCo paper (arXiv:2311.08105), grounded |
| Framework | PRIME (ElasticDeviceMesh + hybrid FSDP2/DiLoCo + int8 all-reduce) | INTELLECT-1 technical report (arXiv:2412.01152), grounded |
| Communication reduction | ~400x vs. standard data-parallel (PRIME); DiLoCo alone reports ~500x in DeepMind's original benchmarks | OpenDiLoCo blog + DiLoCo paper, grounded |
| Largest public run | INTELLECT-1: 10B params, 1T tokens, up to 112 H100s, 5 countries/3 continents | primeintellect.ai/blog/intellect-1, grounded |
| Compute utilization (INTELLECT-1) | 83% cross-continent, 96% US-only nodes | INTELLECT-1 technical report, grounded |
| Trust/incentive layer | "PI protocol" — described as providing on-chain trust primitives and collective model ownership for contributors | General sourcing (third-party coverage), **inferred** — primary-source technical detail not found in this pass |
| Maturity | Production research lab with a live GPU marketplace; INTELLECT-1 is a completed, published run, not a running mainnet protocol in the Gensyn/Bittensor sense | Inferred from available sourcing |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | OPEN QUESTION | No adversarial verification in the training framework; how the PI protocol verifies contributors wasn't found | Known limitations, open follow-up, inferred |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | INTELLECT-1 ran on known, coordinating participants rather than open, untrusted compute | Known limitations; classification inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | EXTERNAL PAPER | DiLoCo (Google DeepMind, arXiv 2311.08105), reimplemented as OpenDiLoCo | primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco, grounded |
| Maturity | RESEARCH | Completed, published training runs plus a live GPU marketplace; not a running mainnet protocol | Inferred from available sourcing |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | The PI protocol is described as offering on-chain primitives, but no chain is identified | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- The DiLoCo/PRIME technical lineage is solidly grounded; the crypto/
  protocol trust-and-ownership layer is not — this entry did not find
  primary documentation (whitepaper-grade) specifying how compute
  contributors are verified or how ownership stakes are actually computed
  and enforced. Flagged as an open follow-up, not resolved here.
- INTELLECT-1's distributed run involved known, coordinating participants
  rather than fully open/untrusted compute contribution — unlike Gensyn's
  design, there is no visible adversarial-verification mechanism (fraud
  proofs, bisection games) in the training framework itself. Worth
  rechecking if Prime Intellect's protocol layer matures to include one.
- Figures above (utilization %, bandwidth reduction) are self-reported by
  Prime Intellect in their own technical report; no independent
  third-party reproduction of the INTELLECT-1 run's numbers was located in
  this pass.

FILE: systems/render-network.md

---
name: Render Network
field: Decentralized GPU / compute marketplace
category: compute-markets
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: inferred (no academic lineage found; patent citation is billing-related, not verification-related)
website: "https://renderfoundation.com"
---

## What it does

Render Network is a decentralized GPU marketplace: idle GPU capacity from
node operators is matched to rendering jobs (3D/VFX) submitted by
creators, paid in the RENDER token. Historically this is a rendering
network, not an AI network. In December 2025 it launched **Dispersed**,
a separate GPU-compute subnet (approved via governance proposals RNP-019
and RNP-021) explicitly marketed for AI workloads — hosting 600+ AI
models at launch, priced at $1.75/hour. ([Solana Compass: Render Network
Launches Dispersed AI Compute
Platform](https://solanacompass.com/learn/breakpoint-25/product-keynote-render-network-render-network-foundation);
[Render Network Foundation Monthly Report — December
2025](https://rendernetwork.medium.com/render-network-foundation-monthly-report-december-2025-43d956808e3f))

**The AI angle is real but recent and structurally separate from the
core network**, not evidence that the original rendering architecture
was AI-specific. Dispersed is general-purpose decentralized GPU compute
being sold into the AI market, not a cryptographically-verified
AI-inference or AI-training primitive like the other systems tracked in
this repo. Treat it as adjacent infrastructure (compute supply), not a
verifiable-AI system.

## Architecture summary

- **Proof-of-Render (PoR)**: the network's anti-fraud / quality-assurance
  mechanism. A node completes a job and submits cryptographic data plus
  a watermarked preview; the job creator visually and technically
  verifies the output before payment release; other nodes reportedly
  spot-check frames before final settlement. ([Web3@KAIST 2025: Render
  Network — Blockchain meets
  AI](https://web3classdao.github.io/kaist2025/reports/render/); general
  sourcing, not Render's own technical docs — see confidence note below)
- Payment is escrow-based: funds are held until PoR verification
  completes.
- **Dispersed** (the AI subnet) aggregates distributed GPUs into a
  single on-demand compute layer for AI/general-purpose workloads,
  separate from the rendering job-matching logic above.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No academic paper lineage was found.** The official whitepaper
(renderfoundation.com/whitepaper, v4.0, originally 2017, last updated
2023) is a product/vision document, not an academic-citation-style
paper. The only external reference recoverable from the whitepaper PDF
is a Google Patents citation:

- **US9197642B1, "Token-based billing model for server-side rendering
  service"** ([patents.google.com/patent/US9197642B1](https://patents.google.com/patent/US9197642B1/en))
  — this patent is about billing/tokenization for server-side rendering
  delivery, **not** about Proof-of-Render's verification mechanism or
  any cryptographic technique. Cited here for completeness, not as
  grounding for the verification claims above.

The whitepaper PDF was heavily corrupted in automated extraction
(compressed/binary streams), so some content may not have been
recoverable — this entry should be rechecked against a clean copy of
the PDF if someone wants to confirm nothing else was missed. Proof-of-
Render's actual verification mechanics (watermarking, spot-checks,
escrow) are documented through third-party explainers and community
docs, not found quoted directly from Render's own primary technical
documentation in this pass.

No new foundations/ file created — there is nothing to ground it to.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Core use case | GPU rendering marketplace (3D/VFX); AI compute is a newer, separate subnet | renderfoundation.com, Render Foundation Dec 2025 report |
| Verification mechanism | Proof-of-Render — watermarked preview + node spot-checks + escrowed payment | Third-party explainers (Web3@KAIST), **not confirmed against primary docs** |
| AI-specific offering | "Dispersed" compute subnet, governance-approved (RNP-019, RNP-021), launched Dec 2025, 600+ models at $1.75/hr | Solana Compass, Render Foundation Medium report — grounded |
| Base chain | Solana (migrated from Ethereum/Polygon in prior iterations) | General sourcing — recheck if precise chain history matters |
| Maturity | Rendering side long-established (since 2017); AI subnet (Dispersed) is new as of Dec 2025 | Render Foundation's own announcement |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | SPOT CHECK | Proof-of-Render: watermarked preview, creator review and node spot-checks before escrow releases | Third-party explainers (Web3@KAIST), inferred, not confirmed against primary docs |
| Trust rests on | OPERATORS | Node operators, checked by the job creator and other nodes before payment | Third-party explainers, inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | The only external reference is a billing patent, unrelated to verification | Whitepaper v4.0 check, grounded (as a negative finding) |
| Maturity | LIVE | Rendering since 2017; the AI compute subnet (Dispersed) launched Dec 2025 | Render Foundation announcement |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | Solana, after earlier Ethereum/Polygon iterations | General sourcing, inferred |

## Known limitations

- **The "AI" framing should be treated with caution.** Most of what's
  written about Render Network and AI is community/press coverage
  describing Dispersed as a new product layer, not evidence that
  Proof-of-Render or the core rendering protocol has any AI-specific
  cryptographic property. This entry exists in the repo as decentralized
  *compute supply* adjacent to the AI space, not as a verifiable-AI
  system comparable to EZKL, Gensyn, etc.
- Proof-of-Render's exact verification algorithm was not confirmed
  against Render's own primary technical documentation in this pass —
  third-party summaries agree on the shape (watermark + spot-check +
  escrow) but no single authoritative source was fetched cleanly.
- The whitepaper PDF extraction was unreliable (binary corruption) —
  worth a manual recheck if precise claims from it matter later.

FILE: systems/ritual.md
========================================================================

---
name: Ritual
field: On-chain AI inference / verifiable compute
category: verifiable-inference
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (consensus/execution architecture); inferred (several matrix cells); no external academic lineage found for the proof-system layer
website: "https://ritual.net"
---

## What it does

Ritual is a decentralized AI infrastructure protocol connecting Ethereum
smart contracts to a network of off-chain AI compute nodes. Developers
submit inference (or other heavy-compute) tasks; the network executes
them off-chain and settles a verifiable result back on-chain.

## Architecture summary

- **Infernet**: the middleware protocol/SDK connecting Ethereum
  contracts to off-chain compute nodes. The Infernet Node is an
  open-source, lightweight client (github.com/ritual-net/infernet-node)
  that executes arbitrary workload containers and reports results
  on-chain. Reported scale: 8,000+ connected nodes (per Ritual's own
  explainer material — not independently verified against chain data
  this pass).
- **Ritual Chain**: a custom L1 built to support heterogeneous
  computation (AI inference, ZK proof verification, TEE execution,
  scheduled transactions) that standard blockchains can't natively
  handle.
- **Symphony**: Ritual's own consensus/execution research (credited to
  Maryam Bahrani, published on ritual.net's blog, ~April 2026),
  describing "Execution-Aware Consensus and Proposer Disaggregation."
  Its core idea is an **Execute-Once-Verify-Many-Times (EOVMT)** model:
  a staked executor runs the expensive/non-deterministic computation
  once and produces a proof; other nodes verify the proof instead of
  re-executing the computation themselves. Deterministic replication
  stays on the critical consensus path; expensive or non-deterministic
  execution is delegated asynchronously, with proof-based settlement.
- **Proof system is deliberately not fixed.** Ritual's own docs
  describe the protocol as proof-system agnostic: settlement can use a
  ZK proof, a TEE attestation, or both, chosen per application based on
  its security/cost/performance needs — not a single scheme the whole
  network commits to.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**No separate `foundations/` entry created for this system** — explained
here rather than forced:

- The closest thing to a foundational technical paper is **Symphony**
  itself, but it is Ritual's own self-published research (Bahrani,
  ritual.net blog), not an independent external line of academic work
  the way PLONK grounds EZKL/Halo2 or TFHE grounds Zama. Self-grounding
  is documented, not treated as equivalent to external validation.
- Ritual's docs name specific cryptographic primitives — **CKKS**
  (homomorphic encryption), **ECIES**, **EIP-712** — but without pinning
  them to a specific academic citation in what was checked this pass.
  These are standard, well-known schemes; the gap is Ritual's own docs
  not citing a specific paper for them, not that the schemes are
  obscure.
- Because Ritual is explicitly proof-system agnostic (ZK or TEE,
  per-app), there is no single cryptographic lineage analogous to
  "this system is built on paper X" the way the other tracked systems
  are. Forcing a `foundations/` file here would mean picking one
  external paper arbitrarily rather than reflecting how the system
  actually works. If a specific Ritual-deployed application turns out
  to commit to one scheme consistently, that would be the better unit
  to ground, not the protocol as a whole.

## Property matrix

| Property | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Verification mechanism | EOVMT: staked executor computes once, produces a proof (ZK, TEE attestation, or both); validators verify the proof rather than re-executing | Symphony research, Ritual docs |
| Consensus model | Symphony — execution-aware consensus with proposer disaggregation; deterministic work stays on critical path, expensive/non-deterministic work delegated async | ritual.net blog (Bahrani, ~Apr 2026) |
| On-chain integration | Infernet middleware links Ethereum smart contracts to off-chain compute nodes; Ritual also runs its own L1 (Ritual Chain) | docs.ritualfoundation.org, github.com/ritual-net/infernet-node |
| Proof system | Not fixed — ZK proof and/or TEE attestation, chosen per application | docs.ritualfoundation.org, grounded |
| Network scale | 8,000+ connected Infernet nodes (as reported) | Ritual explainer material — community-adjacent source, inferred/unverified count |
| Named crypto primitives | CKKS, ECIES, EIP-712 named in docs | docs.ritualfoundation.org — named but not deeply citation-traced this pass |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PER APP | Staked executor computes once and produces a ZK proof and/or TEE attestation; validators verify it instead of re-executing | Symphony research, Ritual docs |
| Trust rests on | PER APP | Depends on which scheme each application picks: ZK, TEE, both, or potentially neither | docs.ritualfoundation.org, grounded |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | TEE execution is supported and CKKS is named in the docs, but no confidentiality claim is traced | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Symphony is Ritual's own self-published research (ritual.net blog); no external paper | ritual.net blog (Bahrani, ~Apr 2026), grounded |
| Maturity | OPEN QUESTION | 8,000+ Infernet nodes reported; Ritual Chain mainnet status not verified | Ritual explainer material, inferred/unverified |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Ritual Chain (custom L1), plus Infernet linking Ethereum contracts to off-chain nodes | docs.ritualfoundation.org, github.com/ritual-net/infernet-node |

## Known limitations

- "Proof-system agnostic" means the actual security guarantee for any
  given deployed application depends on whether that application
  chose ZK, TEE, both, or (potentially) neither — the protocol-level
  description does not by itself guarantee a specific guarantee for a
  specific app. Check per-application before relying on a claim.
- No external, independently-authored academic paper was found
  grounding the protocol's cryptographic/consensus design — Symphony is
  self-published by the Ritual team. Documented as a confidence gap,
  not papered over.
- Node count (8,000+) and current Ritual Chain mainnet/launch status
  were not independently verified against primary chain data this pass.

# Secret Network

## What it does

A Cosmos-based blockchain for confidential smart contracts: data is
encrypted at rest, in transit and during computation inside TEEs. It now
also offers "Secret AI" and SecretVM confidential virtual machines.

## Architecture summary

- Docs sections reviewed: Intel SGX privacy technology (remote
  attestation, sealing, trusted/untrusted core), encryption key
  management (consensus seed rotation), Secret AI (SubscriptionManager,
  WorkerManager, RewardsManager contracts), and SecretVM.
- **Morpheus integration (2026-08-07):** Morpheus built a TEE Provider so
  Secret's confidential AI models are available through its decentralized
  inference marketplace.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None cited in the pages reviewed. **Inferred** link to
`foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md` (SGX origin).

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| TEE | Intel SGX (L1 contracts); SecretVM for VMs | Secret docs index |
| AI economics | On-chain subscription / worker / rewards contracts | Secret docs index |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Intel SGX remote attestation (doc index only; architecture pages unread) | Secret docs index, inferred |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Intel SGX, which has a record of published side-channel attacks | Secret docs index, inferred |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Data encrypted at rest, in transit and during computation inside TEEs; SecretVM for VMs | Secret docs index |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | Secret docs index, inferred link |
| Maturity | LIVE | Running chain; Secret AI models offered via Morpheus since 2026-08-07 | Partnership post; classification inferred |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Cosmos-based chain for confidential smart contracts | Secret docs index |

## Known limitations

- The architecture pages themselves were not read in this pass; only the
  doc index and the partnership post were. Deepen before relying on detail.
- The partnership post calls the stack "unhackable" with no audit or
  benchmark evidence; treat as marketing.
- SGX has a record of published side-channel attacks; check Secret's own
  post-mortems before concluding anything about current exposure.

FILE: systems/sentient-oml.md
========================================================================

---
name: Sentient (OML)
field: AI model ownership / monetization protocols
category: ownership
foundation: foundations/ai-native-cryptography.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded (core paper); inferred/news-sourced (several matrix cells)
---

## What it does

Sentient is a protocol for publishing open-weight AI models while still giving
the model's owners/contributors enforceable ownership, usage tracking, and a
revenue stream — addressing the problem that a fully open model can normally
be copied and monetized by anyone, with no way to trace or compensate the
original builder.

## Architecture summary

- Built around the **OML (Open, Monetizable, Loyal)** framework: a model
  should be inspectable/open (**Open**), trigger compensation to its owners
  on every call (**Monetizable**), and have misuse/unauthorized use be
  detectable (**Loyal**).
- Four-layer protocol stack: **storage** (immutable/available hosting of the
  model artifact), **distribution** (converting the artifact into OML format),
  **access** (authorizing/tracking each query), **incentive** (routing
  collected fees to builders). (Source: openagi.discourse.group summary of
  the Sentient protocol design, cross-confirmed by multiple secondary
  write-ups — not fetched from a single Sentient primary doc in this pass.)
- Production mechanism is reported as the **"Melange" method** — combining
  model fingerprinting, TEE (trusted execution environment) execution, and
  on-chain contract-based revenue distribution. This is a secondary-source
  characterization (search aggregation), not independently confirmed against
  a primary Sentient doc in this pass — flagged as inferred.
- Chain architecture: designed to be **L1-agnostic / EVM-compatible** rather
  than requiring its own base chain (reported compatible with Ethereum and
  other L1s); no dedicated standalone "Sentient Chain" was found. Sentient's
  own network is referred to as **GRID**.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

**Paper:** "OML: Open, Monetizable, and Loyal AI" — Cheng, Contente, Finch,
Golev, Hayase, Miller, Moshrefi, Nasery, Nailwal, Oh, Tyagi, Viswanath.
IACR ePrint 2024/1573 (received 2024-10-05).
[eprint.iacr.org/2024/1573](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1573)

**Grounding:** this is about as direct as grounding gets — 5 of the 12 listed
authors (Contente, Finch, Golev, Nailwal, Tyagi) are affiliated with
**Sentient Foundation** itself, alongside academic co-authors from Princeton,
University of Washington, and UIUC. This paper is not third-party prior work
Sentient cites — it is Sentient's own team publishing the protocol's
founding paper. The paper introduces "AI-native cryptography" as its core
contribution: cryptographic techniques designed around the continuous,
low-dimensional-manifold structure of AI model representations, rather than
the binary correct/incorrect security model of traditional cryptography.
Model fingerprinting (OML 1.0) is presented as the first primitive built in
this new framework.

This lineage is **distinct** from every other foundations/ entry in this
repo (PLONK/ZKML, Proof-of-Learning/decentralized-training, TFHE/FHE-ML,
LSSS-Curl/MPC-ML, Shapley/decentralized-consensus) — see
`foundations/ai-native-cryptography.md`.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Core mechanism | Model fingerprinting (OML 1.0) embedded via fine-tuning | eprint 2024/1573, grounded |
| Theoretical basis | "AI-native cryptography" — exploits continuous/low-dimensional structure of AI representations rather than binary security guarantees | eprint 2024/1573, grounded |
| Protocol layers | Storage, distribution, access, incentive (4-layer stack) | openagi.discourse.group summary, secondary-sourced |
| Production trust mechanism | Reported to combine fingerprinting + TEE execution + on-chain revenue splitting ("Melange" method) | secondary-source aggregation, inferred — not confirmed against a Sentient primary doc this pass |
| Ownership distribution | NFT-based ownership mint used for the Dobby model (reported 650,000-participant mint) | Cointelegraph / Investing.com news coverage, not a primary Sentient doc |
| Base chain | L1-agnostic / EVM-compatible; no dedicated standalone chain found; native network referred to as "GRID" | search aggregation, inferred |
| Released models | Dobby / Dobby Plus (Llama fine-tunes, uncensored-tuned), published on HuggingFace | secondary coverage |
| Maturity | GRID mainnet **not live** as of the most recent coverage found (planned Q2 2026, no committed date confirmed as of Aug 2026); core utility (staking, fee distribution) is gated on this launch | news aggregation, inferred |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NOT COVERED | OML targets ownership: fingerprints detect unauthorized use of a model, not whether an output was computed correctly | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Trust rests on | OPEN QUESTION | Production mechanism reportedly combines fingerprinting, TEE execution and on-chain revenue splits; unconfirmed | Secondary-source aggregation, inferred |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | Models are open-weight by design ("Open") | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | OML paper (ePrint 2024/1573); 5 of 12 authors at Sentient Foundation | eprint 2024/1573, grounded |
| Maturity | PRE-LAUNCH | GRID mainnet not live; no committed date as of Aug 2026; models released on HuggingFace | News aggregation, inferred |
| On-chain | EXISTING CHAINS | L1-agnostic and EVM-compatible; no dedicated chain found | Search aggregation, inferred |

## Known limitations

- The core cryptographic/ML contribution (model fingerprinting via
  "AI-native cryptography") is grounded directly in Sentient's own
  peer-authored paper — strong grounding. The *production* mechanism
  (TEE + on-chain revenue split, the "Melange" method) was not verified
  against a primary Sentient source in this pass and should be rechecked.
- Core on-chain utility — staking, fee distribution, task qualification —
  is reported as gated on the GRID mainnet launch, which had no committed
  date as of the most recent coverage found. Treat any claims about live
  revenue-sharing or staking mechanics as aspirational/not-yet-operational
  until the mainnet status is reconfirmed.
- Ownership-via-NFT-mint (the Dobby distribution model) is a reported
  mechanism from news coverage, not verified against Sentient's own
  documentation of the mint's actual mechanics in this pass.

## What it does

Spectral Labs builds "Spectral Syntax," a platform for creating, deploying,
and monetizing autonomous on-chain agents (the "Onchain Agent Economy") —
agents that interact with DeFi/blockchain systems from natural-language
prompts rather than hand-written smart-contract code. Related products
include an agent launchpad for autonomous trading (on Hyperliquid) and
"Grid AI," described as a spot market for ML inference.

## Architecture summary

- A "coordinator" component manages agent communication, wallet handling,
  and plugin integration — every stage from prompt submission to on-chain
  agent action runs through it. (Source: general sourcing via third-party
  explainer coverage, not independently confirmed against primary docs —
  see confidence note below.)
- **Historical technical core (2023-era): zkML.** Spectral's own account
  posted directly: *"We've been working with @jasonmorton, @CamutoDante
  and @henlojseam at @ezklxyz to implement zkML into our upcoming machine
  learning platform"*
  ([twitter.com/Spectral_Labs/status/1717657586496111034](https://twitter.com/Spectral_Labs/status/1717657586496111034)).
  Those three accounts are EZKL team members — this is Spectral's own
  primary-source statement of a direct collaboration, not an inferred
  connection.
- **Current framing has moved away from that.** Multiple secondary
  sources (crypto-explainer coverage, not Spectral's own primary text)
  report that a more recent version of Spectral's whitepaper shifts
  toward "a decentralized proxy framework with real-time model output
  consumption," explicitly placing *less* emphasis on zkML's role in IP
  protection than earlier material did. I could not independently confirm
  this against the whitepaper's actual text — the public docs site
  (docs.spectrallabs.xyz) redirects to an internal GitBook editor URL,
  not a public reader page, so I couldn't fetch its current content
  directly. Flagging this as reported-but-unverified rather than treating
  it as confirmed.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

Historical grounding runs through a real collaboration, not a citation to
a paper directly: Spectral → (worked with) → EZKL's own team → (EZKL is
built on) → Halo2 → (cites) → PLONK. See
[systems/ezkl.md](ezkl.md) and [foundations/zkml.md](../foundations/zkml.md)
for that downstream lineage; the EZKL-collaboration claim itself is
grounded in Spectral's own tweet (link above), not inferred.

No new foundations file created — this doesn't need to duplicate
`foundations/zkml.md` since it's the same lineage, reached via a direct
team collaboration rather than Spectral citing the paper itself.

**Open question, not resolved here:** whether Spectral's *current*
product (post zkML-de-emphasis) still uses any of this cryptographic
machinery at all, or whether "zkML" was an earlier pivot that's since
been abandoned in favor of something else entirely. The sourcing
available in this pass couldn't settle that either way.

# Story Protocol

## What it does

An on-chain registry for IP: ownership, licensing terms, derivative
permissions and economic rights in machine-readable form.

## Architecture summary

- On 2026-01-29 Story and OpenLedger announced a joint standard for
  licensed AI training: AI systems train on licensed IP, prove how it was
  used, enforce license terms at runtime, and distribute royalties
  automatically (see `/systems/openledger.md`).
- Story's role is the canonical IP registry. This is a press release, not
  independent validation.
- **Deprecation (protocol-core-v1 README):** the repo says the contracts
  were deprecated as of 2026-09-19 with no further features, bug fixes
  or security patches, and that the IP Portal and related services shut
  down on 2026-10-15; it advises against new integrations. What replaces
  them was not found. This is the strongest signal in the file and
  postdates the January joint-standard announcement.
- Mechanics (same repo): IP Assets are ERC-721 NFTs registered in an IP
  Asset Registry, each with an IP Account; modules for Licensing, Royalty,
  Dispute, Grouping and Metadata; the Programmable IP License (PIL) is an
  off-chain legal contract with terms mapped on-chain. Deployed natively
  on Story (Aeneid testnet 1315, Homer mainnet 1514). BUSL-1.1 licensed;
  audit reports are in the repo's `audits/` directory (not read).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None found. Foundation intentionally empty.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Function | IP registry + licensing terms | Joint announcement |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | OPEN QUESTION | Proving how licensed IP was used in training is unsolved; no mechanism described | Joint announcement, inferred |
| Trust rests on | NOT COVERED | Registering IP on-chain doesn't establish the registrant owns it | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | — | File's lineage note, inferred |
| Maturity | DEPRECATED | Core contracts deprecated 2026-09-19; IP Portal shut down 2026-10-15; no new integrations advised | protocol-core-v1 README, grounded |
| On-chain | OWN CHAIN | Contracts deployed natively on the Story chain (mainnet chain id 1514) | protocol-core-v1 README, grounded |

## Known limitations

- "Cryptographically proving how IP is used" in training is the hard,
  unsolved part (see `/foundations/zk-proof-of-training.md`: proofs of
  training do not establish what data overlapped); no mechanism was
  described in the sources.
- Registering IP on-chain does not establish that the registrant owns it.

---
name: Tinfoil

# Tinfoil

## What it does

Open-source confidential AI inference: workloads run in hardware enclaves
and clients verify via remote attestation that the code running matches
what is published on GitHub. Tagline: "Replacing trust with provable
security."

## Architecture summary

- Repos in the `tinfoilsh` GitHub org: `cvmimage` (confidential VM image,
  AGPL-3.0), `tinfoil-config` (workload schema/validator), `modelwrap`
  (reproducible dm-verity images of Hugging Face models),
  `encrypted-http-body-protocol` (EHBP: HPKE encryption of HTTP bodies),
  `tinfoil-proxy`, and OpenAI-compatible clients in Go, JS, Python, Swift.
- Official SDKs verify attestation and the supply chain automatically on
  each connection. V3 attestation is in beta per the docs.
- Red Hat's Office of the CTO is collaborating with the project on
  cloud-native confidential AI (Oct 2025): weights are loaded only after
  mutual attestation, with decryption confined to the enclave.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

No paper cited. Lineage to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md` is
**inferred**. The specific hardware (SEV-SNP / TDX / NVIDIA CC) was not
confirmed from the pages reviewed.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Verification | Client-side attestation + open-source code | Tinfoil docs |
| Transport | EHBP (HPKE) | tinfoilsh repo |
| Model integrity | dm-verity images via modelwrap | tinfoilsh repo |
| Licenses | AGPL-3.0 (core), Apache-2.0 (some clients) | tinfoilsh repo |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Clients verify by remote attestation that the running code matches what is published on GitHub | Tinfoil docs, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | Hardware enclaves; the specific hardware wasn't confirmed | Tinfoil docs; hardware inferred |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Inference in enclaves; HTTP bodies encrypted end to end with HPKE (EHBP) | tinfoilsh repo, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; the link to Intel SGX Explained is inferred from the shared TEE-attestation mechanism | Tinfoil docs, inferred link |
| Maturity | OPEN QUESTION | V3 attestation in beta; no audit or production-deployment evidence found | Tinfoil docs; Known limitations, inferred |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | — | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- "Provable" is a marketing claim; the GitHub org page doesn't describe the
  transparency log or hardware details (read the attestation-architecture
  docs before upgrading this file's confidence).
- No audit or production-deployment evidence found in this pass.

# Vana

## What it does

Lets users export their data from platforms and pool it into data
collectives that negotiate with AI companies and developers.

## Architecture summary

- **DataDAOs / Data Liquidity Pools (DLPs):** a DLP is a smart contract
  that instantiates a DataDAO around one data domain. Contributors get
  DLP-specific tokens (governance proportional to contribution).
- **Proof of Contribution:** each DLP defines its own scoring function
  (e.g. accuracy/completeness for financial data, freshness for health
  data), so scoring is not uniform across DLPs.
- **Validation and privacy:** validation runs on the Satya Network, a set
  of TEE nodes that attest to data quality without exposing the data;
  some DLPs also use zk proofs (zk email, zkTLS). Raw data stays
  encrypted on personal servers or in secure enclaves; only ownership
  proofs, permissions and attestations are on-chain.
- **VANA token:** validator staking, fees, DLP staking (the top 16
  DataDAOs by stake per 3-week epoch share emissions), and the currency AI
  companies use to buy/burn DLP tokens for data access.
- The whitepaper (Dec 2024) is pre-mainnet and forward-looking; nothing
  from 2026 was found, so current status is unknown.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None found. Foundation intentionally empty. Compare `/systems/ocean-protocol.md`
for the older data-marketplace approach.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Quality control | Proof-of-Contribution (details unread) | Vana whitepaper listing |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | ATTESTATION | Per-DLP Proof of Contribution scored by TEE validator nodes (Satya Network); some DLPs add zk proofs | Vana whitepaper, grounded |
| Trust rests on | HARDWARE VENDOR | TEE trust model unspecified in the whitepaper; consensus also unspecified | Vana whitepaper, grounded (absence) |
| Confidentiality | HARDWARE ENCLAVE | Raw data stays encrypted off-chain on personal servers or in enclaves | Vana whitepaper, grounded |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | — | File's lineage note, inferred |
| Maturity | OPEN QUESTION | Nothing from 2026 found; current status unknown | 2024 whitepaper listing, inferred |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- Consensus and the TEE trust model are not specified in the whitepaper.
- Per-DLP scoring means quality bars differ across DataDAOs.
- Some staged-access and burn mechanics are given as examples, not
  confirmed implementations; Dec 2024 content may be stale.

# Venice.ai

## What it does

A consumer and API LLM service built around privacy, with four per-model
privacy modes that make a useful ladder of trust levels.

## Architecture summary

- **Proxy layer:** relays HTTPS requests without storing prompt/response
  content for normal inference.
- **Modes:** Anonymous (identity hidden from the model provider, who may
  store data), Private (zero retention by contract), **TEE** (hardware
  isolated enclaves, "private even from Venice"), **E2EE** (prompts
  decrypted only inside a verified TEE).
- Phala supplies the confidential-computing infrastructure for TEE models
  (see `/systems/phala-dstack.md`).

## Built on (foundational lineage)

No paper cited; **inferred** link to `foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md`
via the Phala TEE stack.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Strongest mode | E2EE inside verified TEE | Venice docs |
| Weaker modes | Contractual / policy, not cryptographic | Venice docs |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | PER APP | Only the TEE and E2EE modes are attested; the others rest on policy | Venice docs |
| Trust rests on | PER APP | Enclave hardware (via Phala) in TEE/E2EE modes; contractual promises in Anonymous/Private modes | Venice docs |
| Confidentiality | PER APP | Four per-model modes, from identity-hiding proxy to E2EE inside a verified TEE | Venice docs |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | No paper cited; TEE link inferred via the Phala stack | Venice docs, inferred link |
| Maturity | LIVE | Consumer and API LLM service; no independent security audit per a 2026 review | Venice docs |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- Anonymous and Private modes are policy promises, not verifiable.
- A third-party post claims basic telemetry (sign-in, browser, IP) is
  logged for abuse prevention; unverified against Venice's policy.
- A 2026 review notes no independent security audit and no way to prove
  every partner follows zero-retention.

# Verified zkEVM

## What it does

An Ethereum Foundation initiative funding formal verification of zkVMs,
EVM implementations and cryptographic proof systems. Relevant to this
radar because the ZKML systems tracked here (e.g. `/systems/ezkl.md`)
depend on the same class of circuits and proof systems.

## Architecture summary

- Site reports 42 grants awarded across 3 tracks and 90 resources, with a
  Verified-zkEVM GitHub org. It names no amounts, teams or tools.
- Secondary sources report: Least Authority on a Lean blueprint for STIR
  and WHIR; Certora on autoprecompiles (Powdr Labs); Nethermind on a
  Lean model of EVM/Yul and Halo2 circuit verification tooling, and a
  RISC Zero RISC-V circuit effort; a reported ~$20M scope covering
  leanMultisig circuits, leanSig hashes and the leanVM specification.
  The dollar figure is single-source.
- **SP1 (Succinct + Nethermind):** Lean checks that SP1 Hypercube's core
  RV64 AIR constraints, plus lookup-implied constraints, implement
  RISC-V semantics against the Sail spec, covering 62 opcodes. An
  Ethereum Foundation post (2026-05-20) says the work has known
  limitations and that additional gaps were recently found and disclosed
  to Succinct. Next: ALU circuits, then Keccak256 / Secp256k1 precompiles.
- **RISC Zero (Nethermind):** a Feb 2025 proof of concept on the Zirgen
  MLIR layer; only the instruction decoder, an IsZero gadget and a OneHot2
  gadget were fully done. Jolt: nothing found.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

None. Foundation intentionally empty: this is verification *of* proof
stacks, not derived from a single paper. Touches `foundations/zkml.md`
indirectly (Halo2 appears in both).

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Method | Lean (per secondary sources; not on the site page) | Least Authority, Nethermind |
| Status | Ongoing for 1+ year; no fully verified zkVM shown | secondary talk summary |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | FORMAL PROOF | Funds Lean proofs of zkVMs, EVM implementations and proof systems; no fully verified zkVM shown yet | Secondary sources (Least Authority, Nethermind), inferred |
| Trust rests on | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Confidentiality | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Lineage | NONE FOUND | Verification of proof stacks, not derived from a single paper | verified-zkevm.org, grounded |
| Maturity | RESEARCH | Ongoing for over a year; 42 grants across 3 tracks; work in progress | verified-zkevm.org + secondary talk summary |
| On-chain | NOT COVERED | — | Not addressed in this file's sources |

## Known limitations

- Work in progress; the sources show no finished, fully verified zkEVM.
- Not about ML: the link to ZKML is that shared proof systems get verified.

FILE: systems/zama-concrete-ml.md

---
name: Zama Concrete-ML
field: FHE for ML
category: private-compute
foundation: foundations/fhe-ml.md
last_updated: 2026-10-20
confidence: grounded
website: "https://github.com/zama-ai/concrete-ml"
---

# Zama Concrete-ML

## What it does

Concrete-ML is an open-source Python framework from Zama that lets you train
a model normally (scikit-learn-compatible APIs, or PyTorch/TensorFlow via
ONNX) and then run inference on **encrypted** inputs, so the service running
the model never sees the plaintext data. Output of `encrypt()` → `run()` →
`decrypt()` never exposes intermediate values to the server.

## Architecture summary

- Built directly on top of **Concrete** (Zama's TFHE compiler, which turns
  Python/numerical programs into their FHE equivalent), which itself is
  built on **TFHE-rs**, Zama's Rust implementation of the TFHE scheme.
- Models are **quantized** (quantization-aware training or post-training
  quantization) to convert floating-point weights/activations into
  integers, since FHE arithmetic operates over integers, not floats.
- Non-linear activation functions (ReLU, sigmoid, etc.) are evaluated via
  **programmable bootstrapping** — TFHE's bootstrap step is repurposed to
  simultaneously refresh noise *and* apply an arbitrary lookup-table
  function, which is what makes homomorphic neural-net inference
  practical rather than prohibitively expensive.

## Built on (foundational lineage)

- **TFHE: Fast Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus** — I. Chillotti,
  N. Gama, M. Georgieva, M. Izabachène, *Journal of Cryptology* 33, 2020
  (https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/421). Base encryption scheme. Grounding:
  this is the standard citation for TFHE across Zama's own repos
  (zama-ai/concrete, zama-ai/tfhe-rs) and third-party papers that build on
  Concrete — confirmed via multiple independent academic citations, though
  the Concrete-ML GitHub README itself does not carry an explicit
  bibliography (see confidence note below).
- **Programmable Bootstrapping Enables Efficient Homomorphic Inference of
  Deep Neural Networks** — I. Chillotti, M. Joye, P. Paillier, Zama
  (https://eprint.iacr.org/2021/091). The specific mechanism Concrete-ML
  relies on to evaluate non-linear layers cheaply.
- **Deep Neural Networks for Encrypted Inference with TFHE** — A. Stoian,
  J. Frery, R. Bredehoft, L. Montero, C. Kherfallah, B. Chevallier-Mames
  (arXiv:2302.10906, Feb 2023). Authored by the Zama/Concrete-ML team
  itself; uses Concrete directly for benchmarks. This is the most directly
  "FHE-for-ML"-specific paper in the lineage — it's the applied bridge
  between the TFHE primitives above and Concrete-ML's DNN support.

**Confidence note:** the Concrete-ML GitHub README links out to
docs.zama.ai/docs.zama.org for technical detail rather than citing papers
inline. The TFHE/programmable-bootstrapping lineage above is grounded via
Zama's own sister repos (tfhe-rs, concrete) and the Stoian et al. paper's
direct authorship/use of Concrete, not via a single README citation list.
Treat as grounded-by-convergence rather than grounded-by-single-citation.

## Property matrix

| Property | Current value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FHE scheme | TFHE (LWE/Ring-LWE based) | zama-ai/concrete, zama-ai/tfhe-rs repos |
| Non-linear evaluation | Programmable bootstrapping (lookup-table via bootstrap) | Chillotti/Joye/Paillier 2021 |
| Precision | Low-bit integer quantization required (model-dependent, typically ≤8-bit activations in practice) | Concrete-ML docs (docs.zama.ai/concrete-ml) |
| Trust model | No trusted setup; client holds secret key, server computes blind | TFHE scheme properties (symmetric/public-key FHE, no CRS) |
| Maturity | Production-maintained OSS library, active releases | github.com/zama-ai/concrete-ml |

## Comparison axes

| Axis | Class | Detail | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correctness | NOT COVERED | FHE hides data from the server; the file describes no check that the server ran the model correctly | Not addressed in this file's sources |
| Trust rests on | MATH | TFHE (LWE-based) hardness; no trusted setup; the client holds the secret key | TFHE scheme properties, grounded |
| Confidentiality | CRYPTOGRAPHIC | Inference on encrypted inputs; the server never sees plaintext or intermediate values | Concrete-ML README, grounded |
| Lineage | OWN PAPER | Seed paper is the Concrete-ML team's DNN-over-TFHE work (arXiv 2302.10906), built on TFHE (eprint 2018/421) | Zama repos + Stoian et al., grounded by convergence |
| Maturity | LIVE | Production-maintained open-source library with active releases | github.com/zama-ai/concrete-ml, grounded |
| On-chain | NO CHAIN | A Python library; no blockchain component in the cited sources | Inferred from absence in the cited sources |

## Known limitations

- Bootstrapping is the dominant cost; deeper/wider networks with more
  non-linearities scale poorly in latency compared to plaintext inference.
- Quantization-aware training adds workflow overhead and can cost accuracy
  versus the unquantized model.
- Encrypted inference latency (seconds–minutes per call depending on model
  size) remains far from plaintext inference speed — not yet suited to
  low-latency, high-throughput serving.

FILE: foundations/ai-native-cryptography.md
========================================================================

---
field: AI model ownership / monetization protocols
paper: "OML: Open, Monetizable, and Loyal AI"
authors: Zerui Cheng, Edoardo Contente, Ben Finch, Oleg Golev, Jonathan Hayase, Andrew Miller, Niusha Moshrefi, Anshul Nasery, Sandeep Nailwal, Sewoong Oh, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath
year: 2024
venue: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2024/1573
link: https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/1573
---

## Why this is the seed for this field

Directly authored by the tracked system's own team: 5 of the 12 authors
(Contente, Finch, Golev, Nailwal, Tyagi) are affiliated with Sentient
Foundation, alongside academics from Princeton, University of Washington,
and UIUC. This is not Sentient citing prior art — it is Sentient's founding
protocol paper. See `systems/sentient-oml.md` for how the system implements
it.

## Core contribution

Introduces **"AI-native cryptography"**: a proposed new branch of
cryptography built specifically around the structure of AI model
representations, rather than adapting traditional binary (secure/broken)
cryptographic security models to AI. The core observation is that AI data
representations live on continuous, low-dimensional manifolds, which can be
exploited to build security primitives traditional cryptography can't
express — e.g. a fingerprint that survives fine-tuning/distillation of a
model without being a literal bit-for-bit watermark. The paper's first
concrete primitive built in this framework is **model fingerprinting**
(labeled OML 1.0): an undetectable marker embedded into a model via
fine-tuning, usable to detect unauthorized use/redistribution of an
ostensibly "open" model.

## Link to tracked system

Sentient's entire ownership/monetization pitch depends on this primitive:
if a model is fully open-weight, nothing stops anyone from copying and
reselling it unless there's a way to detect that a given deployed model is
derived from a specific owned original. OML's fingerprinting is that
detection mechanism. The protocol layers described in
`systems/sentient-oml.md` (storage/distribution/access/incentive) are the
economic/infrastructure machinery built on top of this cryptographic
primitive, not the primitive itself.

FILE: foundations/ccf-confidential-computing.md
========================================================================

---
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
paper: "CCF: A Framework for Building Confidential Verifiable Replicated Services"
authors: Mark Russinovich, Edward Ashton, Christine Avanessians, Miguel Castro, et al.
year: 2019
venue: Microsoft Research Technical Report MSR-TR-2019-16
refined_paper: "Confidential Consortium Framework: Secure Multiparty Applications with Confidentiality, Integrity, and High Availability"
refined_venue: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol 17(2), 2023 (VLDB nominee)
refined_link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11559
---

# CCF: A Framework for Building Confidential Verifiable Replicated Services

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded directly, not inferred: Microsoft's own Azure documentation
states that Azure confidential ledger — the transparency/auditability
component used in Azure AI Confidential Inferencing — "is built on the
Confidential Consortium Framework (CCF)." CCF is itself a Microsoft
Research project (github.com/microsoft/CCF) with its own research page
listing this 2019 technical report as the original design paper, later
refined and published in the peer-reviewed 2023 VLDB paper linked above.
See `/systems/azure-confidential-ai.md` for how this plugs into the
actual Azure product.

## Core contribution

CCF combines two previously separate ideas into one system: (1)
hardware TEEs for remotely-verifiable confidentiality and code
integrity of the compute itself, and (2) state-machine replication
backed by an append-only, auditable ledger for data integrity and high
availability. The result is a framework for building multi-party
applications that can run on cloud infrastructure none of the
participants fully trust, with governance (who can change the rules,
who operates nodes) kept separate from, and verifiable independent of,
the cloud operator. The 2023 refinement formalizes CCF's custom
distributed-consensus and client-consistency model and was itself the
subject of a separate 2025 NSDI verification paper ("Smart Casual
Verification of the Confidential Consortium Framework"), which is
outside this seed paper's scope but worth noting as follow-on
scrutiny of the same system.

## Link to tracked system

Azure's confidential ledger product — and, through it, the
transparency-ledger component of Azure AI Confidential Inferencing —
is built directly on CCF. This is the one part of Microsoft's
"Confidential AI" story with a real, citable Microsoft Research paper
behind it; the TEE hardware layer underneath (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX,
NVIDIA H100 confidential computing) is vendor technology with its own
specs, not an academic contribution from this lineage — see
`/systems/azure-confidential-ai.md`'s "Built on" section for why those
two lineages are kept separate rather than merged into one claim.

FILE: foundations/decentralized-consensus-ml.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized incentive / consensus mechanisms for ML networks
paper: "A Value for n-Person Games"
authors: Lloyd S. Shapley
year: 1952
venue: "Contributions to the Theory of Games, Vol. II (Annals of Mathematics Studies 28), Princeton University Press"
---

# A Value for n-Person Games (Shapley, 1952)

## Why this is the seed for this field

Bittensor's own academic paper, *"Incentivizing Intelligence: The Bittensor
Approach"* (Steeves et al., hosted at
[bittensor.com/academia](https://www.bittensor.com/academia)), explicitly
cites Shapley's 1952 value concept as the theoretical basis for how the
network attributes credit to peers: each participant's reward is meant to
reflect their marginal contribution to the network's informational output,
evaluated across permutations of coalitions of peers — which is exactly what
the Shapley value formalizes. This is the one piece of the Bittensor stack
with a clean, explicit academic citation; the rest of the mechanism (the
specific stake-weighted-median "Yuma Consensus" algorithm used in
production) is documented in community/ecosystem sources rather than in a
peer-reviewed citation trail — see the naming-gap note in
[[systems/bittensor]].

## Core contribution

Shapley's paper answers a fairness question: if a group of people (or
agents) jointly produce some value by cooperating, how should that value be
split among them in a way that fairly reflects each one's contribution,
even when contributions aren't independent (i.e. what one agent adds
depends on who else is already in the group)? The Shapley value is defined
by averaging each agent's marginal contribution across every possible order
in which agents could join the coalition. It's the unique allocation rule
satisfying a small set of fairness axioms (efficiency, symmetry, additivity,
null-player). It's a cooperative-game-theory result, not a machine-learning
or cryptography result — its relevance here is purely as the attribution
principle a decentralized ML incentive system borrows.

## Link to tracked system

Bittensor needs to answer: "how much is this peer's model output actually
worth to the network, given that other peers are also contributing similar
or overlapping information?" Naively rewarding every peer independently
invites redundant, low-effort submissions; the Shapley framing is invoked to
justify rewarding marginal/novel contribution instead. In practice,
production Bittensor does not compute literal Shapley values (that's
computationally intractable at network scale — exact Shapley values require
summing over all coalition permutations); it uses Yuma Consensus's
stake-weighted-median-with-clipping as a tractable proxy mechanism inspired
by the same fairness goal. This is worth flagging explicitly: the citation
grounds the *motivation*, not the *literal algorithm* actually running in
production.

FILE: foundations/decentralized-training.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized / distributed training
paper: "Proof-of-Learning: Definitions and Practice"
authors: Hengrui Jia, Mohammad Yaghini, Christopher A. Choquette-Choo, Natalie Dullerud, Anvith Thudi, Varun Chandrasekaran, Nicolas Papernot
year: 2021
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2021
arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633
---

# Proof-of-Learning: Definitions and Practice

## Why this is the seed for this field

Cited directly by Gensyn's own Verde research post as foundational prior work
("Proof-of-Learning" — [arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.05633)),
alongside Refereed Delegation, Agatha, Toploc, and Proof-of-Training-Data. See
[systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for the full citation list and source
link. Of that list, this paper is the one that directly frames the core problem
Gensyn's verification layer exists to solve: how do you let a party that didn't
do the training convince a verifier that specific gradient-descent work was
actually performed, without full re-execution.

## Core contribution

Introduces "proof-of-learning" (PoL): a party that trained a model produces a
proof — built from checkpoints and the gradient-descent trajectory metadata
recorded during training — that lets a verifier check, cheaply, that training
actually happened as claimed, rather than requiring the verifier to redo the
entire training run. It formalizes what such a proof needs to guarantee and
shows practical constructions and attacks against naive versions of the idea.

## Link to tracked system

Gensyn's verification problem is exactly this: a client needs to trust that a
third-party provider trained a model correctly without re-running the full
job. Gensyn's current production system (Verde) does not implement PoL's
checkpoint-trajectory scheme directly — it instead uses RepOps
(bitwise-reproducible operators) plus a Merkle-tree-based bisection/dispute
game — but PoL is the paper that established the problem framing and the
first concrete proposal in this space, which is why Gensyn cites it as prior
work. See [systems/gensyn.md](../systems/gensyn.md) for how the current
architecture actually differs from PoL's approach.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/differential-privacy.md
========================================================================

---
field: Differential privacy for ML training
paper: "Deep Learning with Differential Privacy"
authors: Martin Abadi, Andy Chu, Ian Goodfellow, H. Brendan McMahan, Ilya Mironov, Kunal Talwar, Li Zhang
year: 2016
venue: ACM CCS 2016
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00133
---

# Deep Learning with Differential Privacy

## Why this is the seed for this field

**Inferred, not grounded.** The Opacus README reviewed does not cite this
paper (it cites its own technical report, arXiv:2109.12298, plus clipping
papers). It is used here as the standard origin of DP-SGD, the algorithm
that Opacus's `noise_multiplier` / `max_grad_norm` parameters implement.
Flower's docs also list DP strategies and accountants (see
`/systems/flower.md`), but Flower's authoritative foundation is secure
aggregation, since DP there is a second, separate feature.

## Core contribution

DP-SGD: clip each example's gradient to a norm bound, add calibrated
Gaussian noise, and track cumulative privacy loss with a "moments
accountant," so a model can be trained with a quantified (epsilon, delta)
guarantee on what it leaks about any single training example.

## Link to tracked systems

`/systems/opacus.md`. Distinct from the cryptographic foundations in this
repo (MPC, FHE, secure aggregation): DP bounds what the *output* reveals;
it does not hide data during computation.
