FILE: foundations/diloco-distributed-training.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized / distributed training
paper: "DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models"
authors: Arthur Douillard, Qixuan Feng, Andrei A. Rusu, Rachita Chhaparia, Yani Donchev, Adhiguna Kuncoro, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Arthur Szlam, Jiajun Shen
year: 2023
venue: Google DeepMind (arXiv preprint)
arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.08105
---

# DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded via direct citation, not inference: Prime Intellect's own
OpenDiLoCo announcement states *"Introducing OpenDiLoCo, an open-source
implementation and scaling of DeepMind's Distributed Low-Communication
(DiLoCo) method"* and separately calls it *"a reproducible implementation
of DeepMind's DiLoCo experiments."*
([primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco](https://www.primeintellect.ai/blog/opendiloco)).
Prime Intellect's subsequent INTELLECT-1 technical report (arXiv:2412.01152)
builds its PRIME framework directly on this same DiLoCo core. See
[systems/prime-intellect.md](../systems/prime-intellect.md) for the full
chain.

This is a different seed paper from the one in
[foundations/decentralized-training.md](./decentralized-training.md)
(Proof-of-Learning, cited by Gensyn) despite sharing the same field — that
paper is about verifying training happened as claimed; this one is about
making distributed training communication-efficient in the first place.

## Core contribution

DiLoCo lets language-model training happen across "islands" of
poorly-connected devices instead of requiring tightly-interconnected
accelerators synchronizing every step. Each worker runs many local
optimization steps with an inner optimizer (AdamW); periodically, an
outer optimizer (SGD with Nesterov momentum) synchronizes pseudo-gradients
across workers. On the C4 dataset with 8 workers, DiLoCo matched fully
synchronous training quality while communicating roughly 500x less, and
the method is robust to workers dropping in and out during training.

## Link to tracked system

Prime Intellect's PRIME framework uses DiLoCo as the inter-node
optimization layer (paired with FSDP2 for intra-node sharding), which is
what let INTELLECT-1 train a 10B-parameter model across five countries and
three continents with nodes syncing only every ~38 minutes. See
[systems/prime-intellect.md](../systems/prime-intellect.md) for the full
architecture and property matrix.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/distributed-compute-scheduling.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized GPU / compute marketplace (orchestration layer)
paper: "Ray: A Distributed Framework for Emerging AI Applications"
authors: Philipp Moritz, Robert Nishihara, Stephanie Wang, Alexey Tumanov, Richard Liaw, Eric Liang, Melih Elibol, Zongheng Yang, William Paul, Michael I. Jordan, Ion Stoica
year: 2018
venue: 13th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI '18)
link: https://www.usenix.org/system/files/osdi18-moritz.pdf
---

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded via a two-hop citation chain, not a direct io.net citation:

- io.net's own architecture docs state directly that its orchestration
  layer, IO-SDK, is *"our specialized fork of Ray, a core technology
  driving io.net's capabilities"* (version base: Ray 2.3.0).
  ([io.net/docs/guides/architecture/io-architecture](https://io.net/docs/guides/architecture/io-architecture))
- Ray is the subject of its own academic systems paper from UC
  Berkeley's RISELab, presented at OSDI 2018.

See `/systems/io-net.md` for the full source chain and for the explicit
distinction between this (orchestration-engine) lineage and io.net's
separate, unsourced trust/verification mechanisms.

## Core contribution

Ray's paper introduces a distributed execution framework for AI
workloads that unifies two previously separate programming models —
fine-grained, stateless task parallelism (as in MapReduce-style
systems) and stateful actor-based computation — under one dynamic task
graph and a single system. It uses a bottom-up distributed scheduler
(rather than a single centralized scheduler) and a fault-tolerant
distributed metadata store, specifically to support workloads common in
AI applications — simulation, training, and serving — that mix
short, latency-sensitive tasks with long-running, stateful ones, which
earlier batch-oriented distributed systems weren't designed for.

## Link to tracked system

io.net uses a fork of Ray as the execution substrate for distributing
and scheduling GPU workloads across its marketplace of
provider-contributed hardware — i.e., Ray solves the general
"orchestrate many parallel/stateful tasks across a cluster" problem,
and io.net's contribution on top is specifically the
decentralization/marketplace/trust layer (payment, resource-integrity
verification, provider onboarding), which this paper does not address
and which io.net's own docs don't tie to any further academic source.
This is a general distributed-systems paper, not an AI-security- or
cryptography-specific one — it's the seed for the *compute
orchestration* side of this field, not the *trust/verification* side.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/distributed-optimization.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized / distributed training
paper: "DeMo: Decoupled Momentum Optimization"
authors: Bowen Peng, Jeffrey Quesnelle, Diederik P. Kingma
year: 2024
venue: arXiv
arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.19870
---

# DeMo: Decoupled Momentum Optimization

## Why this is the seed for this field

Directly grounded, not inferred: the paper is authored by Nous Research
staff, and Nous's own Psyche architecture page states explicitly —
*"Building on DisTrO and its predecessor DeMo, Psyche reduces data
transfer by several orders of magnitude"*
([nousresearch.com/nous-psyche](https://nousresearch.com/nous-psyche)).
See [systems/nous-psyche.md](../systems/nous-psyche.md) for the full
chain. Code: [github.com/bloc97/DeMo](https://github.com/bloc97/DeMo).

This is deliberately kept separate from `decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, arXiv:2103.05633, the seed for Gensyn): both sit in
the same broad field but address different problems — Proof-of-Learning
is about *verifying* that training happened as claimed; DeMo is about
making distributed optimization *communication-efficient* enough to run
over consumer/internet-class links in the first place. Per this repo's
rule of one foundation file per distinct citation lineage, they stay as
two files even though the field label is the same.

## Core contribution

DeMo is a drop-in replacement for momentum-based optimizers (e.g. Adam)
designed to cut the communication volume required for distributed
training. It decouples local momentum updates across workers, applies
a fast orthonormal transform (DCT) to the momentum signal, keeps only
the top-k components (sparsification), and reuses the discarded
momentum as error feedback on the next step rather than dropping it.
The paper reports up to 85x less data transmitted per GPU than
AdamW-DDP on 300M–1B parameter models, while reaching comparable loss —
and the approach is topology-agnostic, meaning it doesn't assume a
particular interconnect (works over Ethernet/multi-datacenter links,
not just high-bandwidth cluster fabric).

## Link to tracked system

Nous's Psyche network is DeMo's direct production application: DisTrO
extends DeMo into a full runtime (adding load balancing and
selective-synchronization on top of the core compression idea), and
Psyche then wraps that runtime in a Solana-coordinated network so
contributors with heterogeneous, geographically dispersed hardware can
train one model together. See [systems/nous-psyche.md](../systems/nous-psyche.md)
for the full system and its known limitations — notably, DeMo/DisTrO
solve the bandwidth problem but explicitly do **not** yet solve
verifying that a remote participant actually ran the claimed
computation honestly.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/fhe-ml.md
========================================================================

---
field: FHE for ML
paper: Deep Neural Networks for Encrypted Inference with TFHE
authors: Andrei Stoian, Jordan Frery, Roman Bredehoft, Luis Montero, Celia Kherfallah, Benoit Chevallier-Mames
year: 2023
venue: arXiv preprint (2302.10906)
---

# Deep Neural Networks for Encrypted Inference with TFHE

## Why this is the seed for this field

Authored by the team behind Zama's Concrete-ML, and uses Concrete directly
for its benchmarks — this is the paper that connects the general TFHE
cryptosystem to the specific problem of running deep neural network
inference on encrypted data, which is exactly what Concrete-ML ships as a
product. It sits one layer above the raw cryptography (TFHE itself, and
Chillotti/Joye/Paillier's programmable bootstrapping) and one layer below
the shipped library — the applied bridge.

## Core contribution

The paper shows how to design and quantize DNN architectures (targeted at
computer-vision tasks) so that they can run entirely under TFHE's
programmable bootstrapping, and benchmarks the resulting latency/accuracy
tradeoffs on Concrete. The core insight it operationalizes: FHE arithmetic
only works cleanly over integers, so every layer of the network has to be
re-expressed in quantized integer form *before* bootstrapping is used to
evaluate non-linearities — the paper is effectively the recipe for doing
that re-expression without destroying accuracy or blowing up latency.

## Link to tracked system

Concrete-ML's quantization-aware training pipeline and its approach to
evaluating activation functions via programmable bootstrapping are the
productionized version of what this paper demonstrates. See
`/systems/zama-concrete-ml.md` for the property matrix this paper's
techniques feed into — specifically the "Precision" and "Non-linear
evaluation" rows.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/model-parallel-decentralized-training.md
========================================================================

---
field: Decentralized / distributed training
paper: "Subspace Networks: Scaling Decentralized Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism"
authors: Sameera Ramasinghe, Thalaiyasingam Ajanthan, Gil Avraham, Yan Zuo, Alexander Long
year: 2025
venue: NeurIPS 2025 (arXiv preprint, originally titled "Protocol Models")
arxiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.01260
---

# Subspace Networks: Scaling Decentralized Training with Communication-Efficient Model Parallelism

## Why this is the seed for this field

Authored directly by the Pluralis Research team (affiliation explicitly
stated in the paper itself — confirmed via
[arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2506.01260v1)), not a
third-party citation. See
[systems/pluralis-research.md](../systems/pluralis-research.md) for the
grounding detail, including the title change between preprint versions
(same arXiv ID, retitled from "Protocol Models" to "Subspace Networks").

This is a **distinct lineage** from `foundations/decentralized-training.md`
(Proof-of-Learning, arXiv:2103.05633, which Gensyn's Verde cites). That
paper addresses verifying that training happened; this paper addresses
making model-parallel training communication-efficient enough to run over
consumer internet connections at all. Same field, different problem, kept
as separate foundation files per this repo's one-file-per-lineage rule.

## Core contribution

When a large model is split across devices (model/pipeline parallelism),
every forward and backward pass requires transferring activation and
gradient tensors between devices — tens to hundreds of MB per step — which
is fine over datacenter interconnects but becomes the binding bottleneck
over consumer internet. The paper's compression algorithm exploits a
recursive structure in transformer networks to confine activations and
gradients to a predefined low-dimensional subspace, permitting full
reconstruction in later layers. This gets up to ~100x compression on
inter-stage communication without materially altering training dynamics or
degrading convergence, which is what makes multi-participant, model-parallel
training over ordinary internet connections practical rather than purely
theoretical.

## Link to tracked system

Pluralis Research's production system, Agora, uses this technique directly
as the mechanism that makes its pipeline-parallel training swarm viable —
without it, the inter-device communication cost of splitting a model across
unreliable, internet-connected consumer hardware would dominate and make
the whole approach impractical. See
[systems/pluralis-research.md](../systems/pluralis-research.md) for the
full system write-up, including the honest gap that this solves the
communication-efficiency problem but not trust/verification of contributor
honesty.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/mpc-ml.md
========================================================================

---
field: Secure MPC for ML
paper: Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase
authors: Miguel de Vega, Andrei Lapets, Stanisław Jarecki, Wicher Malten, Mehmet Ugurbil, Wyatt Howe
year: 2023
venue: self-published / IACR ePrint 2023/1740 (withdrawn 2024-06-28; mirrored at nillion.pub)
---

# Evaluation of Arithmetic Sum-of-Products Expressions in Linear Secret Sharing Schemes with a Non-Interactive Computation Phase

## Why this is the seed for this field

Nillion's own team announced this paper as the direct basis for their
non-interactive MPC protocol for non-linear computation — see
"Introducing the Nillion Non-Interactive MPC Protocol for Non-Linear
Computations"
(https://medium.com/@Nillion_Network/introducing-the-nillion-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations-67e9310ef479),
corroborated by the MPC Alliance's write-up of the same announcement
(https://www.mpcalliance.org/blog/nillion-introduces-a-non-interactive-mpc-protocol-for-non-linear-computations).
Four of the six listed authors (de Vega, Malten, Ugurbil, and one more)
are Nillion staff — this is effectively the project publishing its own
core protocol paper, which is about the strongest grounding available
for a "foundational paper" claim in this exercise.

## Core contribution

Classic linear secret sharing schemes (LSSS) handle addition of shared
secrets for free but need rounds of communication between parties to
handle multiplication — the operation needed for anything non-linear.
This paper describes a way to evaluate arithmetic sum-of-products
expressions (sums of products of shared values — covers the multiply
step) using a **preprocessing phase that doesn't depend on the private
inputs**, so the actual computation-on-private-data step becomes
non-interactive. In plain terms: move the expensive "parties have to
talk to each other" part of secure multiplication to a setup phase that
can happen before anyone's real data is involved, so the live computation
is faster and doesn't require synchronous coordination between nodes.

## Link to tracked system

This is the specific technique underneath Nillion's **Curl** protocol,
which extends LSSS to support the non-linear math (division, square
roots, trig, logarithms) that ML workloads need but plain secret sharing
can't do cheaply. It's the piece that lets Nillion's MPC layer process
more than just linear operations on encrypted data, which is the gap
between "toy secret sharing demo" and "can actually run ML inference
on shared data."

## Open question for future monitoring

The paper was withdrawn from IACR ePrint (2023/1740, withdrawn
2024-06-28) and now only exists as a Nillion-hosted PDF. No public
explanation found for the withdrawal. If a future paper-watch run
surfaces commentary on *why* it was withdrawn (correction vs. priority
dispute vs. something substantive), that's worth a dedicated note since
it bears directly on how much to trust this as the field's seed paper.

FILE: foundations/neural-network-verification.md
========================================================================

---
field: Formal verification of neural networks
paper: "Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions"
authors: Huan Zhang, Tsui-Wei Weng, Pin-Yu Chen, Cho-Jui Hsieh, Luca Daniel
year: 2018
venue: NeurIPS 2018
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.00866
---

# CROWN: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded for α,β-CROWN: its README lists CROWN (2018) first among the
papers users should cite, then auto_LiRPA, α-CROWN, β-CROWN and later
extensions, so the lineage is a documented citation chain. The venue and
author list above are from background knowledge, not from the README, and
should be checked against the arXiv page.

## Core contribution

Linear bound propagation: derive linear lower and upper bounds on each
neuron's output over an input region, for general activations, giving a
sound (possibly loose) certificate that no input in the region violates
a property. Later work adds branch-and-bound (β-CROWN) to make this
complete for ReLU networks and runs it on GPUs.

## Link to tracked systems

`/systems/alpha-beta-crown.md` (grounded). `/systems/marabou.md` is a
different approach (SMT/LP based) and links here only as an inferred peer.
Both address *behavioural properties of a model*, a different problem
than the cryptographic proofs of correct execution in `/foundations/zkml.md`.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/optimistic-ml.md
========================================================================

---
field: Optimistic on-chain AI verification
paper: opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain
authors: KD Conway, Cathie So, Xiaohang Yu, Kartin Wong
year: 2024
venue: arXiv 2401.17555
---

# opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain

## Why this is the seed for this field

Directly grounded, team's-own-paper case — about as strong as this
exercise's grounding gets. Two of the four authors are ORA's own
founding team: **Kartin Wong** (ORA co-founder, ex-Google/TikTok
infrastructure engineer) and **Cathie So** (ORA's Chief Scientist, ex-
Ethereum Foundation zkML researcher). KD Conway is credited elsewhere as
"the author of opML." This isn't a system citing outside research — it's
the system's own team publishing the paper that defines the mechanism
the system runs. (arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.17555)

## Core contribution

Proposes an alternative to zkML for verifying ML inference on-chain:
instead of a cryptographic proof of correct execution (expensive to
generate for large models), accept the result **optimistically** and
only pay the verification cost if someone challenges it. Borrows the
dispute structure from optimistic rollups — a bisection game narrows a
disagreement down to one contested computation step, which then gets
resolved on-chain by a Fraud Proof VM. Security rests on an "AnyTrust"
assumption: as long as at least one honest, economically-incentivized
validator is watching and willing to dispute a bad result within the
challenge window, incorrect inference gets caught. This trades zkML's
stronger cryptographic guarantee for much lower cost and the ability to
run genuinely large models (the paper demonstrates 7B-parameter LLaMA)
without circuit-compilation overhead.

## Link to tracked system

See [systems/ora-protocol.md](../systems/ora-protocol.md). ORA's
On-Chain AI Oracle (OAO) is opML's reference production deployment: ORA
nodes (running the "Tora" client) execute inference off-chain and post
results on-chain; disputes resolve through the exact bisection +
Fraud-Proof-VM mechanism this paper defines. A related ORA-authored
paper, "opp/ai: Optimistic Privacy-Preserving AI on Blockchain" (Cathie
So et al., arXiv 2402.15006), extends the same optimistic-dispute idea
to add privacy — worth a look if a future watch run tracks privacy-
preserving variants of this lineage specifically.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/secure-aggregation.md
========================================================================

---
field: Federated learning / confidential aggregation
paper: "Practical Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning"
authors: Keith Bonawitz, Vladimir Ivanov, Ben Kreuter, Antonio Marcedone, H. Brendan McMahan, Sarvar Patel, Daniel Ramage, Aaron Segal, Karn Seth
year: 2017
venue: ACM CCS 2017
link: http://eprint.iacr.org/2017/281
---

# Practical Secure Aggregation for Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded via a direct citation, not inference: Google's own 2017 federated
learning announcement
([research.google/blog](https://research.google/blog/federated-learning-collaborative-machine-learning-without-centralized-training-data/))
links to this exact paper when describing "a Secure Aggregation protocol
that uses cryptographic techniques so that a coordinating server need
only combine encrypted data from hundreds or thousands of users." It's the
specific crypto contribution underneath Google's federated learning
deployments, distinct from the plain ML algorithm (Federated Averaging,
see `/systems/google-confidential-federated-learning.md`).

## Core contribution

A protocol letting a server compute the *sum* of values held by many
clients (e.g. their model-update vectors) without learning any individual
client's value — only the aggregate. It's built from secret-sharing and
pairwise-masking: each client masks its value with random numbers shared
pairwise with other clients such that the masks cancel out exactly when
all values are summed, revealing the sum but nothing about any individual
contribution. The protocol is also fault-tolerant to clients dropping out
mid-protocol (a real concern on mobile devices), which earlier secure-sum
constructions generally weren't designed to handle well at this scale.

## Link to tracked system

This is the cryptographic mechanism that lets Google's federated learning
systems claim the server never sees an individual device's model update —
only the aggregate across many devices. The later TEE-based "Confidential
Federated Computations" work (2024) layers additional server-side
confidentiality on top of this, authored by overlapping people (Bonawitz
and McMahan both appear on both papers), but Secure Aggregation is the
earlier, foundational crypto piece specifically for the aggregation step
itself. See `/systems/google-confidential-federated-learning.md` for how
the two layers relate.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/tee-remote-attestation.md
========================================================================

---
field: Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference
paper: "Intel SGX Explained"
authors: Victor Costan, Srinivas Devadas
year: 2016
venue: IACR ePrint 2016/086
link: https://eprint.iacr.org/2016/086
---

# Intel SGX Explained

## Why this is the seed for this field

**Inferred, not grounded.** None of the TEE-based inference systems filed
under this foundation (Phala/dstack, Tinfoil, Chutes, NEAR AI Cloud,
Secret Network, Oasis ROFL, Atoma, Venice) cites this paper in the docs
reviewed. It is used here as the standard academic reference for the shared
mechanism they all rely on: hardware-enforced isolation plus *remote
attestation*, where the hardware signs a measurement of the code and
configuration so a remote client can decide whether to trust it. Contrast
`/foundations/ccf-confidential-computing.md`, where Azure's docs name CCF
directly.

## Core contribution

A systematization of how SGX-style enclaves provide isolation, sealing and
attestation, and of the attack surface around them. Newer designs the
tracked systems use (Intel TDX confidential VMs, NVIDIA GPU confidential
computing, AMD SEV-SNP) differ in granularity (VM instead of enclave) but
keep the same trust shape: the hardware vendor's attestation signature is
the root of trust.

## Known attacks and costs (secondary sources)

- **Physical memory-bus attacks, autumn 2025:** WireTap (2025-10-01, DDR4
  interposer, reported against an SGX ECDSA key), Battering RAM (SGX and
  SEV-SNP, DDR4), and TEE.Fail (2025-10-28, DDR5; interposer under
  $1,000). TEE.Fail reportedly extracts keys from Intel TDX and AMD
  SEV-SNP with Ciphertext Hiding, including attestation keys on fully
  updated machines, and those keys reportedly compromise NVIDIA GPU
  Confidential Computing. Root cause given: deterministic AES-XTS. A
  secondary report notes the attacker needed a compromised kernel.
  Primary papers and vendor responses were not checked; nothing dated
  2026 was found. Hosted TEE systems on third-party hardware are most
  exposed, since the host operator is the physical attacker.
- **GPU overhead:** measured data covers Hopper/H100 only: under 7% for
  typical short LLM queries in the original study, ~19% TTFT in a later
  version, and a 2026 preprint (arXiv 2607.19353, unverified) reports
  ~22-28% average TTFT in a TDX CVM. Overhead is mostly CPU-GPU transfer.
  Blackwell TEE-I/O claims came from a weak secondary source.

## Link to tracked systems

See `/systems/phala-dstack.md`, `/systems/tinfoil.md`,
`/systems/chutes.md`, `/systems/near-ai-cloud.md`,
`/systems/secret-network.md`, `/systems/oasis-sapphire-rofl.md`,
`/systems/atoma-network.md`, `/systems/venice-ai.md`. A recurring
caveat across all of them: attestation is evidence of what is running,
not a guarantee it is secure, and side-channel attacks on TEEs are an open
research area.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/verifiable-unlearning.md
========================================================================

---
field: Verifiable machine unlearning
paper: "Verifiable and Provably Secure Machine Unlearning"
authors: Thorsten Eisenhofer, Doreen Riepel, Varun Chandrasekaran, Esha Ghosh, Olga Ohrimenko, Nicolas Papernot
year: 2025
venue: IEEE SaTML 2025
link: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09126
---

# Verifiable and Provably Secure Machine Unlearning

## Why this is here

**Research, not a shipping system.** No tracked system cites it. It extends
the ZK-for-ML cluster (`/foundations/zk-proof-of-training.md`,
`/foundations/zkml.md`) to proving that data was *removed* from a model.
Author names and venue are from search results plus background knowledge
and should be checked; only listings and abstracts were seen.

## Core contribution

A cryptographic definition of verifiable unlearning, plus a protocol using
SNARKs and hash chains: proofs cover correct execution of the unlearning
step and that the deleted point is absent from the new training set.
Tested on linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks.

## Related 2026 work (listings only)

- **ZK-APEX** (MLSys 2026): personalized unlearning on edge devices; a ViT
  proof in ~2 hours, claimed >10^7x faster than retraining-based
  verification.
- **VeriForgot** (March 2026 preprint, not peer reviewed): combines
  membership-inference tests, blockchain unlearning certificates and a ZK
  proof of parameter shift; its authors argue no cryptographically
  verifiable mechanism yet proves unlearning occurred.
- A separate paper titled "Verification of Machine Unlearning is Fragile"
  exists; its findings were not read.

FILE: foundations/zk-proof-of-training.md
========================================================================

---
field: ZK proof of training / verifiable training
paper: "Falafel: Modular Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Training in the Federated Setting"
authors: Tariq Bontekoe, Sven Bootsma, Vincent Dunning, Thom Sijpesteijn, Thomas Attema
year: 2026
venue: IACR ePrint 2026/1335
link: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1335
---

# ZK proofs of training (research cluster)

## Why this is here

**Research, not a shipping system.** No tracked system cites these papers
yet; they sit in the foundations as the leading edge of extending
`/foundations/zkml.md` from proving *inference* to proving *training*.
Seeded with Falafel; two other 2026 papers are grouped with it. All three
abstracts were read; none of the full papers were. Peer-review status was
not checked.

## Papers

- **Falafel** (ePrint 2026/1335, received 2026-06-29): zkPoT for federated
  learning covering local training steps and the central weight update.
  Claims ~70 kB proof for one LeNet round, ~150 s to generate, 10-15x
  smaller than prior zkPoT work, and avoids Fiat-Shamir with arithmetic
  hashes.
- **ZKBoost** (ePrint 2026/202; Melissaris, Polychroniadou, Takahashi,
  Weng, Xu): first zkPoT for XGBoost; VOLE-based; fixed-point XGBoost
  within 1% of standard accuracy.
- **Verifiable Fine-Tuning** (arXiv 2510.16830; Akgul et al., v3 Dec 2025):
  proofs that a released model was fine-tuned from a public base under a
  declared program and committed dataset, using recursive aggregation. No
  code link; the abstract gives no proof-size or prover-cost numbers.

## Open problems (from search results, secondary)

- Proving training correct does not prove anything about training-data
  overlap with private records.
- Governance analyses call ZK for frontier-scale verification promising but
  currently impractical.

FILE: foundations/zkml-stark.md
========================================================================

---
field: ZKML / verifiable inference (STARK-based)
paper: "Scalable, transparent, and post-quantum secure computational integrity"
authors: Eli Ben-Sasson, Iddo Bentov, Yinon Horesh, Michael Riabzev
year: 2018
venue: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2018/046
link: https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/046
---

## Why this is the seed for this field

**Weaker grounding than this repo's other foundations entries — flagged
explicitly rather than smoothed over.** The chain is:

- Giza/Orion compiled models to **Cairo**, StarkWare's STARK-friendly
  CPU architecture (explicit in Orion's own docs/announcement).
- Cairo's own paper (*"Cairo: a Turing-complete STARK-friendly CPU
  architecture,"* Goldberg/Papini/Riabzev, eprint 2021/1063) is the
  natural next hop to this STARK paper, since Cairo exists specifically
  to make programs STARK-provable.
- **This second-hop citation could not be confirmed in-text** (the
  Cairo paper's PDF was inaccessible; its visible abstract/metadata
  didn't explicitly cite 2018/046). The connection is inferred from
  shared authorship/organization — Ben-Sasson co-founded StarkWare,
  which authored the Cairo paper — not from a direct quote, unlike the
  EZKL→Halo2→PLONK chain in `foundations/zkml.md`, where Halo2's own
  docs explicitly name PLONK.

This is included as this field's seed paper because it's the correct
*technical* lineage (STARKs are what make Cairo/Orion's proofs work at
all), with the caveat that the citation chain is inferred, not directly
sourced, at the Cairo→STARK-paper link specifically.

## Core contribution

Introduced zk-STARKs: a proof system for verifying that a computation
was performed correctly, with two properties that distinguish it from
earlier SNARK constructions (like the PLONK lineage in
`foundations/zkml.md`): **no trusted setup** (the verifier's reference
string is public/transparent, generated without a ceremony that could
be compromised) and **conjectured post-quantum security** (relying on
collision-resistant hash functions rather than elliptic-curve
assumptions that quantum computers could break). The tradeoff is
larger proof sizes than SNARKs like PLONK/KZG-based systems.

## Link to tracked system

Giza/Orion's whole value proposition over EZKL was this tradeoff:
transparent setup instead of EZKL's KZG trusted ceremony, at the cost of
STARK proofs generally being larger than PLONK/KZG proofs. See
`systems/giza-orion.md` for why this is now largely historical — the
product built on this lineage is inactive as of October 2026, which
doesn't change the lineage's technical accuracy but does mean there's
currently no actively-maintained reference implementation of it in this
repo's tracked-systems list.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/zkml-sumcheck.md
========================================================================

---
field: ZKML / verifiable inference (sum-check lineage)
paper: "Algebraic methods for interactive proof systems"
authors: Carsten Lund, Lance Fortnow, Howard Karloff, Noam Nisan
year: 1992
venue: Journal of the ACM, 39(4), 859–868
---

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded via a two-hop citation chain:

- Lagrange Labs' DeepProve paper (*"DeepProve: Verifiable End-to-End
  Large Language Model Inference,"* IACR ePrint
  [2026/1112](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1112)) names the
  **sum-check protocol** explicitly, in its own abstract, as a core
  building block for verifying LLM operators.
- The sum-check protocol originates in this 1992 paper. This is the
  standard attribution across the field — sum-check-based SNARKs
  (GKR, Libra, Virgo, Spartan, HyperPlonk, Lasso/Jolt, and now
  DeepProve) all trace back to it, and one of the original authors
  (Lance Fortnow) has publicly noted it became his most-cited paper
  specifically because of this reuse in zkSNARK literature.

This is a **separate lineage** from `foundations/zkml.md` (PLONK,
eprint 2019/953), which grounds EZKL/Halo2's PLONKish arithmetization.
Both are legitimately "ZKML / verifiable inference" foundations, but
they root in different proof techniques — PLONKish circuit
arithmetization vs. sum-check-based verification of arithmetic
operators directly. Kept as distinct files per this repo's
one-foundation-per-lineage rule, not merged just because the field
label matches.

**Not confirmed in this pass:** whether DeepProve's own bibliography
cites this 1992 paper directly, or an intermediate sum-check-based
SNARK paper (e.g. GKR, Libra, or Virgo) that itself cites it. Treat
this as "the standard lineage for a sum-check-based system," not as a
verified direct citation.

## Core contribution

Introduces the sum-check protocol: an interactive proof technique that
lets a prover convince a verifier that the sum of a multivariate
polynomial's evaluations over a Boolean hypercube equals a claimed
value, in a way that's exponentially cheaper to verify than to
brute-force. This became foundational to a large family of later
succinct arguments (GKR and its descendants) because it gives a cheap,
general-purpose way to verify a computation's structure algebraically,
without needing a trusted setup for the sum-check step itself.

## Link to tracked system

DeepProve uses sum-check (plus lookup arguments) to verify individual
LLM operators — attention, layer norm, grouped-query attention, rotary
positional embeddings — directly, rather than compiling the entire
model into one monolithic arithmetic circuit the way PLONKish systems
(like EZKL/Halo2) do. This operator-level verification approach is
part of why DeepProve claims to avoid the quadratic circuit-size blowup
that limited earlier zkML attempts at whole-model proofs. See
`systems/lagrange-labs.md` for the full system entry and its open
follow-up items.

========================================================================
FILE: foundations/zkml.md
========================================================================

---
field: ZKML / verifiable inference
paper: "PLONK: Permutations over Lagrange-bases for Oecumenical Noninteractive arguments of Knowledge"
authors: Ariel Gabizon, Zachary J. Williamson, Oana Ciobotaru
year: 2019
venue: IACR Cryptology ePrint Archive, 2019/953
link: https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953
---

## Why this is the seed for this field

Grounded via a two-hop citation chain, not a direct EZKL citation:

- EZKL's own README names **Halo2** as its backend proof system.
- Halo2's own design documentation states explicitly: *"The
  arithmetization used by Halo 2 comes from
  [PLONK](https://eprint.iacr.org/2019/953), or more precisely its
  extension UltraPLONK that supports custom gates and lookup
  arguments."*
  ([zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html](https://zcash.github.io/halo2/concepts/arithmetization.html))

So the tracked system (EZKL) is built on Halo2, which is explicitly
built on this paper's arithmetization. This is as close to "grounded"
as the chain gets without EZKL citing PLONK by name itself.

## Core contribution

PLONK introduced a practical, universal (not circuit-specific) SNARK
construction: a single structured reference string works for *any*
circuit up to a size bound, instead of needing a fresh trusted setup
per circuit (as earlier SNARKs like the original Groth16/Pinocchio
pipeline required). It does this via a permutation argument over
Lagrange-basis polynomials to enforce wiring constraints between gates,
combined with a polynomial commitment scheme (originally KZG) to make
the whole thing non-interactive and succinct. Follow-on work extended
this base arithmetization with custom gates and lookup arguments
("UltraPLONK" / "PLONKish"), which is the specific extension Halo2
actually implements.

## Link to tracked system

EZKL inherits PLONKish arithmetization transitively through Halo2, then
additionally swaps Halo2's native commitment scheme for KZG commitments
specifically to shrink proof size and verification cost for on-chain
use (see `/systems/ezkl.md` — this specific claim is flagged inferred,
not directly quoted from an EZKL source, so re-verify before treating
it as settled). The universality property of PLONK (one SRS per size
bound, not per circuit) is part of why a general-purpose tool like
EZKL — which has to support arbitrary ONNX graphs rather than one fixed
circuit — is practical at all.

  gradients to come from the locked data. A staking mechanism then
  makes caught attackers train on label-flipped samples. Results are
  reported on CIFAR-10 only. Field: Federated learning / confidential
  aggregation. No tracked system uses it.

  fingerprint like Sentient's OML 1.0. Field: AI model ownership /
  monetization protocols.

### Related, not yet tied to a tracked system

- **Interflow** (arXiv 2610.27431): pipelines MPC correlated-randomness
  generation with online execution, to cut the preprocessing memory and
  stall costs of private inference at the edge. Field: Secure MPC for ML.
- **KNOX** (arXiv 2610.27543): a regulatory sandbox that runs AI agent
  workloads inside TEEs, with an attested policy manifest. Field:
  Confidential computing (TEE) for AI inference.
- **LiBRA** (arXiv 2610.27357): Byzantine-robust FL client selection
  that compares logit fingerprints instead of parameter vectors. The
  authors say this can coexist with secure aggregation, which withholds
  individual updates. Field: Federated learning / confidential
  aggregation.
- **WaveCommitments** (arXiv 2610.26867): an open-sourced speech-asset
  marketplace design. It values data with Data Shapley inside a TEE and
  ties delivery to that valuation with polynomial commitments. Field:
  AI data marketplace / provenance.

## What happened

This is checkpoint zero, not a delta run — there was no prior checkpoint
to compare against yet. It marks the point the baseline was established:
26 systems tracked, 15 foundations grounded, built via a one-time
research sweep across Ethereum-ecosystem ZKML, decentralized
training/compute, agent/marketplace protocols, and TEE-based
confidential-AI systems — not the daily watch mechanism itself.

Starting tomorrow, the actual watch loop takes over on a daily schedule:
pull new items from IACR ePrint and arXiv (cs.CR, cs.LG, cs.DC) since
the last checkpoint, check tracked systems' own repos for notable
releases or merged PRs that would change an existing system's property
matrix, and report what — if anything — actually moved. Most runs are
expected to find nothing; this baseline entry is the only one that
won't follow that pattern, since it's establishing the starting line
rather than measuring a delta from one.
